About this edition

This is the second edition of the MYP 5 mathematics coursebook. It was rebuilt from the pre-rewrite MYP 5 audit, which recorded the chapter scope, the key and related concepts, the global contexts and the inquiry statements of the earlier edition, and identified where the teaching had to be strengthened.

The edition keeps that chapter scope and the visual identity of the collection, and rebuilds the teaching sequence around inquiry: engagement, inquiry questions, investigation, observation, mathematical conclusion, formal development, worked examples, extensive visual practice, and application, assessment and reflection. The register is followed section by section, so the sine and cosine rules, bearings, matrices and determinants, dispersion and standard deviation, and counting with permutations and combinations are all taught here rather than deferred.

The earlier edition carried four confirmed defects, and all four are repaired in the student text rather than only in the answer key. The sine rule's ambiguous case is corrected: two triangles occur when b sin A < a < b, exactly one when b sin A = a, and none when a < b sin A. The matrix product that the capstone asked students to compute had its order mismatched with the question, and is now consistent. The open-top cylinder problem stated its constraint ambiguously, and now states which dimension is fixed. The raw LaTeX that appeared in the Chapter 11 modelling text is gone; every expression in this book is typeset.

All classroom data sets are simulated and are labelled as such. Real data would require provenance, so no claim in this book rests on unverified statistics.

No publisher, ISBN, print specification or commercial print-readiness claim is made in this file. The book is produced as an A4 review copy: fonts are embedded, pagination is continuous and every page has been checked for overflow.

MYP 5 · Student coursebook

How to use this book

Each chapter follows the same sequence, so you always know what is coming next. The sequence is deliberate: you investigate before you are told the rule, because a rule you have discovered is a rule you can defend — and defending it is what Year 5 asks of you.

The chapter sequence

  1. Engagement. A short situation that raises the question the chapter will answer.
  2. Inquiry questions. Factual, conceptual and debatable questions that frame the chapter.
  3. Investigation. A task you complete before the formal teaching: record evidence in a table and look for a pattern.
  4. Observation and discovery. What you noticed, stated in your own words and compared with a partner.
  5. Mathematical conclusion. The rule that the evidence supports, written as a general statement you can justify.
  6. Formal development. The explanation, definitions and notation, with the reasoning made explicit.
  7. Worked examples. Problem, visual representation, mathematical reasoning, step-by-step solution, final answer and interpretation.
  8. Practice. Separated into Criterion A, B, C and D practice, with visual representations throughout.
  9. Application, assessment and reflection. Real-context tasks, criterion-based assessment practice, and a reflection that returns to the statement of inquiry.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookHow to use this book
MYP 5 · Student coursebook

How to use this book

The four MYP mathematics criteria

A · Knowing and understanding

Apply knowledge to familiar and unfamiliar problems, and check results.

B · Investigating patterns

Investigate relationships, describe patterns, formulate a conjecture, test it and justify the generalisation — at Year 5 level a justification is a general argument, not a list of cases.

C · Communicating

Use correct mathematical language, notation and complete representations, and organise reasoning into a coherent structure that a reader can follow.

D · Applying mathematics in real-life contexts

Apply mathematics to authentic situations, identify relevant information, and comment on the accuracy and sense of the result.

Working with this book

  • Practice is separated by criterion so that you can see which skill a task is training. Criterion B practice is additional genuine pattern investigation, not a repeat of the teaching.
  • Visuals are part of the mathematics. Where a task supplies a diagram, grid, table, number line or model, use it; where it asks you to sketch, your drawing is part of the answer.
  • Answers and student-facing reasoning are collected at the back of the book, with a formula bank, a glossary and references.
  • Every chapter ends with project connections: a Service as Action opportunity, a Community Project connection and a Personal Project connection for MYP 5.
  • Chapter 11 is the capstone: a single sustained modelling task that uses mathematics from every part of the year. Chapter 12 adds no new content; it revises what you know and states what the transition to DP Mathematics expects.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookIntroduction
MYP 5 · Student coursebook

MYP mathematics and this coursebook

The IB Middle Years Programme asks students to inquire into concepts through global contexts, to develop approaches to learning (ATL) skills, and to act on what they learn through service as action. In mathematics this means more than practising procedures: students investigate patterns, justify generalisations, communicate with precise language and apply mathematics to situations that matter to them.

MYP mathematics is organised into four branches — number, algebra, geometry and trigonometry, and statistics and probability — and the programme recommends at least 50 hours of teaching per subject each year. This coursebook covers the Year 5 content of those branches across twelve chapters, grouped into five parts.

Year 5 is the extended-leaning level and the last year of the programme. The register for this year records the same four branches as every other year, and the chapters here follow the branch recorded for each of them: number and abstract reasoning, thinking with models, spatial reasoning and reasoning with data, with the modelling capstone and the transition to DP Mathematics at the end.

Assessment in MYP mathematics uses four equally weighted criteria, each with a maximum of 8: A knowing and understanding, B investigating patterns, C communicating, and D applying mathematics in real-life contexts. This book trains each criterion explicitly, and says so on the page where the training happens.

MYP mathematics and this coursebook

Projects, service and action

Service as Action

Each chapter includes a service opportunity with a community need, a mathematical connection, a proposed action, an expected impact and a student reflection. Completing an exercise is not service: service requires action that benefits others and reflection on that action.

Community Project

MYP students completing the programme in Year 3 or Year 4 complete a community project. Each chapter offers a student-led project idea with a research question, the mathematics involved, an action or outcome, beneficiaries and evidence. Follow your school's requirements and supervision.

Personal Project (MYP 5)

Students completing MYP in Year 5 complete a personal project. Each chapter offers an adaptable MYP 5-oriented extension with a personal interest, a learning goal, a product, the mathematics involved, a process and evidence. It is deliberately different from the community project and from service as action.

What this book does not claim

  • Programme requirements quoted here follow the official IB MYP curriculum, mathematics and projects pages and the MYP general regulations. Everything else — the chapter sequence, the investigations, the practice sets and the project ideas — is author-designed material built to serve those requirements, and is not an IB publication.
  • No ISBN, publisher, imprint or print specification is claimed. The file is an A4 review copy with embedded fonts and continuous pagination, produced for proofing and classroom review rather than for commercial print production.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 1 · Polynomials, Factor Theorem and Algebraic Fractions
Chapter 1 · Part I · Number and abstract reasoning
01

Polynomials, Factor Theorem and Algebraic Fractions

A polynomial can be written as a sum of powers or as a product of factors. Each form is the same polynomial, and each makes a different question easy.

Engage

Two students are asked to describe x³ − 7x − 6. One writes it as a sum of three terms; the other writes (x − 3)(x + 1)(x + 2). Neither has changed the polynomial. Which description tells you where the graph crosses the x-axis, and which tells you how steep it is?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Form
Related concepts: Equivalence · Generalisation · Simplification
Global context: Personal and cultural expression
Global context exploration: the language of algebra as a way of making structure visible

Statement of inquiry: The structure of a polynomial — its factors, roots and remainders — determines both what it can be simplified to and what its graph will do.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What is the degree of a polynomial, and what do the remainder and factor theorems say?
  • Conceptual: Why does the factored form of a polynomial reveal its roots, and what does an excluded value protect a simplification from?
  • Debatable: When a calculation produces a solution that the original equation rejects, has the method failed, or has it done its job?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to choose the most useful form of an algebraic expression, students must compare an expanded form with a factorised form of the same polynomial, identify what each form reveals, and justify the choice of form for a stated purpose.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.1
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.1

Polynomials and their behaviour

Inquiry question

What can be read off a polynomial from the form it is written in?

Your task

Take four polynomials of your own: one of degree 1, one of degree 2, one of degree 3 and one you are unsure about. Add and multiply each pair, record the degree of each result, and then try to state a rule that predicts the degree of the answer before you calculate it.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.1
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.1

Polynomials and their behaviour

What do you notice?
  • Adding two polynomials gave the larger of the two degrees, unless the leading terms cancelled.
  • Multiplying two polynomials always gave the sum of the two degrees.
  • A constant has degree 0 and left every degree unchanged when it was multiplied in.
  • The only surprise came from addition, where cancellation can lower the degree.
Observation. The degree of a product is the sum of the degrees, and the degree of a sum is at most the larger of the two degrees.
Mathematical conclusion

The polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication, and multiplication of degrees is exact: the degree of a product is the sum of the degrees of the factors. This is why a factorised form shows the roots while an expanded form shows the degree.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.1 · Polynomials and their behaviour
Chapter 1 · 1.1

Polynomials and their behaviour

A polynomial in x is a sum of terms of the form axN^{N}N where a is a real coefficient and n is a non-negative integer. The degree is the highest power present, and the leading coefficient is the coefficient of that power. The two numbers together describe how the polynomial behaves for very large and very small x.

Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication: performing any of these on two polynomials gives another polynomial. Division is the exception, which is why division is the operation that needs its own technique.

Two polynomials are equal when their corresponding coefficients are equal, not when they look alike. Expanding (x + 1)(x + 2) gives x² + 3x + 2, and the two forms name the same function. Equivalence of form is the idea that makes factorising useful, and the generalisation behind it — that any polynomial can be rewritten in any equivalent form — is what makes algebra a language rather than a set of tricks.

The standard form of a polynomial lists its terms in descending powers with a single coefficient for each power. Rewriting into standard form is the first step in almost every polynomial calculation, because it makes the degree and the leading coefficient visible.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.1 · Worked example 1

Polynomials and their behaviour

Worked example 1.1.1

Problem. Write 3 − 2x⁴ + x² in standard form, state its degree and leading coefficient, and find its value at x = −1.

Mathematical reasoning. Standard form orders the terms by descending power, and the degree and leading coefficient are read directly from it.

  1. Reorder: −2x⁴ + x² + 3.
  2. The highest power is 4, so the degree is 4.
  3. The leading coefficient is −2.
  4. Substitute x = −1: −2(−1)⁴ + (−1)² + 3 = −2 + 1 + 3.
  5. The value is 2.

Final answer. −2x⁴ + x² + 3, degree 4, leading coefficient −2, value 2 at x = −1

Interpretation. Standard form is not cosmetic: it is the form in which the two numbers that govern the polynomial's behaviour can be read off.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.1 · Worked example 2

Polynomials and their behaviour

Worked example 1.1.2

Problem. Show that the product of two polynomials is always a polynomial, and explain why the degree of the product is the sum of the degrees.

Mathematical reasoning. Each term of the first polynomial multiplies each term of the second, and every product is again a constant times a power of x.

  1. Let the polynomials be p and q with degrees m and n.
  2. Every term of p is a constant times x raised to a power i with i at most m, and every term of q is a constant times x raised to a power j with j at most n.
  3. A product term is the product of the two constants times x raised to i + j, and i + j is at most m + n.
  4. The two leading terms multiply to give a non-zero constant times x raised to m + n, so the degree of the product is exactly m + n.
  5. Hence the product is a polynomial of degree m + n.

Final answer. the product is a polynomial of degree m + n

Interpretation. One general argument settles every pair of polynomials, which is why an algebraic proof is worth more than a list of examples.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.2
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.2

Dividing polynomials

Inquiry question

How is one polynomial divided by another, and how is the answer checked?

Your task

Divide x⁴ − 1 by x − 1, then x⁴ − 1 by x + 1, then x⁴ − 1 by x² + 1. Record each quotient and remainder, reconstruct the dividend from your answers, and then explain what the three divisions have in common.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.2
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.2

Dividing polynomials

What do you notice?
  • Three of the six divisors divided x⁴ − 1 exactly, leaving no remainder.
  • The two divisors that left a remainder were not factors of x⁴ − 1.
  • Every reconstruction reproduced the dividend, which is the check that each division was done correctly.
  • The divisors that worked were all built from the factors of x⁴ − 1.
Observation. A divisor that leaves no remainder is a factor, and the quotient is the other factor.
Mathematical conclusion

Dividing p(x) by x − a leaves remainder zero exactly when x − a is a factor of p(x). The reconstruction dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder is the check on every division.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.2 · Dividing polynomials
Chapter 1 · 1.2

Dividing polynomials

Polynomial long division follows the same logic as long division of numbers: match the leading term of the divisor to the leading term of the dividend, write the quotient term, subtract, and repeat on what is left.

The division identity is dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, with the remainder either zero or of lower degree than the divisor. This identity is not a convention; it is the statement that the division has been done correctly.

A missing power in the dividend must be kept as a zero placeholder. Dividing x³ + 1 by x² + 1 requires a 0x term, and omitting it is the commonest source of error.

Synthetic division is a compressed arrangement of the same process for a divisor of the form x − a. It is faster but it hides the reasoning, so the long division is used first and the short form afterwards.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.2 · Worked example 1

Dividing polynomials

Worked example 1.2.1

Problem. Divide 2x³ + 3x² − x + 5 by x + 2, and check the answer.

Mathematical reasoning. Match leading terms, subtract, and repeat until what is left has lower degree than the divisor; then verify with the division identity.

  1. 2x³ ÷ x = 2x². Multiply x + 2 by 2x² to get 2x³ + 4x² and subtract: (2x³ + 3x²) − (2x³ + 4x²) = −x².
  2. Bring down −x. Now −x² ÷ x = −x. Multiply x + 2 by −x to get −x² − 2x and subtract: (−x² − x) − (−x² − 2x) = x.
  3. Bring down +5. Now x ÷ x = 1. Multiply x + 2 by 1 and subtract: (x + 5) − (x + 2) = 3.
  4. The quotient is 2x² − x + 1 and the remainder is 3.
  5. Check: (x + 2)(2x² − x + 1) + 3 = 2x³ − x² + x + 4x² − 2x + 2 + 3 = 2x³ + 3x² − x + 5.

Final answer. quotient 2x² − x + 1, remainder 3

Interpretation. The division identity is the check: if the reconstruction gives back the dividend, the division was correct.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.2 · Worked example 2

Dividing polynomials

Worked example 1.2.2

Problem. Divide x³ + 8 by x² + 2x + 1, keeping every placeholder.

Mathematical reasoning. A missing power is a zero term, and writing it keeps the subtraction aligned.

  1. Write the dividend as x³ + 0x² + 0x + 8.
  2. x³ ÷ x² = x. Subtract x(x² + 2x + 1) = x³ + 2x² + x to get −2x² − x + 8.
  3. −2x² ÷ x² = −2. Subtract −2(x² + 2x + 1) = −2x² − 4x − 2 to get 3x + 10.
  4. 3x has degree 1, below the divisor's degree 2, so the division stops.
  5. Quotient x − 2, remainder 3x + 10. Check: (x² + 2x + 1)(x − 2) + 3x + 10 = x³ + 2x² + x − 2x² − 4x − 2 + 3x + 10 = x³ + 8.

Final answer. quotient x − 2, remainder 3x + 10

Interpretation. Zero placeholders are not decoration: without them the powers drift and the subtraction goes wrong.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.3
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.3

The remainder and factor theorems

Inquiry question

What does the remainder of a division tell you about the polynomial?

Your task

Take the polynomial p(x) = x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6. Evaluate p at x = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and 3, record which values are zero, divide out one factor you have found, and then factorise p completely. State how many roots a cubic can have and how many you found.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.3
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.3

The remainder and factor theorems

What do you notice?
  • Two of the seven values of x made p(x) exactly zero.
  • Those two values gave the two factors x + 3 and x − 2.
  • A cubic has at most three roots, so one root was still missing.
  • Dividing by one factor lowered the degree, making the rest easier.
Observation. A root of the polynomial is a value that makes it zero, and each root gives a linear factor.
Mathematical conclusion

The factor theorem is a generalisation: p(a) = 0 exactly when x − a is a factor of p(x), for every polynomial p and every number a. Finding roots and factorising are therefore the same activity. A cubic has at most three roots, and here p(x) = (x + 3)(x − 2)(x + 1) with roots −3, −1 and 2.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.3 · The remainder and factor theorems
Chapter 1 · 1.3

The remainder and factor theorems

The remainder theorem states that when p(x) is divided by x − a, the remainder is p(a). Evaluating the polynomial at a single number replaces the whole division.

The factor theorem is the special case: x − a is a factor of p(x) exactly when p(a) = 0. So a is a root of the polynomial exactly when x − a divides it exactly. This is the generalisation that turns a search for roots into a search for factors.

A polynomial of degree n has at most n real roots, and if it has n distinct roots then it has exactly n linear factors. Counting roots therefore counts factors, which is how a cubic is factorised completely.

The theorems work together: find one root by inspection, divide out the corresponding factor, and the quotient is a polynomial of one degree lower, which is easier to solve. This is the standard route to solving a cubic or quartic.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.3 · Worked example 1

The remainder and factor theorems

Worked example 1.3.1

Problem. Find the remainder when p(x) = x³ − 4x² + 5x − 7 is divided by x − 2, and hence decide whether x − 2 is a factor.

Mathematical reasoning. By the remainder theorem the remainder is p(a), so evaluate rather than divide.

  1. The divisor is x − 2, so a = 2.
  2. p(2) = 2³ − 4(2²) + 5(2) − 7 = 8 − 16 + 10 − 7.
  3. 8 − 16 = −8, −8 + 10 = 2, 2 − 7 = −5.
  4. The remainder is −5.
  5. Since p(2) ≠\neq= 0, x − 2 is not a factor of p(x).

Final answer. remainder −5, so x − 2 is not a factor

Interpretation. One substitution answers a question that would otherwise need a whole division, and the same substitution also tests whether the divisor is a factor.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.3 · Worked example 2

The remainder and factor theorems

Worked example 1.3.2

Problem. Show that x − 1 is a factor of p(x) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, find the other factors, and hence solve p(x) = 0.

Mathematical reasoning. Find one root, divide out its factor, then solve the quadratic that is left.

  1. p(1) = 1 − 6 + 11 − 6 = 0, so x − 1 is a factor.
  2. Divide p(x) by x − 1: the quotient is x² − 5x + 6.
  3. Check: (x − 1)(x² − 5x + 6) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6.
  4. Factorise the quadratic: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3).
  5. So p(x) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3), and the roots are x = 1, 2 and 3.

Final answer. p(x) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3); roots x = 1, 2, 3

Interpretation. The factor theorem turns a cubic into a quadratic, and a quadratic is already solved.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.4
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.4

Algebraic fractions

Inquiry question

When may an algebraic fraction be cancelled, and what must be stated first?

Your task

Take the four expressions (x² − 9)/(x − 3), (x − 3)/(x² − 9), 1/(x + 3) + 1/(x − 3) and (x + 3 + x − 3)/(x + 3). Simplify each, state the excluded values, and then explain why two of them give the same answer and one of them cannot be simplified at all.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.4
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.4

Algebraic fractions

What do you notice?
  • Two of the four simplified to expressions with the same denominator.
  • The reciprocal of a simplified fraction is the fraction with numerator and denominator swapped.
  • The last expression could not be cancelled at all, because x + 3 is not a factor of 2x.
  • Every excluded value came from a factor of a denominator.
Observation. Cancellation needs a common factor; without one, the fraction is already in its simplest form.
Mathematical conclusion

An algebraic fraction is simplified by cancelling common factors and nothing else, and the excluded values are exactly the values that made the cancelled factors zero. Stating them is part of the answer.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.4 · Algebraic fractions
Chapter 1 · 1.4

Algebraic fractions

An algebraic fraction is cancelled by dividing the numerator and the denominator by a common factor. Cancelling a common term is not cancellation: (x + 3)/x does not become 3, because x is not a factor of x + 3.

Before any cancellation, the values that make the denominator zero must be excluded. The fraction (x² − 1)/(x − 1) simplifies to x + 1 only for x ≠\neq= 1, and the excluded value is part of the answer, not a footnote.

Multiplying fractions multiplies numerators and denominators; adding them requires a common denominator. The two operations are not interchangeable, and the commonest error is to add numerators and denominators separately.

Simplifying a complex fraction means simplifying the numerator and the denominator first, then dividing. The division is multiplication by the reciprocal, and the reciprocal of a sum is not the sum of the reciprocals.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.4 · Worked example 1

Algebraic fractions

Worked example 1.4.1

Problem. Simplify (x² − 5x + 6)/(x² − 4), stating the excluded values.

Mathematical reasoning. Factorise both parts, cancel the common factor, and record the values that made the cancelled factor zero.

  1. Factorise: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) and x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2).
  2. The denominator is zero when x = 2 or x = −2, so both are excluded.
  3. Cancel the common factor x − 2: the fraction becomes (x − 3)/(x + 2).
  4. State the result as (x − 3)/(x + 2) for x ≠\neq= 2 and x ≠\neq= −2.

Final answer. (x − 3)/(x + 2), for x ≠\neq= 2 and x ≠\neq= −2

Interpretation. The excluded values are the values the cancellation removed, and stating them is what makes the simplification honest.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.4 · Worked example 2

Algebraic fractions

Worked example 1.4.2

Problem. Simplify 2/(x + 1) + 3/(x − 1) as a single fraction.

Mathematical reasoning. Build a common denominator by multiplying each fraction by the missing factor, then add.

  1. The common denominator is (x + 1)(x − 1) = x² − 1.
  2. 2/(x + 1) = 2(x − 1)/(x² − 1) = (2x − 2)/(x² − 1).
  3. 3/(x − 1) = 3(x + 1)/(x² − 1) = (3x + 3)/(x² − 1).
  4. Add: (2x − 2 + 3x + 3)/(x² − 1) = (5x + 1)/(x² − 1).
  5. The excluded values are x = 1 and x = −1.

Final answer. (5x + 1)/(x² − 1), for x ≠\neq= 1 and x ≠\neq= −1

Interpretation. Adding fractions is never adding numerators and denominators: it is rewriting both over a common denominator first.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.5
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.5

Rational equations and applications

Inquiry question

Why can solving a rational equation produce an answer the equation rejects?

Your task

Solve (2)/(x) + (3)/(x + 1) = 1. Before you clear the fractions, write down the values x may not take. Solve, then substitute every candidate back into the original equation and say which are genuine and which are extraneous.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.5
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.5

Rational equations and applications

What do you notice?
  • Both candidates were allowed, because neither is 0 nor −1.
  • Both candidates satisfied the original equation when substituted.
  • The equation became a quadratic after clearing, so two answers were possible.
  • Had a candidate been 0 or −1, it would have been extraneous.
Observation. Clearing the fractions can introduce candidates that the original equation rejects, and only substitution finds them.
Mathematical conclusion

A rational equation is solved by clearing the fractions, but every candidate must be tested in the original equation: a value that makes a denominator zero is extraneous and is discarded.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.5 · Rational equations and applications
Chapter 1 · 1.5

Rational equations and applications

A rational equation is solved by multiplying both sides by a common denominator to clear the fractions. The multiplication is only valid for values that do not make that denominator zero.

A solution produced by this method must be substituted back into the original equation. If it makes a denominator zero, it is extraneous: it belongs to the cleared equation but not to the original one.

Applications fall into two families: rate problems, where the rates add, and work problems, where the times add reciprocally. In both, the equation is built from the meaning of the quantities, not from a pattern.

Every application ends with a check for sense. A negative time, a fraction of a person or a speed that exceeds the stated limit are all signals that the model or the algebra needs revisiting.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.5 · Worked example 1

Rational equations and applications

Worked example 1.5.1

Problem. Solve (x + 1)/(x − 2) = 3, and check for extraneous solutions.

Mathematical reasoning. Multiply by the denominator, solve the resulting linear equation, then test the candidate in the original equation.

  1. The denominator is zero when x = 2, so x ≠\neq= 2.
  2. Multiply both sides by x − 2: x + 1 = 3(x − 2).
  3. Expand: x + 1 = 3x − 6, so 7 = 2x and x = 3.5.
  4. Check: x − 2 = 1.5, which is not zero, so the solution is valid.
  5. Verify in the original: (3.5 + 1)/(3.5 − 2) = 4.5/1.5 = 3.

Final answer. x = 3.5, valid

Interpretation. The check is not a formality: it is the step that separates a solution of the original equation from a solution of the cleared one.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.5 · Worked example 2

Rational equations and applications

Worked example 1.5.2

Problem. Two pipes fill a tank in 4 hours and 6 hours respectively. Working together, how long do they take?

Mathematical reasoning. Rates add, so the combined rate is the sum of the individual rates, and the time is its reciprocal.

  1. The first pipe fills 1/4 of the tank per hour and the second 1/6.
  2. Together they fill 1/4 + 1/6 = 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12 per hour.
  3. If the time is t hours, then (5/12)t = 1.
  4. So t = 12/5 = 2.4 hours.
  5. Check: 2.4/4 + 2.4/6 = 0.6 + 0.4 = 1 tank.

Final answer. 2.4 hours, that is 2 hours 24 minutes

Interpretation. Adding the times would give 10 hours, which is longer than either pipe alone and is obviously wrong: rates add, times do not.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.6
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.6

Investigation: factors, roots and sign

Inquiry question

How does the factored form of a polynomial decide where it is positive?

Your task

Take p(x) = (x + 3)(x − 1)²(x − 5). Draw a sign line, test one value in each interval, and solve p(x) > 0 and p(x) ≤ 0. Then sketch the graph from the factored form and mark which roots are crossings and which are touchings.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.6
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.6

Investigation: factors, roots and sign

What do you notice?
  • The squared factor was positive in every interval, so it never changed the sign.
  • The sign changed at x = −3 and at x = 5, both simple roots.
  • The sign did not change at x = 1, the double root.
  • The product was negative on two separate intervals that met at x = 1.
Observation. Only simple factors change sign; a factor with an even power leaves the sign unchanged.
Mathematical conclusion

The factored form of a polynomial decides its sign completely: mark the roots, count the negative factors in each interval, and the inequality is solved. A double root is a touching point and is included when the inequality is not strict. Here p(x) > 0 gives x < −3 or x > 5, and p(x) ≤ 0 gives −3 ≤ x ≤ 5 with x = 1 included.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.6 · Investigation: factors, roots and sign
Chapter 1 · 1.6

Investigation: factors, roots and sign

The sign of a polynomial between its roots is constant, because a polynomial can change sign only by passing through zero. This is why a sign line is a complete method for solving a polynomial inequality.

For a product of factors, the sign is decided by counting the negative factors. Each simple factor changes sign as x passes its root; a factor with an even power does not.

Solving p(x) > 0 means finding the intervals on which the count of negative factors is even. The roots themselves are excluded when the inequality is strict.

A sketch of the graph confirms the algebraic answer: the curve crosses the axis at a simple root and touches it at a double root, and the sign pattern follows the crossing behaviour.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: factors, roots and sign

Worked example 1.6.1

Problem. Solve (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 4) > 0.

Mathematical reasoning. Mark the roots on a sign line, test one value in each interval, and read off where the product is positive.

  1. The roots are x = −2, 1 and 4, and they divide the line into four intervals.
  2. For x < −2: all three factors are negative, so the product is negative.
  3. For −2 < x < 1: only x + 2 is positive, so the product is positive.
  4. For 1 < x < 4: only x − 4 is negative, so the product is negative.
  5. For x > 4: all three are positive, so the product is positive.
  6. The solution is −2 < x < 1 or x > 4, with the roots excluded.

Final answer. −2 < x < 1 or x > 4

Interpretation. One sign line settles every polynomial inequality, however many factors there are.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: factors, roots and sign

Worked example 1.6.2

Problem. Solve (x + 1)²(x − 3) ≥ 0, and explain the difference from the previous example.

Mathematical reasoning. A squared factor is never negative, so only the simple factor decides the sign, and the double root is included when the inequality is not strict.

  1. (x + 1)² ≥ 0 for every x, and it is zero only at x = −1.
  2. So the sign of the product is the sign of x − 3, except at x = −1 where the product is zero.
  3. For x > 3 the product is positive; for x < 3 it is negative.
  4. At x = 3 the product is zero, and at x = −1 it is also zero.
  5. The solution of ≥ 0 is x = −1 or x ≥ 3.

Final answer. x = −1 or x ≥ 3

Interpretation. An even power does not change sign at its root, so the graph touches the axis instead of crossing it, and that root is included.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.7
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which form of each expression makes the next step easiest?

Your task

Choose a method for each of these four tasks and carry it out: divide x⁴ − 16 by x² − 4; find the remainder when x⁴ − 16 is divided by x − 3; simplify (x⁴ − 16)/(x² − 4); and solve (x⁴ − 16)/(x² − 4) = 5. For each, write down which tool you used and why.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 1.7
Chapter 1 · Investigation 1.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • Two of the four tasks used the same underlying division but asked different questions about it.
  • The remainder theorem replaced a whole division with one substitution.
  • Simplifying before clearing the fractions made the last equation linear rather than quartic.
  • The excluded values x = 2 and x = −2 mattered only in the last two tasks.
Observation. The tool is chosen by the question, not by habit: a full quotient needs division, a single remainder needs substitution, and a fraction needs cancellation.
Mathematical conclusion

The four tools of this chapter are interchangeable views of one idea — dividing p(x) by x − a — and choosing the right view is what makes the work short. x⁴ − 16 = (x² − 4)(x² + 4), so the quotient is x² + 4, p(3) = 81 − 16 = 65, and (x⁴ − 16)/(x² − 4) = 5 gives x² + 4 = 5, so x = ±1.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 1 · 1.7

Mixed practice

Choosing a form is a skill in itself. Before calculating, decide whether the expanded form, the factored form or the single-fraction form will answer the question with the least work.

The four tools of this chapter — long division, the remainder theorem, the factor theorem and cancellation of common factors — are selected by the shape of the question. A single evaluation calls for the remainder theorem; a complete factorisation calls for division.

Every rational equation ends with a substitution check, and every simplification ends with a statement of excluded values. These two habits are what separate a correct method from a correct answer.

Mixed practice is where the tools are chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 1 · 1.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 1.7.1

Problem. Solve (x² − 9)/(x² + 4x + 3) = 1.

Mathematical reasoning. Simplify the fraction first, then clear the denominator and check the candidates.

  1. Factorise: (x − 3)(x + 3)/((x + 1)(x + 3)).
  2. Exclude x = −1 and x = −3, then cancel x + 3 to get (x − 3)/(x + 1).
  3. The equation becomes (x − 3)/(x + 1) = 1, so x − 3 = x + 1.
  4. This gives −3 = 1, which is false, so there is no solution.
  5. Note that x = −3 would have made the original denominator zero, so it is excluded anyway.

Final answer. no solution

Interpretation. An equation can be consistent and still have no solution, and recognising that is part of solving it.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook1.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 1 · 1.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 1.7.2

Problem. The polynomial p(x) = x³ + ax² + bx − 12 has x − 2 as a factor and leaves remainder 8 when divided by x − 1. Find a and b.

Mathematical reasoning. Each condition is a value of the polynomial, and two values give two linear equations.

  1. Since x − 2 is a factor, p(2) = 0: 8 + 4a + 2b − 12 = 0, so 4a + 2b = 4 and 2a + b = 2.
  2. Since the remainder on dividing by x − 1 is 8, p(1) = 8: 1 + a + b − 12 = 8, so a + b = 19.
  3. Subtract: (2a + b) − (a + b) = 2 − 19, so a = −17.
  4. Then b = 19 − a = 36.
  5. Check: p(2) = 8 + 4(−17) + 72 − 12 = 8 − 68 + 72 − 12 = 0.

Final answer. a = −17 and b = 36

Interpretation. The remainder theorem turns two statements about division into two equations, and the rest is simultaneous linear algebra.

Chapter 1 · Application and assessment

Applying chapter 1

These tasks use polynomial division, the factor theorem, algebraic fractions and rational equations. State the excluded values before you cancel anything, and check every solution in the original equation.

A1 · The container specification

A container's capacity is modelled by V(x) = x³ + 6x² + 11x + 6 cm³ and its base area by A(x) = (x + 1)(x + 2) cm². Find the height, state the restriction on x that the physical situation imposes, and explain what the restriction protects the answer from.

Criteria A and D · factorise, divide, then apply the physical domain.

A2 · The shared job

Two machines together complete a batch in 4 hours. The older machine takes 6 hours longer than the newer one. Find each machine's time alone, check the answer, and explain why adding the two times is not the answer.

Criteria A and C · build the equation from the rates, and set out the check clearly.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 1 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • The degree of a product of polynomials is the sum of the degrees.
  • Dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder is the check on every division.
  • The remainder theorem gives the remainder on dividing by x − a as p(a).
  • The factor theorem says x − a is a factor exactly when p(a) = 0.
  • An algebraic fraction is cancelled only by a common factor.
  • Excluded values are the values that made a cancelled factor zero.
  • A rational equation is solved by clearing fractions, then checking every candidate.
  • The factored form of a polynomial decides its sign completely.

Vocabulary

polynomial · degree · leading coefficient · long division · quotient · remainder · remainder theorem · factor theorem · root · linear factor · algebraic fraction · excluded value · extraneous solution · sign line · double root

Returning to the statement of inquiry

The structure of a polynomial — its factors, roots and remainders — determines both what it can be simplified to and what its graph will do.

Acting on what you have learned

Algebra is a language for making structure visible. Choose the form that shows the structure you need, and say what the choice costs.

Service as Action

Community need
Public budgets and building specifications are published as simplified expressions whose restrictions are not stated.
Mathematical connection
Algebraic fractions, excluded values and rational equations.
Proposed action
Collect three published specifications, rewrite each as a single simplified expression, and publish the restrictions that were dropped.
Expected impact
A reader can tell where a published formula stops being valid.

Record the specifications, the simplifications and the restrictions you found.

Timetables, budgets and lab recipes are quoted as formulas with unstated limits.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 2 · Functions: Transformations, Composites and Inverses
Chapter 2 · Part II · Thinking with models
02

Functions: Transformations, Composites and Inverses

A function is a relationship between two quantities. The same relationship can be written as a rule, as a table, as a graph or as a machine, and each representation makes a different operation visible.

Engage

A sensor reports a temperature that a model then converts into a pressure. The sensor is recalibrated so that every reading is 3 degrees higher. Which part of the model has to change, and does the graph of the model move up, down, left or right?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Relationships
Related concepts: Change · Representation · Patterns
Global context: Scientific and technical innovation
Global context exploration: models that translate a measurement into a prediction

Statement of inquiry: A function is a rule that pairs each input with exactly one output; transforming, composing and inverting are operations on the rule itself, and each leaves a trace on the graph.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What are the domain and range of a function, and what does the notation f(x) mean?
  • Conceptual: Why does f(x) + k move a graph vertically while f(x + k) moves it horizontally, and what makes a function invertible?
  • Debatable: If two representations of the same function look nothing alike, which one is the function?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to predict the effect of a transformation on a model, students must compare a parent graph with its image, identify which coordinate has changed and how, and justify the algebraic rule that produces the same change.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.1
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.1

Domain, range and function notation

Inquiry question

What does the notation f(x) actually assert?

Your task

Take four rules of your own: a linear one, a quadratic one, one with a square root and one with a fraction. For each, find the largest domain you can state on the real numbers, find the range, and record one input that is not permitted. Then say which representation — table, formula, graph or machine — shows the domain most clearly.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.1
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.1

Domain, range and function notation

What do you notice?
  • Two of the six rules accepted every real input.
  • The square root rule excluded everything below a single number.
  • The fraction rule excluded exactly one value, and its range excluded exactly one value too.
  • The last rule looked like a constant but was undefined at one point.
Observation. The domain is decided by the operations in the rule: division excludes zeros of the denominator and roots exclude negative inputs.
Mathematical conclusion

A function is a rule together with a domain, and the range is what the rule can produce from that domain. The domain is not decoration: the same formula on a different domain is a different function, which is why the domain is stated before anything else is claimed.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.1 · Domain, range and function notation
Chapter 2 · 2.1

Domain, range and function notation

A function is a rule that assigns exactly one output to each input of a stated set, and the relationships it can express are limited by that set. The domain is the set of permitted inputs and the range is the set of outputs the rule can produce. A rule without a stated domain is incomplete, because the same formula can describe different functions on different domains.

Function notation f(x) names the output for the input x. Writing f(2) = 5 is a statement about one input; writing f(x) = 2x + 1 is a statement about all of them. The notation distinguishes the rule from its values, which is what makes composition possible.

Two functions are equal only when they agree on every input of a common domain. The formulas x²/x and x agree everywhere except at x = 0, so they are not the same function unless 0 is excluded from the domain of both.

A mapping diagram, a table, a formula and a graph are four representations of one relationship between input and output. Each is complete, and each makes a different operation easy: a table shows values, a formula shows rules, a graph shows behaviour, and the patterns in each are the same patterns seen from a different angle.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.1 · Worked example 1

Domain, range and function notation

Worked example 2.1.1

Problem. The function f is defined by f(x) = √(x − 2) + 1. State its domain and range, and explain why the domain cannot be larger.

Mathematical reasoning. The expression under a square root must be non-negative, and the root itself is never negative, which fixes the range from below.

  1. The expression under the root is x − 2, so x − 2 ≥ 0 and x ≥ 2.
  2. The domain is therefore x ≥ 2.
  3. √(x − 2) takes every value from 0 upwards, so f(x) takes every value from 1 upwards.
  4. The range is f(x) ≥ 1.
  5. The domain cannot be larger because any x below 2 makes the root undefined.

Final answer. domain x ≥ 2, range f(x) ≥ 1

Interpretation. The domain is part of the definition, not an afterthought: the same formula with a smaller domain is a different function.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.1 · Worked example 2

Domain, range and function notation

Worked example 2.1.2

Problem. Show that f(x) = x²/x and g(x) = x are not the same function, and explain what has to change for them to become equal.

Mathematical reasoning. Two functions are equal only when they agree on every input of a common domain, so a single disagreement is decisive.

  1. f(0) = 0²/0, which is undefined because division by zero is not defined.
  2. g(0) = 0, which is defined.
  3. So the two functions disagree at x = 0.
  4. If the domain of both is restricted to x ≠\neq= 0, then they agree everywhere and become equal.
  5. Hence f and g are different functions on the real numbers but the same function on x ≠\neq= 0.

Final answer. they differ at x = 0; restricting the domain of g to x ≠\neq= 0 makes them equal

Interpretation. Equality of functions is equality on a domain, not similarity of formulas.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.2
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.2

Transformations of graphs

Inquiry question

Why does f(x) + 3 move a graph up but f(x + 3) move it left?

Your task

Take the parent graph y = x². Write the equation of the image after each of these: a translation 2 right and 3 down; a reflection in the y-axis; a stretch by factor 3 parallel to the y-axis; and a translation 1 left followed by a stretch by factor 2 parallel to the x-axis. For each, plot the image of the point (1, 1) and check it satisfies your equation.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.2
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.2

Transformations of graphs

What do you notice?
  • The reflection in the y-axis left this particular graph unchanged, because x² is symmetric.
  • The stretch parallel to the y-axis multiplied the y-coordinate.
  • The stretch parallel to the x-axis divided the x-coordinate, so the graph widened.
  • Every image point satisfied the equation it was supposed to satisfy.
Observation. A change inside the bracket acts on the input and moves the graph horizontally; a change outside acts on the output.
Mathematical conclusion

The equation of an image is the parent equation with the coordinate rule substituted into it, so y = f(x) translated by (a, b) becomes y = f(x − a) + b. Reading the equation as a coordinate rule is the check that the transformation has been described correctly.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.2 · Transformations of graphs
Chapter 2 · 2.2

Transformations of graphs

A translation of the graph of y = f(x) by the vector (a, b) has equation y = f(x − a) + b. The number inside the bracket acts on x before the function, so it moves the graph in the opposite direction to its sign.

The reason for the reversal is order of operations. To obtain the same output as f at x = 0, the translated graph must be evaluated at x = −a, so the whole graph sits a units to the left of where it started.

A reflection in the x-axis has equation y = −f(x), and a reflection in the y-axis has equation y = f(−x). A stretch parallel to the y-axis by factor k has equation y = kf(x), and a stretch parallel to the x-axis by factor k has equation y = f(x/k).

The two descriptions of a transformation — as a coordinate rule and as an equation — must agree. Reading the equation as a coordinate rule is the standard way to check that a transformation has been described correctly.

Formal development

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.2 · Worked example 1

Transformations of graphs

Worked example 2.2.1

Problem. Describe the transformation taking y = x² to y = (x − 3)² + 2, and state the image of the point (1, 1).

Mathematical reasoning. Compare the equation with y = f(x − a) + b to read off the translation, then apply it to the point.

  1. The parent graph is f(x) = x² and the new graph is f(x − 3) + 2.
  2. So a = 3 and b = 2, which is a translation by the vector (3, 2).
  3. The vertex moves from (0, 0) to (3, 2).
  4. The point (1, 1) moves to (1 + 3, 1 + 2) = (4, 3).
  5. Check: (4 − 3)² + 2 = 1 + 2 = 3, which is the y-coordinate.

Final answer. translation by (3, 2); the image of (1, 1) is (4, 3)

Interpretation. The equation encodes the coordinate rule, and reading it as a coordinate rule is the fastest check.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.2 · Worked example 2

Transformations of graphs

Worked example 2.2.2

Problem. Describe the transformation taking y = x² to y = −2(x + 1)², and explain the order of the two changes.

Mathematical reasoning. Separate the change inside the bracket, which acts on the input, from the changes outside, which act on the output.

  1. Inside the bracket, x + 1 means x − (−1), so a = −1: a translation 1 unit left.
  2. Outside, the factor 2 multiplies the output: a stretch parallel to the y-axis by factor 2.
  3. The leading minus sign reflects in the x-axis.
  4. The vertex moves from (0, 0) to (−1, 0) and the graph opens downwards.
  5. Check with a point: on the parent, x = 0 gives 0; on the new graph, x = −1 gives 0.

Final answer. translation 1 left, stretch by factor 2 parallel to the y-axis, then reflection in the x-axis

Interpretation. Changes inside the bracket move the graph horizontally; changes outside move it vertically or reflect it. Confusing the two is the commonest transformation error.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.3
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.3

Composite functions

Inquiry question

In what order do the functions in f(g(x)) act?

Your task

Take f(x) = 3x − 2 and g(x) = x + 5. Compute f(g(x)), g(f(x)), f(f(x)) and g(g(x)), and record the value of each at x = 1. Then find a pair of functions of your own for which the two orders give the same answer, and explain why.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.3
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.3

Composite functions

What do you notice?
  • All four composites were linear, because both functions were linear.
  • The two orders differed by a constant, 10, rather than by a whole function.
  • Repeating a function changed its gradient, so f(f(x)) had gradient 9.
  • A pair of linear functions with the same gradient would commute.
Observation. The order matters, but for linear functions the two orders differ only by a constant.
Mathematical conclusion

The composite f(g(x)) applies g first, and the two orders are different functions in general. Two functions commute exactly when they are specially related — for example when both are translations, or when they are powers of one another.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.3 · Composite functions
Chapter 2 · 2.3

Composite functions

The composite function f(g(x)) applies g first and then f. The inner function acts first, which is the opposite of the order in which the functions are written, and this reversal is the single commonest source of error.

The domain of f(g(x)) is the set of inputs x for which g(x) is defined and g(x) lies in the domain of f. Both conditions must hold, so the domain of a composite is usually smaller than either domain alone.

Composition is associative: f(g(h(x))) can be built as f∘\circ∘(g∘\circ∘h) or as (f∘\circ∘g)∘\circ∘h with the same result. It is not commutative in general, and f(g(x)) = g(f(x)) only for specially related functions.

A function machine is a faithful picture of composition: the output of the first box is the input of the second. Drawing the machine before writing the algebra prevents the order being reversed.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.3 · Worked example 1

Composite functions

Worked example 2.3.1

Problem. Given f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x² − 3, find f(g(x)), g(f(x)) and f(g(2)), and state the domain of f(g(x)).

Mathematical reasoning. Substitute the inner function into the outer one, and note that the two orders differ.

  1. f(g(x)) = 2(g(x)) + 1 = 2(x² − 3) + 1 = 2x² − 5.
  2. g(f(x)) = (f(x))² − 3 = (2x + 1)² − 3 = 4x² + 4x − 2.
  3. The two are different: f(g(1)) = −3 while g(f(1)) = 6.
  4. f(g(2)) = 2(4) − 5 = 3.
  5. Both f and g accept every real input, so the domain of f(g(x)) is all real x.

Final answer. f(g(x)) = 2x² − 5, g(f(x)) = 4x² + 4x − 2, f(g(2)) = 3, domain all real x

Interpretation. Composition is not commutative, and the two orders are different functions with different graphs.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.3 · Worked example 2

Composite functions

Worked example 2.3.2

Problem. Given f(x) = √x and g(x) = x − 4, find f(g(x)) and state its domain.

Mathematical reasoning. The composite is defined only where the inner function is defined and its output lies in the domain of the outer one.

  1. f(g(x)) = √(x − 4).
  2. The square root requires x − 4 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 4.
  3. g itself is defined for all x, so the only restriction comes from f.
  4. The domain of f(g(x)) is x ≥ 4.
  5. Note that this is smaller than the domain of f alone, which is x ≥ 0.

Final answer. f(g(x)) = √(x − 4), domain x ≥ 4

Interpretation. The domain of a composite is the intersection of two conditions, and it is usually smaller than either domain alone.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.4
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.4

Inverse functions

Inquiry question

When does a function have an inverse, and how is it found?

Your task

Take six functions of your own: two linear, one quadratic, one with a square root, one rational and one cubic. For each, decide whether it is one-to-one on its natural domain. If it is, find the inverse and verify it by composition; if it is not, restrict the domain so that it becomes one-to-one and find the inverse on that restriction. Record the domain and range of every inverse you find.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.4
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.4

Inverse functions

What do you notice?
  • Four of the six functions were already one-to-one and needed no restriction.
  • The squaring function needed the restriction x ≥ 0 before an inverse existed.
  • The rational function was one-to-one because its graph never turned back.
  • Every inverse swapped the domain of the original with its range.
Observation. A function is invertible exactly when no horizontal line meets its graph twice, and restriction is the tool for making that true.
Mathematical conclusion

The inverse function exists exactly when the original is one-to-one, and it is verified by composition in both directions. Where the original is not one-to-one, a restricted domain is stated as part of the definition, and the inverse's domain is the original's range.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.4 · Inverse functions
Chapter 2 · 2.4

Inverse functions

The inverse function f−1^{-1}−1 reverses the relationship: if f(a) = b then f−1^{-1}−1(b) = a. It exists exactly when f is one-to-one on its domain, because two different inputs with the same output could not be told apart on the way back.

The horizontal line test decides invertibility. If any horizontal line meets the graph more than once, two inputs share an output and no inverse exists on that domain.

Restricting the domain can make a function one-to-one. The squaring function is not one-to-one on the real numbers, but it is one-to-one on x ≥ 0, and its inverse there is the square root.

The inverse is found by writing y = f(x), rearranging to make x the subject, and then swapping the letters. The check is composition: f−1^{-1}−1(f(x)) = x and f(f−1^{-1}−1(x)) = x on the restricted domains.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.4 · Worked example 1

Inverse functions

Worked example 2.4.1

Problem. Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 5, state its domain and range, and check it by composition.

Mathematical reasoning. Rearrange to make x the subject, then swap the letters, and verify by composition.

  1. Write y = 3x − 5.
  2. Add 5: y + 5 = 3x, so x = (y + 5)/3.
  3. Swap the letters: f−1^{-1}−1(x) = (x + 5)/3.
  4. Check: f−1^{-1}−1(f(x)) = (3x − 5 + 5)/3 = x.
  5. Also f(f−1^{-1}−1(x)) = 3((x + 5)/3) − 5 = x + 5 − 5 = x.

Final answer. f−1^{-1}−1(x) = (x + 5)/3, domain all real x, range all real x

Interpretation. The composition check is the definition of an inverse: it undoes the function in both directions.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.4 · Worked example 2

Inverse functions

Worked example 2.4.2

Problem. Show that f(x) = x² has no inverse on the real numbers, find a domain on which it does, and state the inverse there.

Mathematical reasoning. A horizontal line meeting the graph twice means two inputs share an output, so the function is not one-to-one and has no inverse on that domain.

  1. The line y = 4 meets y = x² at x = −2 and x = 2.
  2. So f(−2) = f(2) = 4, and the two inputs cannot be distinguished on the way back.
  3. Restrict the domain to x ≥ 0. Then every horizontal line meets the graph at most once.
  4. On x ≥ 0 the inverse is f−1^{-1}−1(x) = √x, with domain x ≥ 0.
  5. Check: f−1^{-1}−1(f(x)) = √(x²) = x for x ≥ 0, and f(f−1^{-1}−1(x)) = (√x)² = x for x ≥ 0.

Final answer. no inverse on the real numbers; on x ≥ 0 the inverse is √x with domain x ≥ 0

Interpretation. Restricting the domain is how a many-to-one relationship becomes a one-to-one one, and the restriction must be stated.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.5
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.5

Modelling with transformations

Inquiry question

How does a transformation of a model show up in the situation it describes?

Your task

Take the parent model P(n) = 5n, the price of n items at 5 each. Write models for: a 3 currency unit delivery charge added; a 20 per cent discount; a shop that charges for n + 2 items; and a shop whose item costs half. For each, say whether the change is vertical or horizontal, and find the number of items at which the discounted model costs the same as the original.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.5
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.5

Modelling with transformations

What do you notice?
  • The delivery charge raised every price by the same amount, so it was a vertical translation.
  • The discount multiplied every price by 0.8, so it was a vertical stretch.
  • Charging for n + 2 items was a horizontal translation, and it only mattered for positive n.
  • Two of the models met the original only at n = 0, because both passed through the origin.
Observation. An additive change in the situation is a vertical translation; a multiplicative change is a vertical stretch; a change of origin is a horizontal translation.
Mathematical conclusion

A transformation of a model is a change in the situation, and the direction of the change tells you what changed. Reading the transformation is often faster than recalculating the model, and it explains why two models cross.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.5 · Modelling with transformations
Chapter 2 · 2.5

Modelling with transformations

A model is a function whose input and output both carry units. A transformation of the model is therefore a change in the situation, and reading the transformation tells you what changed without recalculating anything.

A vertical translation changes the output at every input, which is an additive change in the situation: a fixed charge added to a bill, a starting temperature added to a reading. A horizontal translation changes the input, which is a shift in time or in the zero of a scale.

A vertical stretch multiplies every output, which is a multiplicative change: a price rise, a calibration factor. A horizontal stretch divides every input, which is a change of unit or of time scale.

Combining transformations builds a family of models from one parent. A single parent function plus a small set of parameters describes a whole class of situations, and each parameter has a physical meaning.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.5 · Worked example 1

Modelling with transformations

Worked example 2.5.1

Problem. A taxi charges a flag fall of 4 currency units and then 2 per kilometre. A rival charges a flag fall of 6 and 1.5 per kilometre. Model both, describe the transformation between them, and find the distance at which they cost the same.

Mathematical reasoning. Model each as a linear function, read the transformation as a translation and a stretch, and solve for the crossing.

  1. First model: C₁(d) = 2d + 4. Second model: C₂(d) = 1.5d + 6.
  2. The second is the first translated up by 2 and stretched parallel to the x-axis by factor 2/1.5 = 4/3.
  3. Set them equal: 2d + 4 = 1.5d + 6.
  4. Then 0.5d = 2, so d = 4 km.
  5. Check: C₁(4) = 12 and C₂(4) = 12.

Final answer. C₁ = 2d + 4, C₂ = 1.5d + 6; they cost the same at 4 km

Interpretation. The transformation description explains the crossing before any algebra: a higher fixed charge with a lower rate must cross.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.5 · Worked example 2

Modelling with transformations

Worked example 2.5.2

Problem. A cooling model is T(t) = 20 + 60(0.8)T^{T}T for t minutes after 14:00. Write the model for s minutes after the same start, and then for s minutes after 15:00.

Mathematical reasoning. A change of time origin is a horizontal translation, so the new input is the old input minus the shift.

  1. For s minutes after 14:00 the model is identical: T(s) = 20 + 60(0.8)S^{S}S.
  2. For s minutes after 15:00, the old input is t = s + 60, because 15:00 is 60 minutes after 14:00.
  3. So T(s) = 20 + 60(0.8)^(s + 60) = 20 + 60(0.8)⁶⁰(0.8)S^{S}S.
  4. Using the index law, (0.8)^(s + 60) = (0.8)S^{S}S × (0.8)⁶⁰, and (0.8)⁶⁰ is essentially 0.
  5. So the 15:00 model is essentially T(s) ≈ 20, which is why the canteen switched to a different model later in the day.

Final answer. T(s) = 20 + 60(0.8)S^{S}S after 14:00; T(s) = 20 + 60(0.8)^(s + 60) after 15:00

Interpretation. A change of origin is a horizontal translation, and the index law is what makes the translated exponential readable.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.6
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.6

Investigation: when is a function invertible?

Inquiry question

What property of a graph decides whether an inverse exists?

Your task

Take six graphs of your own: a straight line, a parabola, a cubic, an exponential curve, a reciprocal curve and a step function. For each, apply the horizontal line test, and where it fails, find a restricted domain on which it passes. Sketch the inverse on the same axes, using the line y = x as the mirror, and record the domain and range of each inverse.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.6
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.6

Investigation: when is a function invertible?

What do you notice?
  • Four of the six graphs passed the test without any restriction.
  • The parabola needed a restriction to one side of its vertex.
  • The step function could not be rescued by any restriction, because it is constant on whole intervals.
  • Each inverse was the reflection in the line y = x, so every domain and range swapped.
Observation. The horizontal line test is a complete criterion, and the algebraic version is that equal outputs must force equal inputs.
Mathematical conclusion

A function is invertible exactly when it is one-to-one, which the horizontal line test decides graphically and the implication f(a) = f(b) implies a = b decides algebraically. Where a function fails, a restricted domain is stated, and the inverse's graph is the reflection of the original in y = x.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.6 · Investigation: when is a function invertible?
Chapter 2 · 2.6

Investigation: when is a function invertible?

The horizontal line test is a complete criterion: a function is one-to-one exactly when no horizontal line meets its graph more than once. The test works because a horizontal line collects all the inputs with one particular output, so a second meeting is a repeated pattern among the outputs.

The algebraic version of the same test is that f(a) = f(b) must force a = b. Proving that implication is proving that the function is one-to-one, and it is the form used when no graph is available.

A function that is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on its whole domain is one-to-one, because equal outputs would force a reversal. This is why monotonicity is the standard sufficient condition.

The graph of an inverse is the reflection of the graph in the line y = x, because the inverse swaps the coordinates of every point. Drawing the line of reflection is a quick check that an inverse has been found correctly.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: when is a function invertible?

Worked example 2.6.1

Problem. Decide whether f(x) = 2x + 7 is one-to-one, and prove it algebraically.

Mathematical reasoning. Suppose f(a) = f(b) and deduce a = b; the implication is the definition of one-to-one.

  1. Suppose f(a) = f(b), so 2a + 7 = 2b + 7.
  2. Subtract 7 from both sides: 2a = 2b.
  3. Divide by 2: a = b.
  4. So equal outputs force equal inputs, and f is one-to-one.
  5. The inverse is f−1^{-1}−1(x) = (x − 7)/2, and its graph is the reflection in y = x.

Final answer. one-to-one; f−1^{-1}−1(x) = (x − 7)/2

Interpretation. The algebraic test is the same claim as the horizontal line test, written as an implication.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: when is a function invertible?

Worked example 2.6.2

Problem. Decide whether f(x) = x² − 4x is one-to-one on the real numbers, and find a restricted domain on which it is.

Mathematical reasoning. Complete the square to find the axis of symmetry, and note that points equidistant from it share an output.

  1. Complete the square: f(x) = (x − 2)² − 4.
  2. The axis of symmetry is x = 2, so f(2 + h) = f(2 − h) for every h.
  3. For example f(1) = f(3) = −3, so the function is not one-to-one.
  4. Restrict the domain to x ≥ 2. Then the function is strictly increasing and therefore one-to-one.
  5. On x ≥ 2 the inverse is f−1^{-1}−1(x) = 2 + √(x + 4), with domain x ≥ −4.

Final answer. not one-to-one on the real numbers; one-to-one on x ≥ 2, where f−1^{-1}−1(x) = 2 + √(x + 4)

Interpretation. Completing the square locates the axis of symmetry, and the axis is exactly where the function stops being one-to-one.

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which representation makes the next step easiest?

Your task

Take the function f(x) = 2x − 6. Carry out all of the following and record the answer to each: f(5); f−1^{-1}−1(5); f(f(5)); the image of (3, 0) under y = f(x) + 4; the image of (3, 0) under y = f(x + 4); and the image of (3, 0) under y = f−1^{-1}−1(x). Then explain which two of the six answers are the same and why.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 2.7
Chapter 2 · Investigation 2.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • f(5) and the vertical translation gave the same y-coordinate, because adding 4 after the function and evaluating at the same x differ.
  • The horizontal translation moved the point left, not right, because the change was inside the bracket.
  • The inverse image was the reflection of the original point in y = x.
  • The composition f(f(5)) was neither of the translations.
Observation. Each operation acts on a different part of the rule: substitution evaluates, the inverse reverses, and a transformation moves the graph.
Mathematical conclusion

The operations on functions are distinguished by where they act: inside the bracket changes the input, outside changes the output, and composition feeds one function into another. Choosing the right operation is the first step in any question about functions.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 2 · 2.7

Mixed practice

Every question about a function can be approached from four directions: the formula, the table, the graph or the machine. Choosing the representation that shows the needed quantity directly is the skill this section practises.

Transformations, composition and inversion are operations on the rule. Keeping the three operations distinct — and knowing which one a question is asking for — prevents the commonest confusions between f(x) + 2, f(x + 2) and f(f(x)).

The checks are always available: a transformation is checked against a coordinate rule, a composition is checked against a value, and an inverse is checked by composition. Using a check is faster than finding an error later.

Mixed practice is where the operation is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 2 · 2.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 2.7.1

Problem. The function f is defined by f(x) = (3x + 2)/(x − 1). Find f−1^{-1}−1 and state its domain, and find the value of x for which f(x) = f−1^{-1}−1(x).

Mathematical reasoning. Rearrange to make x the subject, then swap the letters and state the domain from the new denominator.

  1. Write y = (3x + 2)/(x − 1) and multiply by x − 1: y(x − 1) = 3x + 2.
  2. Expand: yx − y = 3x + 2, so yx − 3x = y + 2.
  3. Factor: x(y − 3) = y + 2, so x = (y + 2)/(y − 3).
  4. Swap: f−1^{-1}−1(x) = (x + 2)/(x − 3), with domain x ≠\neq= 3.
  5. Setting f(x) = f−1^{-1}−1(x) gives (3x + 2)/(x − 1) = (x + 2)/(x − 3); cross-multiplying gives 3x² − 7x − 6 = x² + x − 2, so 2x² − 8x − 4 = 0 and x = 2 ± √6.

Final answer. f−1^{-1}−1(x) = (x + 2)/(x − 3), domain x ≠\neq= 3; f(x) = f−1^{-1}−1(x) at x = 2 ± √6

Interpretation. A rational function's inverse is rational again, and the excluded value moves from the original denominator to the new one.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook2.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 2 · 2.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 2.7.2

Problem. The graph of y = f(x) passes through (2, 5) and (−1, 3). Find the corresponding points on y = −f(x − 2) + 1 and on y = f−1^{-1}−1(x).

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the coordinate rule of the transformation, and swap the coordinates for the inverse.

  1. For y = −f(x − 2) + 1 the coordinate rule is (x, y) →\rightarrow→ (x + 2, −y + 1).
  2. So (2, 5) maps to (4, −4) and (−1, 3) maps to (1, −2).
  3. For y = f−1^{-1}−1(x) the coordinates swap, so (2, 5) gives (5, 2) and (−1, 3) gives (3, −1).
  4. Check the first: f(2 − 2) = f(0), and −f(0) + 1 = −5 + 1 = −4, which is the image's y-coordinate.
  5. Note the inverse requires f to be one-to-one, which the two points alone cannot establish.

Final answer. (2, 5) →\rightarrow→ (4, −4) and (5, 2); (−1, 3) →\rightarrow→ (1, −2) and (3, −1)

Interpretation. Transformations move points by a rule; inverses swap the coordinates. The two operations look similar on a graph and are completely different.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 2 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A function is a rule with a stated domain that gives exactly one output per input.
  • f(x) + k translates vertically; f(x − a) translates horizontally by a.
  • A stretch parallel to the y-axis has factor k; one parallel to the x-axis divides the input by k.
  • The composite f(g(x)) applies g first.
  • The domain of a composite is where the inner output is a permitted input of the outer function.
  • An inverse exists exactly when the function is one-to-one.
  • The horizontal line test decides invertibility; algebraically, f(a) = f(b) must force a = b.
  • The graph of an inverse is the reflection in the line y = x.

Vocabulary

function · domain · range · mapping · one-to-one · composite · inner function · translation · reflection · stretch · inverse function · horizontal line test · fixed point · coordinate rule
