MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 3 · Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
Chapter 3 · Part II · Thinking with models
03

Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

Some quantities change by adding a fixed amount and some by multiplying by a fixed factor. Logarithms are the inverse language of multiplication, and they turn a multiplicative relationship into an additive one.

Engage

A population doubles every 8 years. A student models it as 8 times the initial population after 64 years. Another models it as 2 to the power 8. Which is right, and why does the difference matter for a forecast a century ahead?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Change
Related concepts: Equivalence · Patterns · Representation
Global context: Scientific and technical innovation
Global context exploration: populations, medicines, sound and seismic energy

Statement of inquiry: Exponential change is repeated multiplication; logarithms are the inverse language that turns multiplication into addition and makes the rate visible.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What do the logarithm laws say, and how is a logarithm defined?
  • Conceptual: Why does an exponential model outgrow every linear model, and what does a logarithm measure?
  • Debatable: If a model fits the past decade exactly, is it a better model than one that fits approximately and states its limits?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to judge whether a growth claim is plausible, students must compare a linear and an exponential model of the same situation, identify the quantity that changes multiplicatively, and justify the choice of model.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.1
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.1

Exponential growth and decay

Inquiry question

Why does repeated multiplication outgrow repeated addition?

Your task

Take 1000 currency units. Model it under three schemes: simple interest at 5 per cent per year, compound interest at 5 per cent per year, and compound interest at 5 per cent per half-year. Record the value after 1, 2, 5 and 10 years for each, and then say which two agree and why the third is different.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.1
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.1

Exponential growth and decay

What do you notice?
  • Simple interest added the same amount every year, so its graph was a straight line.
  • Compound interest added a growing amount, so its graph curved upwards.
  • Compounding twice a year gave slightly more, because interest earned interest sooner.
  • The gap between the schemes widened every year, which is the signature of exponential against linear change.
Observation. Simple interest is a linear model and compound interest is an exponential one, and the exponential model pulls ahead without bound.
Mathematical conclusion

An exponential model N = N₀bT^{T}T compounds a multiplier b for each unit of time, so equal percentage changes occur in equal intervals. The base b is the multiplier, and the exponent counts units of time, not the amount of the quantity. Here 1000 × 1.05T^{T}T is the yearly model and 1000 × 1.025^(2t) the half-yearly one.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.1 · Exponential growth and decay
Chapter 3 · 3.1

Exponential growth and decay

An exponential model has the form N = N₀bT^{T}T, where N₀ is the initial quantity, b is the base or multiplier per unit time, and t is the time. The base is the whole story: b > 1 gives growth, 0 < b < 1 gives decay, and b = 1 gives no change at all.

A constant multiplicative rate means equal percentage changes in equal time intervals. This is what distinguishes exponential change from linear change, where equal absolute changes occur in equal intervals instead.

The graph of an exponential model is a curve with a horizontal asymptote. Growth curves steepen; decay curves flatten towards the asymptote; neither ever reaches it in finite time.

Any exponential model can be written with any positive base, because bT^{T}T = e^(kt) for k = ln b. The equivalence of the two forms is exact, and choosing a base is choosing a representation rather than changing the model.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.1 · Worked example 1

Exponential growth and decay

Worked example 3.1.1

Problem. A population of 400 bacteria doubles every 3 hours. Write the model, find the population after 10 hours, and find when it reaches 25 600.

Mathematical reasoning. The multiplier per period is 2 and the period is 3 hours, so the exponent is t/3; then solve for t by equating.

  1. The model is N(t) = 400 × 2^(t/3).
  2. After 10 hours: N(10) = 400 × 2^(10/3) = 400 × 2^3.333.
  3. 2^3.333 ≈ 10.08, so N(10) ≈ 4032 bacteria.
  4. Set 400 × 2^(t/3) = 25 600, so 2^(t/3) = 64.
  5. Since 64 = 2⁶, t/3 = 6 and t = 18 hours.

Final answer. N(t) = 400 × 2^(t/3); about 4032 after 10 hours; 25 600 after 18 hours

Interpretation. The exponent counts periods, not hours, and confusing the two is the commonest error in exponential modelling.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.1 · Worked example 2

Exponential growth and decay

Worked example 3.1.2

Problem. A car loses 15 per cent of its value each year. Write the model and find its value after 5 years if it cost 24 000.

Mathematical reasoning. A percentage loss is a multiplier below 1, and the model compounds it each year.

  1. Losing 15 per cent leaves 85 per cent, so the multiplier is 0.85.
  2. The model is V(t) = 24000 × 0.85T^{T}T.
  3. After 5 years: V(5) = 24000 × 0.85⁵.
  4. 0.85⁵ ≈ 0.4437, so V(5) ≈ 10 675.
  5. The value never reaches zero in finite time, because 0.85T^{T}T > 0 for every t.

Final answer. V(t) = 24000 × 0.85T^{T}T; about 10 675 after 5 years

Interpretation. A decay model with a positive base is always positive, so the asymptote at zero is a limit rather than a value that is reached.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.2
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.2

The number e and continuous change

Inquiry question

What does it mean for change to be continuous rather than periodic?

Your task

Investigate 1000 currency units at a nominal 10 per cent per year, compounded annually, half-yearly, quarterly, monthly, daily and continuously. Record the value after one year for each, and describe the pattern in the extra amounts as the compounding becomes more frequent.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.2
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.2

The number e and continuous change

What do you notice?
  • Each increase in frequency raised the final value, but by less each time.
  • The daily and continuous values differed by less than one hundredth of a currency unit.
  • The limiting value is 1000e^0.1 ≈ 1105.17, which is the continuous model.
  • The gains formed a decreasing sequence, which is the signature of convergence.
Observation. More frequent compounding raises the accumulated value towards a limit, and the limit is reached by the continuous model.
Mathematical conclusion

Compounding a nominal rate r in n periods per year gives 1000(1 + r/n)N^{N}N, and as n grows this approaches 1000eR^{R}R. The number e is the limit of (1 + 1/n)N^{N}N, and the continuous model N = N₀eKT^{KT}KT is the limit of every periodic model with the same annual rate.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.2 · The number e and continuous change
Chapter 3 · 3.2

The number e and continuous change

Compounding more and more often raises the accumulated value towards a limit, and that limit is the number e ≈ 2.71828. A nominal annual rate r compounded continuously gives a growth factor of eR^{R}R per year.

The continuous model N = N₀eKT^{KT}KT has rate k per unit time. Any base-b model can be rewritten in this form with k = ln b, and the two forms describe exactly the same change.

The natural logarithm ln is the logarithm to base e, and it is the inverse of the exponential function with base e. It is the convenient logarithm for continuous models for the same reason that e is the convenient base.

Continuous models appear wherever the rate of change is proportional to the quantity: populations, radioactive decay, cooling, and the accumulation of interest in a limit.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.2 · Worked example 1

The number e and continuous change

Worked example 3.2.1

Problem. A population is modelled by P(t) = 400(1.05)T^{T}T. Write the model for s years in continuous form, and find the continuous rate.

Mathematical reasoning. Match the two forms by setting eK^{K}K = 1.05 and taking natural logarithms.

  1. The model is P(t) = 400(1.05)T^{T}T.
  2. Write 1.05T^{T}T = eKT^{KT}KT, so eK^{K}K = 1.05.
  3. Taking natural logarithms gives k = ln 1.05 ≈ 0.04879.
  4. So the continuous model is P(t) = 400e^(0.04879t).
  5. Check: e^(0.04879 × 1) ≈ 1.05, as required.

Final answer. P(t) = 400e^(0.04879t), continuous rate about 4.879 per cent per year

Interpretation. The two models are the same function in different clothes, and the continuous rate is slightly below the nominal rate.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.2 · Worked example 2

The number e and continuous change

Worked example 3.2.2

Problem. A substance decays so that 30 per cent remains after 5 hours. Find the half-life, and state the continuous model.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the multiplier per hour from the given data, then solve for the time at which half remains.

  1. Let the model be N(t) = N₀bT^{T}T. Then b⁵ = 0.30, so b = 0.30^(1/5) ≈ 0.7860.
  2. The continuous form is N = N₀eKT^{KT}KT with k = ln 0.7860 ≈ −0.2408.
  3. Half remains when bT^{T}T = 0.5, so t = ln 0.5 ÷ ln 0.7860.
  4. ln 0.5 ≈ −0.6931 and ln 0.7860 ≈ −0.2408, so t ≈ 2.88 hours.
  5. The half-life is about 2.88 hours.

Final answer. half-life about 2.88 hours; N = N₀e^(−0.2408t)

Interpretation. The half-life is independent of the starting quantity, which is why it is the standard way to report a decay rate.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.3
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.3

Logarithms and their laws

Inquiry question

Why do logarithms turn multiplication into addition?

Your task

Build a table of log₂(n) for n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 3, 6, 12 and 24, using only log₂ 2 = 1 and log₂ 3 ≈ 1.585. Then use your table to evaluate log₂ 48, log₂(1/6) and log₂ 9, and state the law you used in each case.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.3
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.3

Logarithms and their laws

What do you notice?
  • Every value came from adding or subtracting the two given values.
  • The power law multiplied by the exponent, so log₂ 16 = 4 log₂ 2 = 4.
  • The product law added, so log₂ 6 = log₂ 2 + log₂ 3.
  • log₂ 1 was 0 because 2⁰ = 1, and that single fact made every quotient work.
Observation. The logarithm laws are the index laws read backwards, and two values generate a whole table.
Mathematical conclusion

The logarithm to base b is the inverse of bX^{X}X, so log_b x = y means exactly bY^{Y}Y = x. Its laws — the product, quotient and power laws — are the index laws read backwards, and they turn multiplication into addition, division into subtraction and powers into multiplication. Here log₂ 48 = log₂(16 × 3) = 4 + 1.585 = 5.585, log₂(1/6) = −2.585 and log₂ 9 = 2 × 1.585 = 3.170.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.3 · Logarithms and their laws
Chapter 3 · 3.3

Logarithms and their laws

The logarithm to base b, written log_b, is the inverse of the exponential function with base b. The statement log_b x = y means exactly bY^{Y}Y = x, and the two statements are equivalent ways of describing the same relationship between x and y.

The three logarithm laws follow from the index laws: log_b(xy) = log_b x + log_b y, log_b(x/y) = log_b x − log_b y, and log_b(xK^{K}K) = k log_b x. Each is the index law read backwards.

The change of base formula log_b a = log a ÷ log b allows any logarithm to be computed from any other. It is the reason a calculator with only two logarithm buttons is sufficient.

A logarithm is an exponent, so its laws are the laws of exponents. Treating a logarithm as a number to be manipulated rather than as a label is what makes the laws usable.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.3 · Worked example 1

Logarithms and their laws

Worked example 3.3.1

Problem. Solve log₂(x) + log₂(x − 2) = 3.

Mathematical reasoning. Combine with the product law, remove the logarithm with its definition, then check the domain.

  1. Both logarithms require a positive argument, so x > 0 and x − 2 > 0, giving x > 2.
  2. Combine: log₂(x(x − 2)) = 3.
  3. Remove the logarithm: x(x − 2) = 2³ = 8.
  4. So x² − 2x − 8 = 0, giving (x − 4)(x + 2) = 0.
  5. x = 4 or x = −2; only x = 4 satisfies x > 2.

Final answer. x = 4

Interpretation. The domain restriction comes before the algebra, and it is what rejects the extraneous root.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.3 · Worked example 2

Logarithms and their laws

Worked example 3.3.2

Problem. Given log 2 ≈ 0.3010 and log 3 ≈ 0.4771, find log 12 and log(2/3) without a calculator.

Mathematical reasoning. Factorise into primes and apply the laws, using the given values.

  1. 12 = 4 × 3 = 2² × 3, so log 12 = 2 log 2 + log 3.
  2. log 12 = 2(0.3010) + 0.4771 = 0.6021 + 0.4771 = 1.0791.
  3. 2/3 has log 2 − log 3 = 0.3010 − 0.4771 = −0.1761.
  4. Check: 10^1.0791 ≈ 12, and 10^(−0.1761) ≈ 0.667.
  5. The laws turned two given values into many others.

Final answer. log 12 ≈ 1.0791 and log(2/3) ≈ −0.1761

Interpretation. Logarithms of composite numbers are sums of logarithms of primes, which is why logarithm tables were short.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.4
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.4

Solving exponential equations

Inquiry question

When can an exponential equation be solved, and what is the method?

Your task

Solve each of these by first trying to match bases, and then by taking logarithms: 2^(x+1) = 32; 4X^{X}X = 8^(x−1); 3^(2x−1) = 27; and 10X^{X}X = 7. Record which method you used for each and why, and check every answer.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.4
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.4

Solving exponential equations

What do you notice?
  • Three of the four equations yielded to matching bases, because the numbers were all powers of small integers.
  • The fourth needed logarithms, because 7 is not a power of 10.
  • Matching bases gave exact answers; logarithms gave approximations.
  • Every answer passed the substitution check.
Observation. Matching bases is exact and should always be tried first; logarithms are the general method.
Mathematical conclusion

An exponential equation is solved by matching bases when that is possible, and otherwise by taking logarithms of both sides and using the power law. The check is substitution into the original equation, and it also confirms that every logarithm taken had a positive argument.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.4 · Solving exponential equations
Chapter 3 · 3.4

Solving exponential equations

If both sides of an exponential equation can be written as powers of the same base, the exponents can be equated, because a one-to-one power function has one input per output.

If the bases cannot be matched, take logarithms of both sides. The power law brings the unknown down from the exponent, which converts the exponential equation into a linear or quadratic one.

Every solution must be checked in the original equation, because taking logarithms requires positive arguments. A candidate that makes an argument non-positive is extraneous.

Equations with the unknown in two places, such as 2X^{X}X = 3x + 1, cannot be solved algebraically. They are solved numerically, and a graph or an iterative method gives the answer to any required accuracy.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.4 · Worked example 1

Solving exponential equations

Worked example 3.4.1

Problem. Solve 3^(2x) = 81.

Mathematical reasoning. Write both sides as powers of 3, then equate the exponents.

  1. 81 = 3⁴, so the equation becomes 3^(2x) = 3⁴.
  2. Equal powers of the same base have equal exponents: 2x = 4.
  3. So x = 2.
  4. Check: 3^(2 × 2) = 3⁴ = 81.

Final answer. x = 2

Interpretation. Matching bases is always the first move, because it is exact and avoids rounding.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.4 · Worked example 2

Solving exponential equations

Worked example 3.4.2

Problem. Solve 5^(x) = 250, giving the answer to three significant figures.

Mathematical reasoning. Take logarithms of both sides, apply the power law, and rearrange.

  1. Take logarithms: log(5X^{X}X) = log 250.
  2. Apply the power law: x log 5 = log 250.
  3. So x = log 250 ÷ log 5.
  4. log 250 ≈ 2.3979 and log 5 ≈ 0.6990, so x ≈ 3.430.
  5. Check: 5^3.43 ≈ 249.9, which is close to 250.

Final answer. x ≈ 3.43

Interpretation. Any base of logarithm works, because the change of base formula cancels the base out of the quotient.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.5
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.5

Modelling with logarithms

Inquiry question

What does a logarithmic scale show that a linear scale cannot?

Your task

Take a quantity that doubles every day: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Plot the values on a linear axis and on a logarithmic axis, and describe what each plot shows. Then take the first seven square numbers and plot them on a log-log axis, and describe what you see.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.5
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.5

Modelling with logarithms

What do you notice?
  • On a linear axis the doubling quantity curved steeply upwards.
  • On a logarithmic axis the same values lay on a straight line, because each step multiplied by the same factor.
  • The squares also lay on a straight line on the log-log axis, with gradient 2.
  • The gradient of a log-log line is the power in a power law.
Observation. A straight line on semi-log paper means exponential change, and a straight line on log-log paper means a power law.
Mathematical conclusion

A logarithmic scale compresses equal ratios into equal distances, so multiplicative change appears as a straight line and the gradient measures the rate. Taking logarithms of both variables turns an exponential law into a linear one and a power law into a line whose gradient is the power. This is why the Richter, decibel and pH scales are logarithmic.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.5 · Modelling with logarithms
Chapter 3 · 3.5

Modelling with logarithms

A logarithmic scale compresses equal ratios into equal distances, so a quantity that grows by a constant factor appears as a straight line and its patterns become readable. This is why logarithmic axes are used for anything spanning many orders of magnitude.

Semi-log graph paper has a linear axis and a logarithmic one. Data that plot as a straight line on semi-log paper are exponential, and the gradient of the line is the continuous rate.

The Richter scale for earthquakes, the decibel scale for sound and the pH scale for acidity are all logarithmic. A difference of one unit is a fixed ratio, not a fixed difference, which is why the scales are described as logarithmic.

Taking logarithms of both variables of a power law y = kxN^{N}N gives log y = n log x + log k, a straight line. Log-log graph paper therefore identifies power laws, just as semi-log paper identifies exponential ones.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.5 · Worked example 1

Modelling with logarithms

Worked example 3.5.1

Problem. An earthquake of magnitude 6 releases how many times the energy of one of magnitude 4, if energy is proportional to 10^(1.5M)?

Mathematical reasoning. Form the ratio of the energy factors and simplify using the index laws.

  1. Energy is proportional to 10^(1.5M).
  2. The ratio for M = 6 against M = 4 is 10^(1.5 × 6) ÷ 10^(1.5 × 4).
  3. By the quotient law this is 10^(9 − 6) = 10³.
  4. So a magnitude 6 earthquake releases 1000 times the energy.
  5. One step of magnitude is a factor of 10^1.5 ≈ 31.6.

Final answer. 1000 times

Interpretation. The magnitude scale is logarithmic, so differences in magnitude are ratios in energy, and the ratios grow very fast.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.5 · Worked example 2

Modelling with logarithms

Worked example 3.5.2

Problem. Sound intensity level is L = 10 log(I/I₀) decibels. Find the ratio of intensities for levels of 60 dB and 40 dB.

Mathematical reasoning. Subtract the two level equations and use the quotient law.

  1. L₁ − L₂ = 10 log(I₁/I₀) − 10 log(I₂/I₀) = 10 log(I₁/I₂).
  2. So 60 − 40 = 10 log(I₁/I₂), giving 20 = 10 log(I₁/I₂).
  3. Hence log(I₁/I₂) = 2, so I₁/I₂ = 10² = 100.
  4. The 60 dB sound is 100 times as intense as the 40 dB sound.
  5. Note that a 20 dB difference sounds roughly four times as loud, because loudness is not logarithmic in the same way.

Final answer. 100 times

Interpretation. A difference on a logarithmic scale is a ratio, and the ratio is found by dividing the difference by the scale factor.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.6
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.6

Investigation: how many digits?

Inquiry question

How many digits does a large power have, and can it be predicted?

Your task

Investigate the number of digits of 2N^{N}N for n = 1 to 12. Form a conjecture and justify it. Then investigate the leading digit of 2N^{N}N over the same range, and describe the pattern you find.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.6
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.6

Investigation: how many digits?

What do you notice?
  • The digit count increased by 1 about every 3.32 powers.
  • The increases happened at n = 4, 7, 10 and 12, which is not a fixed period.
  • The leading digit cycled through 2, 4, 8, 1, 3, 6, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 4.
  • The leading digit was 1 at n = 4, 7 and 10, more often than any other digit.
Observation. The digit count grows linearly in n with slope log₁₀2, and the leading digit cycles irregularly.
Mathematical conclusion

The number of digits of bN^{N}N is the whole part of n log₁₀b, plus one, because bN^{N}N lies between 10K^{K}K and 10K+1^{K+1}K+1 where k is that whole part. The fractional part of n log₁₀b gives the leading digits, and its distribution explains why small leading digits are common — the observation behind Benford's law.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.6 · Investigation: how many digits?
Chapter 3 · 3.6

Investigation: how many digits?

A positive integer with n digits lies between 10N−1^{N-1}N−1 and 10N^{N}N, so the number of digits of a number x is the least integer strictly greater than log₁₀x. Counting digits is therefore a logarithm problem.

The number of digits of bN^{N}N is the whole part of n log₁₀b, plus one. The fractional part of n log₁₀b determines the leading digits, because 10 raised to that fractional part lies between 1 and 10.

This is the basis of floating-point representation in every computer: a number is stored as a mantissa between 1 and 10 and an exponent, which is exactly the decomposition that logarithms describe.

The leading-digit pattern of powers is not uniform. Benford's law observes that in many real data sets the leading digit is 1 far more often than 9, and the logarithmic distribution explains it.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: how many digits?

Worked example 3.6.1

Problem. How many digits does 2¹⁰⁰ have?

Mathematical reasoning. Compute n log₁₀2, take its whole part and add one.

  1. log₁₀2 ≈ 0.30103.
  2. So 100 log₁₀2 ≈ 30.103.
  3. The whole part is 30, and the number of digits is 30 + 1 = 31.
  4. Check: 2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 1.2677 × 10³⁰, which indeed has 31 digits.
  5. The fractional part 0.103 gives the leading digits, because 10^0.103 ≈ 1.27.

Final answer. 31 digits

Interpretation. One multiplication and one truncation answer a question about a number with 31 digits.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: how many digits?

Worked example 3.6.2

Problem. How many digits does 7²⁰ have, and what are its leading digits?

Mathematical reasoning. Separate n log b into its whole part and its fractional part.

  1. log₁₀7 ≈ 0.84510.
  2. 20 log₁₀7 ≈ 16.902.
  3. The whole part is 16, so the number of digits is 17.
  4. The fractional part is 0.902, and 10^0.902 ≈ 7.98.
  5. So 7²⁰ begins with the digits 79, and is about 7.98 × 10¹⁶.

Final answer. 17 digits, beginning with 79

Interpretation. The same calculation that counts the digits also reveals the leading ones, which is how a computer stores a number.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.7
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which representation of the change makes the rate visible?

Your task

A company's revenue is 4 million in year 0 and 5.8 million in year 5. Fit an exponential model, state the annual rate, find the doubling time, and predict the revenue in year 12. Then state one assumption the model makes and one reason it might fail.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 3.7
Chapter 3 · Investigation 3.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • The base came from the ratio of the two known values, raised to the power 1/5.
  • The annual rate was just under 8 per cent.
  • The doubling time was independent of the starting revenue.
  • The prediction for year 12 was more than three times the starting value.
Observation. Two data points fix an exponential model, and the rate and the doubling time are read straight off it.
Mathematical conclusion

An exponential model is fitted by finding the base from two data points, and the base gives both the rate and the doubling time. The model assumes the rate stays constant, which is the assumption most likely to fail: markets saturate, competitors enter and costs rise. Here the fitted model is R(t) = 4 × 1.0771T^{T}T million, with a doubling time of about 9.3 years.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 3 · 3.7

Mixed practice

Every exponential question can be approached in three ways: match the bases, take logarithms, or read the rate off a model. The method is chosen by the shape of the question, and choosing well saves work.

The base form N = N₀bT^{T}T and the continuous form N = N₀eKT^{KT}KT are equivalent representations of the same change, related by k = ln b. Converting between them is a routine step, not a change of model.

Logarithm laws are used to solve equations, to simplify expressions and to interpret scales. In each case the underlying move is the same: turn a multiplicative statement into an additive one.

Mixed practice is where the representation is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 3 · 3.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 3.7.1

Problem. A town's population grows from 12 000 to 15 000 in 4 years. Assuming exponential growth, find the annual growth rate and predict the population after a further 6 years.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the two known values to find the base, then extrapolate.

  1. The model is P(t) = 12000 bT^{T}T and P(4) = 15000.
  2. So b⁴ = 15000/12000 = 1.25.
  3. Hence b = 1.25^(1/4) ≈ 1.0574, an annual rate of about 5.74 per cent.
  4. After a further 6 years, t = 10, so P(10) = 12000 × 1.0574¹⁰.
  5. 1.0574¹⁰ ≈ 1.7575, so P(10) ≈ 21 090.

Final answer. about 5.74 per cent per year; about 21 090 after 10 years

Interpretation. Two data points fix an exponential model completely, which is why exponential extrapolation is so easy and so dangerous.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook3.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 3 · 3.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 3.7.2

Problem. A bank offers 6 per cent nominal annual interest compounded continuously. How long does it take for a deposit to double?

Mathematical reasoning. Set the model equal to twice the initial value and take natural logarithms.

  1. The model is A(t) = P e^(0.06t).
  2. Doubling means A(t) = 2P, so e^(0.06t) = 2.
  3. Taking natural logarithms: 0.06t = ln 2 ≈ 0.6931.
  4. So t ≈ 0.6931 ÷ 0.06 ≈ 11.55 years.
  5. The answer is independent of P, which is why the doubling time is quoted.

Final answer. about 11.55 years

Interpretation. The doubling time of a continuous model is ln 2 ÷ k, a formula worth remembering because it does not depend on the deposit.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 3 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • An exponential model N = N₀bT^{T}T compounds the base b for each unit of time.
  • The base-b form and the continuous form N₀eKT^{KT}KT describe the same change, with k = ln b.
  • Compounding more frequently approaches the continuous model, whose limit is eR^{R}R.
  • A logarithm is an exponent: log_b x = y means exactly bY^{Y}Y = x.
  • The logarithm laws are the index laws read backwards.
  • Exponential equations are solved by matching bases or by taking logarithms.
  • Every solution must be checked for a positive logarithm argument.
  • A logarithmic scale compresses equal ratios into equal distances.

Vocabulary

exponential · base · multiplier · asymptote · half-life · continuous growth · natural logarithm · logarithm laws · change of base · semi-log · log-log · Benford's law · floating point · decibel · Richter scale

Chapter 3 · Review

Returning to the statement of inquiry

Statement of inquiry

Exponential change is repeated multiplication; logarithms are the inverse language that turns multiplication into addition and makes the rate visible.

Reflect on the chapter

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 4 · Sequences and Series
Chapter 4 · Part I · Number and abstract reasoning
04

Sequences and Series

A sequence is a list generated by a rule, and a series is the sum of a sequence. Both can be summarised by a formula, and the formula's behaviour decides whether the sum is finite, unbounded or convergent.

Engage

Two savers each deposit 100 currency units in the first month. The first adds 10 every month; the second increases each deposit by 10 per cent of the previous month's deposit. After twelve months who has saved more, and after ten years?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Form
Related concepts: Patterns · Generalisation · Simplification
Global context: Fairness and development
Global context exploration: saving, loans and the long-term decisions that shape opportunity

Statement of inquiry: A sequence is form made visible: one rule generates every term, and the sum of those terms simplifies to a formula whose behaviour — finite, unbounded or convergent — is decided by a single number.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What are the formulas for the nth term and the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic and of a geometric sequence?
  • Conceptual: Why does a geometric series converge exactly when the common ratio is between −1 and 1?
  • Debatable: If two savings plans agree for the first year, does the one that is better after ten years make the other unfair?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to judge whether a savings plan is fair, students must compare two sequences that begin identically, identify the rule that generates each, and justify which is the better long-term choice.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.1
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.1

Arithmetic sequences

Inquiry question

What single number generates an arithmetic sequence?

Your task

Take six lists of your own: three arithmetic and three not. For the arithmetic ones, find the common difference and the general term. For the others, explain precisely which property of an arithmetic sequence fails, and state whether the list is geometric.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.1
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.1

Arithmetic sequences

What do you notice?
  • Two of the six lists were arithmetic, with common differences 3 and −3.
  • Two were geometric, with ratios 3 and 0.9.
  • The squares failed the arithmetic test because their differences grew.
  • The Fibonacci-type list failed both tests, because its rule used two earlier terms.
Observation. An arithmetic sequence has a constant difference; a geometric one has a constant ratio; a list can be neither.
Mathematical conclusion

An arithmetic sequence is generated by adding a fixed common difference d, so u(n) = u(1) + (n − 1)d is a generalisation that covers every term from the first term and d alone. The test for the type is whether consecutive differences, or consecutive ratios, are constant, and a list can fail both tests.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.1 · Arithmetic sequences
Chapter 4 · 4.1

Arithmetic sequences

An arithmetic sequence has a common difference d between consecutive terms, so u(n) = u(1) + (n − 1)d. The sequence is completely determined by its first term and its common difference.

The common difference is found by subtracting any term from the next one, and it must be the same for every consecutive pair, so the pattern is a single number repeated. A list that fails this test is not arithmetic, however regular it looks.

The graph of an arithmetic sequence, with n on the horizontal axis, is a set of equally spaced points on a straight line. The common difference is the gradient of that line, which is why arithmetic sequences are the discrete analogue of linear functions.

The nth-term formula is a generalisation: it claims something about every term from a single rule, and its simplification u(n) = dn + c is a straight line. It is proved by checking that consecutive terms differ by d.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 4 · 4.1 · Worked example 1

Arithmetic sequences

Worked example 4.1.1

Problem. Find the nth term of the sequence 7, 11, 15, 19, … and hence find the 50th term.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the common difference, write the general term, and substitute.

  1. Consecutive differences are all 4, so d = 4.
  2. The first term is 7, so u(n) = 7 + (n − 1) × 4.
  3. Simplify: u(n) = 4n + 3.
  4. Check: u(1) = 7, u(2) = 11, u(3) = 15, as required.
  5. So u(50) = 4(50) + 3 = 203.

Final answer. u(n) = 4n + 3; u(50) = 203

Interpretation. The general term is a formula that covers every term, and it is verified by checking the first few.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 4 · 4.1 · Worked example 2

Arithmetic sequences

Worked example 4.1.2

Problem. The 3rd term of an arithmetic sequence is 14 and the 9th term is 34. Find the first term and the common difference.

Mathematical reasoning. Write two equations from the general term and solve simultaneously.

  1. Let the first term be a and the common difference be d.
  2. Then a + 2d = 14 and a + 8d = 34.
  3. Subtracting gives 6d = 20, so d = 10/3.
  4. Substituting back: a = 14 − 2(10/3) = 14 − 20/3 = 22/3.
  5. Check: u(9) = 22/3 + 8(10/3) = 22/3 + 80/3 = 102/3 = 34.

Final answer. first term 22/3, common difference 10/3

Interpretation. Any two terms determine an arithmetic sequence, because the general term is linear in n.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.2
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.2

Arithmetic series and sigma notation

Inquiry question

How does a sum simplify to a formula?

Your task

Take the arithmetic sequence u(r) = 5r + 2. Compute ∑r=110\sum_{r=1}^{10}∑r=110​ u(r) by direct addition, then by the sum formula, then by splitting the sum into two parts. Record all three answers and explain why they must agree.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.2
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.2

Arithmetic series and sigma notation

What do you notice?
  • All three methods gave 295, as they had to.
  • The formula method used only the first and last terms.
  • The splitting method used the known sum of the first ten integers.
  • The formula method was fastest and the direct method was the check.
Observation. The sum formula and the linearity of summation are two descriptions of the same total.
Mathematical conclusion

The sum of an arithmetic series simplifies to (n/2)(u(1) + u(n)) because the terms can be paired so that every pair has the same total. Sigma notation records the same sum compactly, and its linearity lets the sum be split into parts that are easier to evaluate. Here all three routes gave 295.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.2 · Arithmetic series and sigma notation
Chapter 4 · 4.2

Arithmetic series and sigma notation

The sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence is S(n) = (n/2)(2u(1) + (n − 1)d), or equivalently S(n) = (n/2)(u(1) + u(n)). The second form pairs the first with the last, and each pair has the same sum.

Sigma notation writes the sum of a list compactly: S(n) = ∑r=1n\sum_{r=1}^{n}∑r=1n​ u(r). The letter r is the index, 1 is its start and n its finish, and changing the index changes nothing about the value.

The pairing argument is the proof of the formula: write the sum forwards and backwards, add the two rows, and every pair sums to u(1) + u(n). There are n such pairs, so twice the sum is n(u(1) + u(n)), and the simplification to (n/2)(u(1) + u(n)) follows immediately.

Linearity of summation lets a sum be split: ∑\sum∑ (a(r) + b(r)) = ∑\sum∑ a(r) + ∑\sum∑ b(r), and ∑\sum∑ k a(r) = k ∑\sum∑ a(r). These are the rules that make sigma notation usable.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 4 · 4.2 · Worked example 1

Arithmetic series and sigma notation

Worked example 4.2.1

Problem. Find the sum of the first 60 positive integers.

Mathematical reasoning. Pair the first term with the last, and note that each pair has the same sum.

  1. The sequence is 1, 2, 3, …, 60, with u(1) = 1 and u(60) = 60.
  2. Pair 1 with 60, 2 with 59, and so on: each pair sums to 61.
  3. There are 60 terms, so there are 30 pairs.
  4. The sum is 30 × 61 = 1830.
  5. Check with the formula: (60/2)(1 + 60) = 30 × 61 = 1830.

Final answer. 1830

Interpretation. The pairing argument explains the formula rather than merely applying it, and it works for every arithmetic series.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 4 · 4.2 · Worked example 2

Arithmetic series and sigma notation

Worked example 4.2.2

Problem. Evaluate ∑r=112\sum_{r=1}^{12}∑r=112​ (3r − 2).

Mathematical reasoning. Recognise the terms as an arithmetic sequence and apply the sum formula.

  1. The terms are 1, 4, 7, …, with u(1) = 1 and d = 3.
  2. The last term is u(12) = 3(12) − 2 = 34.
  3. There are 12 terms, so the sum is (12/2)(1 + 34).
  4. That is 6 × 35 = 210.
  5. Check by splitting: 3 × (sum of 1 to 12) − 2 × 12 = 3 × 78 − 24 = 234 − 24 = 210.

Final answer. 210

Interpretation. The linearity check confirms the formula by a different route, which is what a check should do.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.3
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.3

Geometric sequences

Inquiry question

What distinguishes a geometric sequence from an arithmetic one?

Your task

Take four geometric sequences of your own with r = 2, r = 0.5, r = −1 and r = −0.5, each with first term 8. Compute the first six terms of each, describe the behaviour of the terms as n grows, and record whether the terms grow, shrink, alternate or collapse.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.3
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.3

Geometric sequences

What do you notice?
  • With r = 2 the terms doubled each step and grew without bound.
  • With r = 0.5 the terms halved and approached zero.
  • With r = −1 the terms alternated between two values and never settled.
  • With r = −0.5 the terms alternated and shrank, approaching zero.
Observation. The magnitude of r decides growth or decay, and the sign of r decides whether the terms alternate.
Mathematical conclusion

A geometric sequence multiplies by a fixed ratio r, so u(n) = u(1)r^(n−1) is a generalisation covering every term. The behaviour of the sequence is decided by |r| alone: growth above 1, decay below 1, and neither at exactly 1. The sign of r only decides whether the terms change sign, not whether they grow.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.3 · Geometric sequences
Chapter 4 · 4.3

Geometric sequences

A geometric sequence has a common ratio r between consecutive terms, so u(n) = u(1) × r^(n−1). Each term is the previous one multiplied by the same factor, which is why the growth is multiplicative rather than additive.

The sign of r matters. A positive r keeps every term the same sign as the first; a negative r makes the terms alternate in sign; r = 0 collapses the sequence to zero after the first term.

The magnitude of r decides the behaviour. With |r| > 1 the terms grow without bound; with |r| = 1 they stay constant or alternate; with 0 < |r| < 1 they shrink towards zero. These three patterns exhaust the possibilities.

A geometric sequence with a positive first term and r > 0 is an exponential function of n in disguise, and its graph is the set of points on an exponential curve.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 4 · 4.3 · Worked example 1

Geometric sequences

Worked example 4.3.1

Problem. Find the nth term of the sequence 3, 6, 12, 24, … and hence find the 10th term.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the common ratio and write the general term, then substitute.

  1. Consecutive ratios are all 2, so r = 2.
  2. The first term is 3, so u(n) = 3 × 2^(n−1).
  3. Check: u(2) = 3 × 2 = 6 and u(3) = 3 × 4 = 12, as required.
  4. So u(10) = 3 × 2⁹ = 3 × 512 = 1536.
  5. Note the exponent is n − 1, not n, because the first term corresponds to r⁰.

Final answer. u(n) = 3 × 2^(n−1); u(10) = 1536

Interpretation. The exponent counts the number of multiplications, which is one fewer than the number of terms.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 4 · 4.3 · Worked example 2

Geometric sequences

Worked example 4.3.2

Problem. A ball is dropped from 2 m and rebounds to 60 per cent of its previous height each time. Find the height of the fifth rebound and the total distance travelled before it comes to rest.

Mathematical reasoning. Model the rebound heights as a geometric sequence and sum the distances, counting each rebound twice.

  1. The rebound heights are 2, 1.2, 0.72, … with r = 0.6.
  2. So the height of the nth rebound is 2 × 0.6N^{N}N.
  3. The fifth rebound is 2 × 0.6⁵ ≈ 0.1555 m.
  4. The total distance is the initial 2 m plus twice the sum of the rebound heights.
  5. That sum is 2 × 0.6 ÷ (1 − 0.6) = 3, so the total distance is 2 + 2 × 3 = 8 m.

Final answer. fifth rebound about 0.156 m; total distance 8 m

Interpretation. The total distance is finite even though the ball bounces infinitely often, which is the first surprise of convergent series.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.4
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.4

Geometric series and convergence

Inquiry question

When is an infinite sum finite?

Your task

Investigate the series 1 + r + r² + r³ + … for r = 0.9, r = 0.99, r = −0.5, r = −0.99, r = 1 and r = −1. For each, compute the partial sums after 5, 10 and 20 terms, and state whether a sum to infinity exists.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.4
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.4

Geometric series and convergence

What do you notice?
  • Every series with |r| < 1 approached a limit, however slowly.
  • With r = 0.99 the limit was 100, and 20 terms had reached only 9.81.
  • With negative r the partial sums alternated above and below the limit.
  • With r = 1 and r = −1 the partial sums did not settle at all.
Observation. The partial sums settle exactly when |r| < 1, and the limit is u(1)/(1 − r).
Mathematical conclusion

A geometric series converges exactly when |r| < 1, and its sum to infinity is u(1)/(1 − r); otherwise the partial sums grow without bound or oscillate. The single number r decides the behaviour, which is why the convergence condition is checked before the formula is used. Here the limits were 10, 100, 2/3 and about 0.5025.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.4 · Geometric series and convergence
Chapter 4 · 4.4

Geometric series and convergence

The sum of the first n terms of a geometric sequence is S(n) = u(1)(1 − rN^{N}N)/(1 − r) when r ≠\neq= 1. The formula is proved by subtracting r S(n) from S(n), which cancels every term but two.

The infinite series ∑n=0∞\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}∑n=0∞​ u(1)rN^{N}N converges exactly when |r| < 1, and its sum is u(1)/(1 − r). When |r| ≥ 1 the partial sums grow without bound and no sum exists.

The condition |r| < 1 is not a technicality. With r = 0.9 the partial sums approach 10; with r = −0.9 they approach 1/1.9 ≈ 0.526; with r = 1.1 they grow without bound. A single number decides the behaviour.

A convergent series is a limit of partial sums, not an infinite addition performed all at once. The distinction matters when the terms are not all positive, because rearranging the terms of a conditionally convergent series can change its sum.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 4 · 4.4 · Worked example 1

Geometric series and convergence

Worked example 4.4.1

Problem. Find the sum of the geometric series 12 + 6 + 3 + 1.5 + … to infinity.

Mathematical reasoning. Identify the first term and the common ratio, check the convergence condition, and apply the formula.

  1. The first term is 12 and the common ratio is 6/12 = 0.5.
  2. Since |r| = 0.5 < 1, the series converges.
  3. The sum to infinity is u(1)/(1 − r) = 12/(1 − 0.5) = 12/0.5 = 24.
  4. Check with partial sums: after 4 terms the sum is 22.5, and after 10 terms it is 23.976, approaching 24.
  5. The remaining distance after n terms is 24 × 0.5N^{N}N, which tends to zero.

Final answer. 24

Interpretation. The limit 24 is never reached by a partial sum, but the partial sums get arbitrarily close to it, which is what convergence means.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 4 · 4.4 · Worked example 2

Geometric series and convergence

Worked example 4.4.2

Problem. Show that the series 1 + 1.1 + 1.21 + 1.331 + … has no sum to infinity, and explain why.

Mathematical reasoning. The common ratio is greater than 1 in magnitude, so the convergence condition fails.

  1. The common ratio is 1.1, so |r| = 1.1 > 1.
  2. The condition |r| < 1 fails, so the series diverges.
  3. The partial sums are S(n) = 1(1.1N^{N}N − 1)/(1.1 − 1) = 10(1.1N^{N}N − 1).
  4. As n grows, 1.1N^{N}N grows without bound, so the partial sums do too.
  5. Hence there is no sum to infinity.

Final answer. no sum; the series diverges because |r| > 1

Interpretation. The single number r decides everything, and the threshold is exactly 1 in magnitude.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.5
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.5

Annuities, loans and saving

Inquiry question

How does a series model a long-term financial decision?

Your task

Investigate saving 100 currency units a month for 20 years at three rates: 0 per cent, 3 per cent and 6 per cent per year compounded monthly. Record the total paid in and the final value for each, and describe the pattern in the interest earned.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.5
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.5

Annuities, loans and saving

What do you notice?
  • With no interest the final value was exactly the amount paid in.
  • At 3 per cent the interest was about 37 per cent of the total deposited.
  • At 6 per cent the interest was about 93 per cent of the total deposited, nearly doubling the savings.
  • Doubling the rate far more than doubled the interest, because the earliest deposits had longer to grow.
Observation. The final value is a geometric series sum, and the rate enters through the ratio.
Mathematical conclusion

A regular saving plan accumulates to P((1 + i)N^{N}N − 1)/i, where P is the deposit, i the rate per period and n the number of periods. The formula is the geometric series sum applied to deposits, and the same formula read backwards repays a loan. Here 100 a month for 20 years grew to 32 883 at 3 per cent and 46 204 at 6 per cent.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.5 · Annuities, loans and saving
Chapter 4 · 4.5

Annuities, loans and saving

A regular deposit into an account paying interest is a geometric series: each deposit grows by the interest factor for the number of periods it remains invested. The accumulated value is the sum of a finite geometric series.

The future value of a deposit of P made at the end of each period for n periods at rate i per period is P((1 + i)N^{N}N − 1)/i. The formula is the geometric sum formula applied to the deposits.

A loan repaid by regular instalments is the same formula read backwards: the present value of the instalments must equal the amount borrowed. Solving for the instalment gives the standard repayment formula.

The fairness of a plan depends on the interest rate, the frequency of compounding and the length of the term. Two plans with the same nominal rate can differ substantially once these are stated, which is why the assumptions are part of the model.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 4 · 4.5 · Worked example 1

Annuities, loans and saving

Worked example 4.5.1

Problem. A saver deposits 500 currency units at the end of each year into an account paying 4 per cent per year. Find the value after 10 years.

Mathematical reasoning. Recognise the accumulated deposits as a geometric series and apply the sum formula.

  1. The deposits are 500 each, and the deposit made k years before the end has grown by 1.04K^{K}K.
  2. So the total is 500(1 + 1.04 + 1.04² + … + 1.04⁹).
  3. This is a geometric series with r = 1.04 and 10 terms.
  4. The sum is 500 × (1.04¹⁰ − 1)/(1.04 − 1) = 500 × 12.0061.
  5. So the value is about 6003 currency units.

Final answer. about 6003 currency units

Interpretation. The deposits together earn about 1003 currency units of interest, and the earliest deposit earns the most.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 4 · 4.5 · Worked example 2

Annuities, loans and saving

Worked example 4.5.2

Problem. A loan of 20 000 currency units is repaid in 5 equal annual instalments at 6 per cent per year. Find the annual instalment.

Mathematical reasoning. Equate the present value of the instalments to the loan and solve for the instalment.

  1. Let the instalment be R, paid at the end of each year for 5 years.
  2. The present value of the instalments is R(1 + 1.06−1^{-1}−1 + … + 1.06−4^{-4}−4).
  3. This is a geometric series with ratio 1/1.06 and 5 terms, summing to 4.2124.
  4. So 20000 = 4.2124R, giving R ≈ 4748.4.
  5. The total repaid is 5 × 4748.4 ≈ 23 742, so the interest is about 3742.

Final answer. about 4748 currency units per year

Interpretation. The same geometric series that grows a saving shrinks a loan, because the ratio is below 1 instead of above it.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.6
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.6

Investigation: infinite sums

Inquiry question

Can infinitely many numbers add to a finite total?

Your task

Investigate four series: ∑\sum∑ 1/n², ∑\sum∑ 1/n, ∑\sum∑ 1/2N^{N}N and ∑\sum∑ (−1)N+1^{N+1}N+1/n. For each, compute the partial sums after 5, 10 and 20 terms and describe the behaviour.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.6
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.6

Investigation: infinite sums

What do you notice?
  • The series of 1/n² converged, while the series of 1/n did not, even though both have terms tending to zero.
  • The geometric series converged fastest, reaching 1 to four decimal places by 20 terms.
  • The alternating series converged by approaching its limit from above and below in turn.
  • The slowest convergence belonged to 1/n², which needed thousands of terms for two decimal places.
Observation. Convergence depends on how fast the terms shrink, not merely on whether they shrink.
Mathematical conclusion

An infinite series converges when its partial sums settle, and the harmonic series diverges because its terms shrink too slowly, as the doubling-block argument shows. Faster shrinkage, as in a geometric series or in 1/n², gives convergence. The threshold between the two behaviours is a rate, which is what the comparison test formalises.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.6 · Investigation: infinite sums
Chapter 4 · 4.6

Investigation: infinite sums

An infinite series is a sequence of partial sums, and it converges when that sequence settles. Adding infinitely many numbers is not a single operation but a limit of finitely many additions, which is why convergence has to be defined rather than assumed.

The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + … diverges even though its terms tend to zero. The terms shrink too slowly for the partial sums to settle, which shows that tending to zero is not sufficient for convergence.

Grouping the harmonic series in blocks of doubling length shows that each block contributes at least a half, so the partial sums exceed every bound. This argument is the standard proof that the harmonic series diverges.

A series whose terms shrink fast enough — geometrically, for instance — does converge, and the threshold between the two behaviours is a rate rather than a size. The comparison test makes the comparison precise.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 4 · 4.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: infinite sums

Worked example 4.6.1

Problem. Show that the partial sums of 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … exceed 2 after enough terms, and explain why this suggests divergence.

Mathematical reasoning. Group the terms in blocks of doubling length and show that each block contributes at least a half.

  1. The first block is the single term 1, which is at least 1/2.
  2. The second block is 1/2, exactly 1/2.
  3. The third block is 1/3 + 1/4 ≥ 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
  4. The fourth block is 1/5 + … + 1/8, which is 8 terms each at least 1/8, so at least 1/2.
  5. Every further block contributes at least 1/2, so the partial sums exceed every bound and the series diverges.

Final answer. the series diverges, because each doubling block contributes at least 1/2

Interpretation. Terms tending to zero is not enough: the harmonic series diverges because its terms do not shrink fast enough.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 4 · 4.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: infinite sums

Worked example 4.6.2

Problem. Find the sum of 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … to infinity and compare it with the harmonic series.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the geometric sum formula and note the contrast with the harmonic series.

  1. The first term is 1/2 and the ratio is 1/2.
  2. Since |r| < 1, the series converges.
  3. The sum is (1/2)/(1 − 1/2) = 1.
  4. The partial sums approach 1 from below, and the remaining distance halves each time.
  5. By contrast the harmonic series, whose terms are larger from the third term onwards, diverges.

Final answer. 1; the harmonic series diverges by comparison

Interpretation. Two series whose terms both tend to zero can behave in opposite ways, and the difference is the rate at which the terms shrink.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.7
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which formula simplifies this sequence or series?

Your task

Take the sequence 2, 6, 18, 54, …. Compute the sum of the first 10 terms, the sum of the first 20 terms, and the sum to infinity if it exists. Then find the smallest n for which the partial sum exceeds 1000, and record the method you used for each part.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 4.7
Chapter 4 · Investigation 4.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • The finite sums grew extremely fast, because r = 3.
  • There was no sum to infinity, because the convergence condition failed.
  • The smallest n for which the sum exceeded 1000 was 7, found by evaluating successive partial sums.
  • The same formula answered three of the four questions.
Observation. The geometric sum formula answers finite questions, and the convergence condition decides whether an infinite question has an answer at all.
Mathematical conclusion

A sequence is summarised by a general term and a series by a sum, and each family has its own formula chosen by the type. The convergence condition |r| < 1 is checked before any sum to infinity is claimed, because the formula is a statement about a limit rather than about an endless addition. Here the sums were 59 048 and 3 486 784 400, and no infinite sum existed.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 4 · 4.7

Mixed practice

Every sequence question begins by identifying the type: constant difference means arithmetic, constant ratio means geometric, and neither means the rule must be found some other way. Identifying the type is choosing the formula.

Series questions require the convergence condition to be checked before the sum formula is applied. Applying a sum-to-infinity formula to a divergent series produces a number that is not a sum.

The two families of formulas — arithmetic and geometric — cover a large part of what sequences and series can do. The remaining cases are handled by the general idea of a partial sum and its limit.

Mixed practice is where the type is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 4 · 4.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 4.7.1

Problem. A sequence has u(n) = 3n − 1. Find the sum of the first 40 terms.

Mathematical reasoning. Recognise the sequence as arithmetic and apply the sum formula.

  1. u(n) = 3n − 1 has common difference 3, so it is arithmetic.
  2. The first term is u(1) = 2 and the last is u(40) = 119.
  3. The sum is (40/2)(2 + 119) = 20 × 121 = 2420.
  4. Check by splitting: 3 × (sum of 1 to 40) − 40 = 3 × 820 − 40 = 2460 − 40 = 2420.

Final answer. 2420

Interpretation. The check uses a different route to the same total, which is what makes it a check.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook4.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 4 · 4.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 4.7.2

Problem. Find the sum to infinity of 27 + 18 + 12 + 8 + …

Mathematical reasoning. Find the ratio, check the condition, and apply the formula.

  1. The ratio is 18/27 = 2/3.
  2. Since |2/3| < 1, the series converges.
  3. The sum to infinity is 27/(1 − 2/3) = 27/(1/3) = 81.
  4. Check with partial sums: after 4 terms the sum is 65, and after 10 terms it is 79.4, approaching 81.

Final answer. 81

Interpretation. The convergence check comes first, and it is what licenses the formula.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 4 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • An arithmetic sequence has a common difference d, and u(n) = u(1) + (n − 1)d.
  • A geometric sequence has a common ratio r, and u(n) = u(1) r^(n−1).
  • The sum of an arithmetic series is (n/2)(u(1) + u(n)).
  • The sum of a finite geometric series is u(1)(rN^{N}N − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠\neq= 1.
  • A geometric series converges to u(1)/(1 − r) exactly when |r| < 1.
  • The harmonic series diverges even though its terms tend to zero.
  • An annuity accumulates to P((1 + i)N^{N}N − 1)/i.
  • A loan repayment is the same formula read backwards.

Vocabulary

sequence · term · arithmetic · common difference · geometric · common ratio · series · partial sum · sigma notation · index · convergent · divergent · sum to infinity · annuity · instalment · present value · harmonic series
