MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 5 · Quadratic Inequalities and Linear Programming
Chapter 5 · Part II · Thinking with models
05

Quadratic Inequalities and Linear Programming

An inequality describes a set of possibilities rather than a single value. A system of inequalities bounds that set, and a linear objective function turns the bounded set into a choice.

Engage

A workshop makes two kinds of basket. Each large basket uses 3 units of cane and 2 hours of labour; each small one uses 1 unit of cane and 1 hour. Only 24 units of cane and 20 hours are available. How many of each should be made to earn the most, and how do you know no better choice exists?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Relationships
Related concepts: Change · Equivalence · System
Global context: Globalization and sustainability
Global context exploration: production planning under resource limits

Statement of inquiry: A system of inequalities describes what is possible; a linear objective turns possibility into choice. Solving a quadratic inequality and optimising under linear constraints are the same habit: compare, bound, and justify.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What does the solution set of a quadratic inequality look like, and how is it found?
  • Conceptual: Why does a linear objective function on a bounded feasible region take its extreme values at a vertex?
  • Debatable: If an optimal plan ignores the workers' preferences, is it still the best plan?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to decide how much of each product a workshop should make, students must translate resource limits into inequalities, bound the feasible region, and justify the optimal choice against alternatives.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.1
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.1

Quadratic inequalities in one variable

Inquiry question

How does a graph solve an inequality?

Your task

Take six quadratic inequalities of your own: two with two distinct roots, one with a repeated root, one with no real roots, one with a negative leading coefficient and one in the form of a fraction whose denominator changes sign. Solve each, and record the solution set and the reason the sign behaves as it does.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.1
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.1

Quadratic inequalities in one variable

What do you notice?
  • Two of the six had two distinct roots, and their solution sets were the intervals between or beyond them.
  • The repeated-root case excluded exactly one value.
  • The no-real-roots case was true everywhere, because the parabola never crossed the axis.
  • The fraction case was not a quadratic at all, and its sign was decided by the denominator alone.
Observation. The sign of a quadratic is decided by its leading coefficient and its roots, and a repeated root leaves the sign unchanged.
Mathematical conclusion

A quadratic inequality is solved by finding the roots and reading the sign from the shape of the parabola: between the roots for an upward-opening parabola with the expression negative, and beyond them for the expression positive. The leading coefficient and the number of real roots decide the pattern, and the strictness of the inequality decides whether the roots themselves are included.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.1 · Quadratic inequalities in one variable
Chapter 5 · 5.1

Quadratic inequalities in one variable

A quadratic inequality such as x² − 3x − 4 < 0 asks for the values of x for which a quadratic expression is negative. The boundary of the solution set is the set of roots, and the sign of the expression between and beyond the roots is constant.

The sign of a quadratic is decided by its leading coefficient and by the number of real roots. With two distinct roots the sign alternates across them; with a repeated root the sign does not change; with no real roots the sign is constant everywhere.

The method is to find the roots, sketch the parabola, and read off the intervals where the graph lies below or above the axis. The sketch is the justification, not a decoration.

A strict inequality excludes the boundary values and a non-strict one includes them, which is recorded with round and solid markers on a number line. The distinction matters at the endpoints only, but it matters there completely.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 5 · 5.1 · Worked example 1

Quadratic inequalities in one variable

Worked example 5.1.1

Problem. Solve x² − 3x − 4 < 0.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the roots, sketch the parabola, and read off where it lies below the axis.

  1. Factorise: x² − 3x − 4 = (x − 4)(x + 1), so the roots are x = −1 and x = 4.
  2. The parabola opens upwards, so it is negative between its roots.
  3. Hence the solution is −1 < x < 4.
  4. The endpoints are excluded because the inequality is strict.
  5. Check: at x = 0 the expression is −4 < 0, as required.

Final answer. −1 < x < 4

Interpretation. The sketch turns an algebraic question into a reading question, and the reading is what is justified.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 5 · 5.1 · Worked example 2

Quadratic inequalities in one variable

Worked example 5.1.2

Problem. Solve x² + 4x + 4 ≥ 0.

Mathematical reasoning. A perfect square is never negative, so the inequality holds everywhere.

  1. Factorise: x² + 4x + 4 = (x + 2)².
  2. A square is never negative, so (x + 2)² ≥ 0 for every x.
  3. The solution set is therefore all real x.
  4. The single value x = −2 makes the expression zero and is included because the inequality is non-strict.
  5. Check: at x = 0 the expression is 4 ≥ 0, as required.

Final answer. all real x

Interpretation. A repeated root means the parabola touches the axis and turns back, so the sign does not change.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.2
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.2

Inequalities in two variables

Inquiry question

What does the solution set of a linear inequality look like?

Your task

Take a workshop that makes two products, A and B, with x of A and y of B. Write and draw a system of inequalities of your own using at least four constraints of these kinds: an upper limit on x, an upper limit on y, a shared resource limit, and a minimum output requirement. Shade the feasible region, label its vertices, and test one interior point.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.2
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.2

Inequalities in two variables

What do you notice?
  • Two constraints were shared resources, so their boundary lines sloped downwards.
  • The minimum-output constraints were vertical or horizontal lines.
  • The feasible region was a polygon whose vertices were intersections of pairs of boundary lines.
  • The interior point satisfied every constraint, confirming that the shaded side of each line was chosen correctly.
Observation. Each constraint is a half-plane, and the feasible region is their intersection.
Mathematical conclusion

A system of linear inequalities is solved by the intersection of its half-planes, and each half-plane is chosen by testing one point. The resulting feasible region is a polygon whose vertices are the intersections of its boundary lines, and those vertices are what an objective function is evaluated at.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.2 · Inequalities in two variables
Chapter 5 · 5.2

Inequalities in two variables

A linear inequality in two variables, such as 2x + 3y ≤ 12, describes a half-plane bounded by the line 2x + 3y = 12. The line is drawn solid when the inequality is non-strict and dashed when it is strict.

Which side of the line is the solution region is decided by testing one point, conventionally the origin when the line does not pass through it. The test is a single substitution, and it settles the question for the whole half-plane.

The boundary line itself is part of the solution exactly when the inequality is non-strict, so ≤ and ≥ include the line and < and > exclude it. The distinction is visible in the drawing and decisive in the algebra.

A system of linear inequalities is satisfied by the points that lie in every half-plane at once, so its solution set is the intersection of the regions. This intersection is the feasible region, and it is usually a polygon.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 5 · 5.2 · Worked example 1

Inequalities in two variables

Worked example 5.2.1

Problem. Shade the region satisfying x + 2y ≤ 8, x ≥ 1 and y ≥ 0, and find the coordinates of its vertices.

Mathematical reasoning. Draw each boundary, test which side satisfies each inequality, and find the intersections.

  1. The line x + 2y = 8 meets the x-axis at (8, 0) and the y-axis at (0, 4).
  2. x ≥ 1 excludes everything to the left of the vertical line x = 1.
  3. y ≥ 0 excludes everything below the x-axis.
  4. Testing (4, 1): 4 + 2 = 6 ≤ 8, so the region containing (4, 1) is kept.
  5. The vertices are (1, 0), (8, 0) and (1, 3.5).

Final answer. a triangle with vertices (1, 0), (8, 0) and (1, 3.5)

Interpretation. The region is the intersection of three half-planes, and each vertex is the meeting of two of its boundaries.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 5 · 5.2 · Worked example 2

Inequalities in two variables

Worked example 5.2.2

Problem. Explain why the system x + y ≤ 5 and x + y ≥ 8 has no solution, and draw what happens.

Mathematical reasoning. The two inequalities demand contradictory bounds on the same quantity, so no point satisfies both.

  1. The first inequality demands x + y ≤ 5.
  2. The second demands x + y ≥ 8.
  3. No number is both at most 5 and at least 8.
  4. So no point (x, y) satisfies both, and the feasible region is empty.
  5. The two boundary lines are parallel and lie on opposite sides of the strip between them.

Final answer. no solution; the feasible region is empty

Interpretation. An empty feasible region is a meaningful answer: it says the constraints cannot all be met.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.3
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.3

Feasible regions and vertices

Inquiry question

Why does the optimum lie at a vertex?

Your task

Take the feasible region bounded by x + y ≤ 6, x + 3y ≤ 9, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Find its vertices, then maximise P = 2x + y, minimise it, and then find the objective that is parallel to one of the edges and explain what that means for the number of solutions.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.3
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.3

Feasible regions and vertices

What do you notice?
  • The maximum was 12 at (6, 0) and the minimum was 0 at (0, 0).
  • The objective 2x + y had slope −2, while the edges had slopes −1 and −1/3, so no edge was parallel to it.
  • The objective x + 3y was parallel to the edge from (0, 3) to (4.5, 1.5).
  • Every point of that edge gave the same value, 9, so there were infinitely many solutions.
Observation. A linear objective on a bounded polygon takes its extremes at vertices, unless it is parallel to an edge.
Mathematical conclusion

A linear objective function takes constant values on parallel iso-lines, so its extremes on a bounded feasible region occur at the last point of contact, which is a vertex. When the objective is parallel to an edge, every point of that edge is optimal and the solution is not unique. Here the maximum of 2x + y was 12 and the minimum was 0.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.3 · Feasible regions and vertices
Chapter 5 · 5.3

Feasible regions and vertices

A linear objective function P = ax + by takes constant values along parallel lines called iso-lines. As the line moves across the feasible region, P changes steadily, so its largest and smallest values on a bounded region occur at the last point of contact.

The last point of contact of an iso-line with a polygon is always a vertex, because a polygon's boundary consists of line segments and the extreme point of a line segment is an endpoint. Hence the optimum is at a vertex, or along a whole edge when the objective is parallel to it.

The method is therefore to find the vertices of the feasible region and evaluate the objective at each one. The vertex with the largest value gives the maximum, and the one with the smallest value gives the minimum.

When the objective is parallel to an edge, every point of that edge is optimal, and there are infinitely many solutions. This case is reported as an edge rather than as a single vertex, because the choice within the edge is free.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 5 · 5.3 · Worked example 1

Feasible regions and vertices

Worked example 5.3.1

Problem. Maximise P = 3x + 5y subject to x + 2y ≤ 8, x ≥ 1, y ≥ 0 and x ≤ 5.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the vertices of the feasible region and evaluate the objective at each.

  1. The constraints give the vertices (1, 0), (5, 0), (5, 1.5) and (1, 3.5).
  2. Evaluate P = 3x + 5y at each: 3, 15, 22.5 and 20.5.
  3. The largest value is 22.5, at (5, 1.5).
  4. Check that (5, 1.5) is feasible: 5 + 3 = 8 ≤ 8, 5 ≤ 5, 1.5 ≥ 0 and 5 ≥ 1.
  5. So the maximum is 22.5, achieved at x = 5 and y = 1.5.

Final answer. maximum P = 22.5 at (5, 1.5)

Interpretation. Evaluating the objective at the vertices is both necessary and sufficient for a linear objective on a polygon.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 5 · 5.3 · Worked example 2

Feasible regions and vertices

Worked example 5.3.2

Problem. Minimise C = 2x + 4y subject to x + y ≥ 4, x ≤ 3, y ≤ 5, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, and identify the case that arises.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the vertices, evaluate the objective, and check whether any edge is parallel to the objective.

  1. The constraints give the vertices (0, 4), (3, 1), (3, 5) and (0, 5).
  2. Evaluate C = 2x + 4y: 16, 10, 26 and 20.
  3. The smallest value is 10, at (3, 1).
  4. The objective 2x + 4y has slope −1/2, and the edge from (3, 1) to (0, 4) has slope −1, so no edge is parallel to the objective.
  5. Hence the minimum is unique, at (3, 1).

Final answer. minimum C = 10 at (3, 1)

Interpretation. The check for a parallel edge is part of the justification, because it rules out infinitely many solutions.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.4
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.4

Linear programming

Inquiry question

How is a real problem turned into a linear program?

Your task

Formulate and solve a linear program of your own for a school fair. Two stalls sell drinks and snacks. Each drink needs 1 unit of storage and 2 minutes of service; each snack needs 2 units of storage and 1 minute. There are 60 units of storage and 60 minutes. Profit is 2 per drink and 3 per snack. Find the optimal plan and the maximum profit.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.4
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.4

Linear programming

What do you notice?
  • Both constraints were used at the optimum, so the plan sat at their intersection.
  • The plan was 20 drinks and 20 snacks, giving a profit of 100.
  • The vertex (30, 0) used all the service time but left storage unused, so it was not optimal.
  • The vertex (0, 30) used all the storage but left service time unused.
Observation. The optimum is the vertex that uses the resources most profitably, and it usually sits where two constraints meet.
Mathematical conclusion

A linear program is formulated by naming the decision variables, writing one inequality per limit, and stating the objective. It is solved by finding the vertices of the feasible region and evaluating the objective at each. Here the optimal plan was 20 drinks and 20 snacks for a profit of 100.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.4 · Linear programming
Chapter 5 · 5.4

Linear programming

A linear program has three parts: decision variables, a linear objective function, and linear constraints. Writing these down in that order is the whole translation, and the relationships between the resources are what the constraints record.

The constraints come from the limits of the situation: availability of resources, minimum outputs, and the non-negativity of the quantities. Each limit is a relationship between the variables, and a limit that is not stated is a limit that has been assumed away.

The solution of a linear program is the vertex that optimises the objective, together with the statement of the optimal value. Reporting the value without the point that achieves it, or the point without the value, is an incomplete answer.

Sensitivity analysis asks how much a constraint can change before the optimum moves. The answer is read from the slack in the binding constraints, and it is what makes a recommendation robust.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 5 · 5.4 · Worked example 1

Linear programming

Worked example 5.4.1

Problem. A workshop makes tables and chairs. A table needs 4 hours of carpentry and 2 of finishing; a chair needs 2 and 1. There are 40 hours of carpentry and 15 of finishing. Profit is 30 per table and 20 per chair. Formulate the problem and solve it.

Mathematical reasoning. Define the variables, write the constraints and the objective, then solve by evaluating the vertices.

  1. Let x be the number of tables and y the number of chairs.
  2. The constraints are 4x + 2y ≤ 40, 2x + y ≤ 15, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.
  3. The objective is P = 30x + 20y.
  4. The vertices of the feasible region are (0, 0), (7.5, 0), (5, 5) and (0, 15).
  5. Evaluating P gives 0, 225, 250 and 300, so the maximum is 300 at (0, 15), that is 15 chairs and no tables.

Final answer. 15 chairs and no tables, profit 300

Interpretation. The optimum is a vertex, and reporting the plan without the profit, or the profit without the plan, is incomplete.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 5 · 5.4 · Worked example 2

Linear programming

Worked example 5.4.2

Problem. A farmer has 100 hectares to plant with wheat and barley. Wheat needs 3 units of fertiliser per hectare and barley 2, with 240 units available. Profit is 400 per hectare of wheat and 300 of barley. Formulate and solve.

Mathematical reasoning. Formulate with two variables and two resource constraints, then evaluate the vertices.

  1. Let w be the hectares of wheat and b the hectares of barley.
  2. The constraints are w + b ≤ 100, 3w + 2b ≤ 240, w ≥ 0 and b ≥ 0.
  3. The objective is P = 400w + 300b.
  4. The vertices are (0, 0), (80, 0), (40, 60) and (0, 100).
  5. Evaluating P gives 0, 32000, 34000 and 30000, so the maximum is 34000 at (40, 60).

Final answer. 40 ha of wheat and 60 ha of barley, profit 34 000

Interpretation. Both resource constraints are used at the optimum, so the solution sits at the intersection of both boundaries.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.5
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.5

Modelling and optimisation

Inquiry question

When is a linear model the right model?

Your task

Take the problem of maximising P = 5x + 4y subject to x + y ≤ 7, x + 3y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Solve the relaxed problem, then find the integer optimum, and then find how much the right-hand side of the second constraint can fall before the optimum changes.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.5
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.5

Modelling and optimisation

What do you notice?
  • The relaxed optimum was not a lattice point, so rounding was needed.
  • Rounding (4.5, 2.5) down to (4, 2) gave 28, but (5, 2) gave 33, so rounding was not optimal.
  • The true integer optimum was (5, 2) with profit 33.
  • The binding constraint could fall by 1 unit before the optimum moved.
Observation. Rounding a relaxed optimum is not generally optimal, and the integer optimum must be found by testing nearby lattice points.
Mathematical conclusion

A linear model is appropriate when the contributions are independent and the range is limited, and the modeller must check both. When the variables are whole numbers, the relaxed optimum is an upper bound and the true optimum is found by testing nearby lattice points. Here the relaxed optimum was 32.5 at (4.5, 2.5) and the integer optimum was 33 at (5, 2).

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.5 · Modelling and optimisation
Chapter 5 · 5.5

Modelling and optimisation

A linear model assumes that the contribution of each variable is independent of the level of the others, so that doubling the inputs doubles the output. This assumption gives an equivalence between the model and the situation that holds only over a limited range, and the range is part of the model.

Real problems rarely have exactly linear constraints. Costs have fixed components, resources have minimum order quantities, and outputs are whole numbers. Each of these breaks linearity, and the modeller must decide whether the break matters.

When the variables must be whole numbers, the optimum of the relaxed problem is an upper bound, and the true integer optimum is found by testing the nearby lattice points. Rounding the relaxed optimum is not in general optimal.

Sensitivity analysis reports how much a constraint can change before the optimum moves. It converts a single answer into a recommendation, because it says how fragile the answer is.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 5 · 5.5 · Worked example 1

Modelling and optimisation

Worked example 5.5.1

Problem. A factory makes two products with profit 8 and 12 per unit. The constraints are x + y ≤ 10, x + 2y ≤ 14, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Solve, and then solve again with the requirement that x and y are whole numbers.

Mathematical reasoning. Solve the relaxed problem, then check whether the optimum is a whole-number point.

  1. The relaxed vertices are (0, 0), (10, 0), (6, 4) and (0, 7).
  2. Evaluating P = 8x + 12y gives 0, 80, 96 and 84.
  3. The relaxed maximum is 96 at (6, 4).
  4. Both coordinates are whole numbers, so the integer optimum is the same point.
  5. The integer optimum is x = 6, y = 4 with profit 96.

Final answer. x = 6, y = 4, profit 96 (the same for both problems)

Interpretation. When the relaxed optimum happens to be a lattice point, the integer problem needs no further work — but that has to be checked.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 5 · 5.5 · Worked example 2

Modelling and optimisation

Worked example 5.5.2

Problem. In the same problem, suppose a third constraint 2x + y ≤ 13 is added. Find the new optimum and explain the change.

Mathematical reasoning. Add the constraint, recompute the vertices, and re-evaluate.

  1. The new constraint 2x + y ≤ 13 cuts off the old optimum at (6, 4), since 2(6) + 4 = 16 > 13.
  2. The new vertices are (0, 0), (6.5, 0), (5, 3) and (0, 7).
  3. Evaluating P gives 0, 52, 76 and 84.
  4. The new maximum is 84 at (0, 7).
  5. The profit has fallen from 96 to 84, and the plan has changed completely.

Final answer. maximum 84 at (0, 7)

Interpretation. Adding one constraint can move the optimum to the opposite corner, which is why sensitivity analysis matters.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.6
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.6

Investigation: integer solutions and the vertex

Inquiry question

When is the vertex the answer, and when is it only a bound?

Your task

Take P = 5x + 4y with constraints x + 2y ≤ 9, 2x + y ≤ 9, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Find the relaxed optimum, then find the integer optimum by testing lattice points, and then find a second problem of your own where rounding the relaxed optimum gives the wrong answer.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.6
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.6

Investigation: integer solutions and the vertex

What do you notice?
  • The relaxed vertex was (3, 3) with P = 27, which is a lattice point.
  • But (4, 2) is also feasible and gives 28, which is larger.
  • So the relaxed optimum was not the integer optimum even though it was a lattice point, because the objective was not maximised there.
  • The true integer optimum was (4, 2) with P = 28.
Observation. The relaxed optimum is an upper bound, and the integer optimum is found by testing lattice points near it.
Mathematical conclusion

The vertex of a relaxed linear program is an upper bound on the integer optimum, and it is exact only when the vertex is itself an optimal lattice point. Otherwise the integer optimum must be found by testing nearby lattice points, and rounding the vertex is a heuristic that can fail. Here the integer optimum was 28 at (4, 2), above the relaxed vertex value of 27.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.6 · Investigation: integer solutions and the vertex
Chapter 5 · 5.6

Investigation: integer solutions and the vertex

The vertex of a relaxed linear program is an upper bound on the integer optimum, because the integer points are a subset of the feasible region. The bound is exact only when the vertex is itself a lattice point.

When the vertex is not a lattice point, the integer optimum is found by testing the lattice points near it. In two variables this is a short list, and in higher dimensions it becomes a substantial problem in its own right.

Rounding the vertex is a heuristic, not a method. Rounding down can leave the feasible region, and rounding to the nearest lattice point can miss the true optimum, as a single example shows.

The gap between the relaxed and integer optima is a measure of how much the whole-number requirement costs. When the gap is small, the relaxation is a good guide; when it is large, the problem needs a genuine integer method.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 5 · 5.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: integer solutions and the vertex

Worked example 5.6.1

Problem. Maximise P = 4x + 3y subject to 2x + y ≤ 7, x + 2y ≤ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Find the relaxed optimum and then the integer optimum.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the relaxed vertex and check whether it has whole-number coordinates.

  1. Solving the two boundary equations gives x = 2 and y = 3.
  2. The relaxed optimum is (2, 3) with P = 4(2) + 3(3) = 17.
  3. Both coordinates are whole numbers, so the integer optimum is the same point.
  4. The nearby lattice points give smaller values, confirming the result.
  5. The integer optimum is x = 2, y = 3 with P = 17.

Final answer. relaxed and integer optima both at (2, 3) with P = 17

Interpretation. When the vertex is a lattice point the relaxation is exact, and that is the best possible case.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 5 · 5.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: integer solutions and the vertex

Worked example 5.6.2

Problem. Maximise P = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 5, x ≤ 3.4, y ≤ 3.4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Find the relaxed optimum and the integer optimum, and explain the difference.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the relaxed optimum, then test the lattice points near it.

  1. The relaxed optimum is where x = 3.4 meets x + y = 5, so y = 1.6.
  2. The relaxed value is P = 3(3.4) + 2(1.6) = 13.4.
  3. This point is not a lattice point, so it is not a feasible integer solution.
  4. Testing nearby lattice points: (3, 2) gives 13, (2, 3) gives 12 and (3, 1) gives 11.
  5. The integer optimum is (3, 2) with P = 13, which is 0.4 below the relaxed bound.

Final answer. relaxed optimum 13.4 at (3.4, 1.6); integer optimum 13 at (3, 2)

Interpretation. The gap of 0.4 is the cost of the whole-number requirement, and rounding the relaxed point to (3, 2) happens to work here but not in general.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.7
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which method does this problem need?

Your task

Take a recycling centre that processes glass and plastic. Each tonne of glass needs 2 hours of sorting and earns 40 currency units; each tonne of plastic needs 3 hours and earns 50. There are 36 hours and at least 4 tonnes must be processed. Formulate, solve, and then re-solve with the requirement that the tonnages are whole numbers.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 5.7
Chapter 5 · Investigation 5.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • The plastic earned more per hour, so the optimum put everything into plastic.
  • The relaxed optimum was already a lattice point, so the integer problem needed no extra work.
  • The minimum-output constraint was satisfied automatically.
  • The profit of 600 used all 36 hours.
Observation. The optimum uses the binding resource fully, and the integer check confirms whether the relaxed answer stands.
Mathematical conclusion

An inequality problem is solved by identifying its type first: roots and sign for a quadratic inequality, region and vertices for a linear system. The answer to a linear program is the point, the value and the feasibility check together, and when whole numbers are required the relaxed optimum is only a bound. Here the optimum was 12 tonnes of plastic for a profit of 600.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 5 · 5.7

Mixed practice

Quadratic inequalities are solved by roots and sign; linear systems are solved by region and vertices. Recognising which of the two a question needs is the first step, and the two methods are easily confused because both involve graphs.

A linear programming answer has three parts: the point, the value and the justification that the point is feasible. Missing any one of the three leaves the answer incomplete.

When a problem asks for whole numbers, the relaxed optimum is a bound and the answer must be checked against lattice points. Reporting the relaxed optimum as the answer is a category error.

Mixed practice is where the method is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 5 · 5.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 5.7.1

Problem. Solve 2x² − 5x − 3 > 0.

Mathematical reasoning. Factorise, find the roots, and read the sign from the shape of the parabola.

  1. Factorise: 2x² − 5x − 3 = (2x + 1)(x − 3).
  2. The roots are x = −1/2 and x = 3.
  3. The parabola opens upwards, so the expression is positive outside the roots.
  4. Hence x < −1/2 or x > 3.
  5. Check: at x = 0 the expression is −3, which is not positive, so the interval between the roots is correctly excluded.

Final answer. x < −1/2 or x > 3

Interpretation. The check confirms the interval that is excluded, which is as informative as the one that is included.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook5.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 5 · 5.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 5.7.2

Problem. A bakery makes loaves and rolls. A loaf needs 200 g of flour and a roll 50 g, with 10 kg available. Profit is 3 per loaf and 1 per roll, and at least 20 items must be made. Formulate and solve.

Mathematical reasoning. Formulate with the flour limit and the minimum output, then evaluate the vertices.

  1. Let x be loaves and y be rolls. The flour limit is 200x + 50y ≤ 10000.
  2. The minimum output is x + y ≥ 20, with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.
  3. The objective is P = 3x + y.
  4. The vertices are (0, 20), (0, 200), (50, 0) and (20, 0), giving P = 20, 200, 150 and 60.
  5. The maximum is 200 at (0, 200), that is 200 rolls and no loaves.

Final answer. 200 rolls and no loaves, profit 200

Interpretation. The profit per gram of flour is higher for rolls, so the optimum puts everything into rolls, and the minimum-output constraint is satisfied automatically.

Applying chapter 5

These tasks use inequalities and linear programming. Draw the region, label the constraints, evaluate the objective at each vertex, and justify the choice.

A1 · The workshop plan

A workshop makes two products. Product A needs 2 hours of cutting and 1 of assembly; product B needs 1 of cutting and 2 of assembly. There are 40 hours of cutting and 36 of assembly. Criteria A and D · formulate, solve by vertices, and justify the recommendation.

A2 · The fair's budget

A school fair has a budget of 300 currency units and 20 volunteers. A food stall costs 40 and needs 3 volunteers; a games stall costs 25 and needs 2. The fair must have at least 2 food stalls. Maximise the total income, modelled as 90 per food stall and 60 per games stall, and comment on whether the model is realistic.

Criteria A and C · formulate, solve, and evaluate the model's assumptions.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 5 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A quadratic inequality is solved by finding the roots and reading the sign from the parabola.
  • A linear inequality in two variables describes a half-plane bounded by a line.
  • A system of inequalities is solved by the intersection of its half-planes.
  • A linear objective takes constant values on parallel iso-lines.
  • The optimum of a linear program on a bounded region is at a vertex, or along an edge parallel to the objective.
  • When the objective is parallel to an edge there are infinitely many solutions.
  • An integer optimum is found by testing lattice points near the relaxed vertex.
  • Rounding a relaxed optimum is a heuristic, not a method.

Vocabulary

inequality · solution set · feasible region · vertex · constraint · objective function · iso-line · linear program · decision variable · binding constraint · slack · sensitivity · integer programming · lattice point · relaxed problem

Chapter 5 · Review

Returning to the statement of inquiry

Statement of inquiry

A system of inequalities describes what is possible; a linear objective turns possibility into choice. Solving a quadratic inequality and optimising under linear constraints are the same habit: compare, bound, and justify.

Reflect on the chapter

Answer in your own words, using evidence from this chapter.

  • Write the statement of inquiry for this chapter in your own words.
  • Which mathematical ideas from this chapter did you use to understand it? Name at least two.
  • How did the key concept of relationships and the related concepts of change, equivalence and system appear in your work?

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 6 · Circle Geometry and Geometric Proof
Chapter 6 · Part III · Spatial reasoning
06

Circle Geometry and Geometric Proof

A circle is the set of points at a fixed distance from a centre, so all its points lie in one space at one distance. That single definition generates a small number of theorems, and those theorems justify every measurement made in a circle.

Engage

A stained-glass window is designed as a circle with chords meeting at a point. The designer needs to know the angle between two chords before cutting the glass. Which property of the circle decides it, and how is that property proved?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Logic
Related concepts: Space · Generalisation · Justification
Global context: Personal and cultural expression
Global context exploration: the geometry of architecture and ornament

Statement of inquiry: A circle conceals equal angles and fixed distances; a few theorems, proved from radii and triangles, let us deduce measurements and justify every claim.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What do the angle at the centre, the angle in a semicircle and the alternate segment theorems say?
  • Conceptual: Why does a tangent meet a radius at right angles, and what does a proof need in order to be complete?
  • Debatable: If a diagram convinces you a claim is true, is a proof still needed?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to justify a measurement in an architectural drawing, students must identify the circle property that applies, state it as a general claim, and construct a proof from radii and triangles.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.1
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.1

Angles in circles

Inquiry question

What relationships between angles does a circle force?

Your task

Draw a circle with centre O and three points A, B and C on it, with C on the major arc AB. Measure the angle AOB, the angle ACB and the angle in the alternate segment. Repeat for three different positions of C and for two different arcs, and record the relationships you find.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.1
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.1

Angles in circles

What do you notice?
  • The angle at C did not change when C moved along the same arc.
  • The angle at C was always half the angle at the centre.
  • The two angles at C, one on each arc, always summed to 180 degrees.
  • Changing the arc changed every angle, but not the relationship between them.
Observation. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, and the two angles in the two segments are supplementary.
Mathematical conclusion

The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc, and this one theorem explains angles in the same segment, the right angle in a semicircle, and the supplementary opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral. The measurements confirmed it in every configuration, with the angle at C always half the centre angle.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.1 · Angles in circles
Chapter 6 · 6.1

Angles in circles

The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference standing on the same arc. This is the fundamental circle theorem, and the others are consequences of it, so one generalisation covers many cases.

The proof splits into cases according to whether the centre lies on a side of the inscribed angle. Each case reduces to an isosceles triangle and the exterior angle theorem, and together the cases cover every configuration.

Angles in the same segment are equal, because each is half the same angle at the centre. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, because the angle at the centre is 180 degrees.

A cyclic quadrilateral has opposite angles summing to 180 degrees, because the two opposite angles stand on arcs that together make the whole circumference. This is the theorem that makes cyclic quadrilaterals recognisable.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 6 · 6.1 · Worked example 1

Angles in circles

Worked example 6.1.1

Problem. An angle at the centre of a circle is 118 degrees and stands on the same arc as an angle at the circumference. Find the angle at the circumference.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the angle at the centre theorem directly.

  1. The angle at the centre is 118 degrees and the angle at the circumference stands on the same arc.
  2. By the theorem, the centre angle is twice the circumference angle.
  3. So the circumference angle is 118 ÷ 2 = 59 degrees.
  4. Check: 2 × 59 = 118, as required.
  5. A point on the other arc would give 180 − 59 = 121 degrees, because opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180.

Final answer. 59 degrees

Interpretation. The theorem relates two angles through the arc they share, which is why naming the arc is part of the justification.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 6 · 6.1 · Worked example 2

Angles in circles

Worked example 6.1.2

Problem. Prove that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

Mathematical reasoning. Treat the diameter as an arc of 180 degrees and apply the angle at the centre theorem.

  1. Let AB be a diameter and C a point on the circle distinct from A and B.
  2. The arc AB is a semicircle, so the angle AOB at the centre is 180 degrees.
  3. The angle ACB stands on the same arc AB.
  4. By the angle at the centre theorem, angle ACB is half of 180 degrees.
  5. Hence angle ACB is 90 degrees, as required.

Final answer. the angle in a semicircle is 90 degrees

Interpretation. The proof names the theorem it uses and the arc it applies to, which is what makes it a proof rather than a description.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.2
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.2

Cyclic quadrilaterals

Inquiry question

What does a quadrilateral being cyclic tell you?

Your task

Draw four cyclic quadrilaterals of your own, each with a different shape, and measure all four interior angles of each. Check that opposite angles are supplementary in every case. Then draw one quadrilateral that is not cyclic and show that the property fails.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.2
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.2

Cyclic quadrilaterals

What do you notice?
  • Every cyclic quadrilateral had opposite angles summing to 180 degrees.
  • The non-cyclic quadrilateral failed one of the two pairs, which was enough to rule it out.
  • The test is an if and only if, so failing it proves non-cyclicity.
  • The irregular case confirmed the property is not restricted to symmetric shapes.
Observation. Cyclicity is decided by one pair of supplementary opposite angles.
Mathematical conclusion

A quadrilateral is cyclic exactly when a pair of opposite angles is supplementary, and then both pairs are. The exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle, which is the quickest way to find an unknown angle. The measurements confirmed the property in every cyclic case and its failure in the non-cyclic one.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.2 · Cyclic quadrilaterals
Chapter 6 · 6.2

Cyclic quadrilaterals

A cyclic quadrilateral is one whose four vertices lie on a circle, so its four points share one space of fixed radius. Its defining property is that opposite angles sum to 180 degrees, and the converse is also true: a quadrilateral with supplementary opposite angles is cyclic.

The proof of the defining property uses the angle at the centre theorem twice. Each opposite pair of angles stands on arcs that together form the whole circumference, so their halves sum to 180 degrees.

The converse gives a test for cyclicity that is used constantly: if one pair of opposite angles is supplementary, the fourth vertex lies on the circle through the other three. This is how a circle is constructed to pass through given points.

An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle, because the interior angle is supplementary to its opposite and the exterior angle is supplementary to the interior. This is the property used to find an unknown angle quickly.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 6 · 6.2 · Worked example 1

Cyclic quadrilaterals

Worked example 6.2.1

Problem. A cyclic quadrilateral has angles 3x, 5x, 2x and 4x in order. Find each angle.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the supplementary property on both pairs of opposite angles.

  1. Opposite angles sum to 180, so 3x + 2x = 180, giving x = 36.
  2. Check the other pair: 5x + 4x = 9x = 9 × 36 = 324, which is not 180, so the ordering must be reconsidered.
  3. The angles are in order around the quadrilateral, so opposite pairs are (3x, 2x) and (5x, 4x).
  4. Both pairs must sum to 180, which requires 5x = 180, so x = 36, and then 5x = 180 is impossible for a genuine quadrilateral angle.
  5. The only consistent reading is 3x + 5x = 180 and 2x + 4x = 180, both giving x = 22.5, so the angles are 67.5, 112.5, 45 and 90 degrees.

Final answer. 67.5°, 112.5°, 45° and 90°

Interpretation. Naming which pairs are opposite is part of the justification, and the two conditions must be checked together.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 6 · 6.2 · Worked example 2

Cyclic quadrilaterals

Worked example 6.2.2

Problem. Prove that an exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the cyclic property and the straight-line property together.

  1. Let ABCD be cyclic and let AE extend the side DA beyond A.
  2. Then angle DAB + angle BCD = 180 degrees, because ABCD is cyclic.
  3. Also angle DAE + angle DAB = 180 degrees, because they lie on a straight line.
  4. Both angle DAE and angle BCD equal 180 degrees minus angle DAB.
  5. Hence angle DAE = angle BCD, as required.

Final answer. the exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle

Interpretation. The proof chains two known facts, and each step cites the fact it uses.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.3
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.3

Tangents and radii

Inquiry question

Why is a tangent perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact?

Your task

Draw a circle and an external point P. Draw the two tangents from P, touching at A and B. Measure PA, PB, the angles at P and the angles at A and B. Repeat for three different positions of P and record what stays the same and what changes.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.3
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.3

Tangents and radii

What do you notice?
  • The two tangent lengths were equal in every case.
  • The angles at the points of contact were always 90 degrees.
  • The angle at P shrank as P moved away from the circle.
  • Moving P to the other side changed nothing except the orientation.
Observation. The tangent lengths from a point are equal, and the tangent is always perpendicular to the radius.
Mathematical conclusion

A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, which is proved by contradiction from the definition of a tangent. Two consequences follow immediately: the two tangents from an external point are equal, and the line from the centre to that point bisects the angle between them. The measurements confirmed both, with PA = PB in every case.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.3 · Tangents and radii
Chapter 6 · 6.3

Tangents and radii

A tangent to a circle is a line that meets the circle at exactly one point, called the point of contact. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to that point, and this is a theorem rather than a definition.

The proof is by contradiction. If the tangent were not perpendicular to the radius, a foot of the perpendicular from the centre to the line would give a second point of the circle on the line, contradicting the definition of a tangent.

Two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length, and the line from the centre to that point bisects the angle between them. Both facts follow from congruent right-angled triangles.

The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment, which is the alternate segment theorem. It is the theorem that makes tangents useful for computing angles, and it is proved from the tangent-radius property.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 6 · 6.3 · Worked example 1

Tangents and radii

Worked example 6.3.1

Problem. A point P is 13 cm from the centre O of a circle of radius 5 cm. A tangent from P touches the circle at T. Find the length PT.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the tangent-radius property to get a right angle, then apply Pythagoras.

  1. The tangent PT is perpendicular to the radius OT, so triangle OTP is right-angled at T.
  2. By Pythagoras, OP² = OT² + PT².
  3. So 13² = 5² + PT², giving 169 = 25 + PT².
  4. Hence PT² = 144 and PT = 12 cm.
  5. The two tangents from P are both 12 cm, by the equal-tangents theorem.

Final answer. PT = 12 cm

Interpretation. The tangent-radius property converts a tangent problem into a Pythagoras problem, which is why it is used so often.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 6 · 6.3 · Worked example 2

Tangents and radii

Worked example 6.3.2

Problem. Prove that the two tangents drawn to a circle from an external point are equal in length.

Mathematical reasoning. Show the two right-angled triangles are congruent and read off the equal hypotenuses.

  1. Let the tangents from P touch the circle at A and B, and let O be the centre.
  2. The radii OA and OB are equal, and OP is common to both triangles.
  3. Both triangles are right-angled, because a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
  4. So triangles OAP and OBP are congruent by the right angle, hypotenuse, side criterion.
  5. Hence PA = PB, as required.

Final answer. the two tangents are equal in length

Interpretation. The proof uses the tangent-radius property as one of its congruency conditions, which is why that property is proved first.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.4
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.4

Chords, secants and the alternate segment

Inquiry question

How do the lengths of intersecting chords relate?

Your task

Draw a circle and two chords intersecting inside it. Measure the four segments and check the intersecting chords theorem. Then draw a tangent and a chord from the point of contact, and check the alternate segment theorem against an angle in the alternate segment. Repeat for a second circle.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.4
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.4

Chords, secants and the alternate segment

What do you notice?
  • The two products were equal in both circles.
  • The tangent-chord angle equalled the angle in the alternate segment in both cases.
  • The second circle had the angle pairs swapped, which showed the relationship is not a coincidence of one diagram.
  • Both theorems held regardless of where the chords crossed.
Observation. Intersecting chords give equal products, and a tangent-chord angle equals the alternate segment angle.
Mathematical conclusion

The intersecting chords theorem follows from the similarity of the triangles formed by the chords, which in turn follows from equal angles. The alternate segment theorem follows from the tangent-radius property and the angle at the centre theorem. The measurements confirmed both, with the products equal and the angle pairs equal in each circle.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.4 · Chords, secants and the alternate segment
Chapter 6 · 6.4

Chords, secants and the alternate segment

When two chords AB and CD intersect inside a circle at X, the products AX × XB and CX × XD are equal. This is the intersecting chords theorem, and it follows from the similarity of the triangles formed.

The similarity comes from the equal angles: the angles at X are vertically opposite, and the angles subtended by the same arc are equal. Equal angles give similar triangles, and similar triangles give the equal ratios.

When two secants meet outside the circle, the product of the whole secant and its external part is the same for both. The tangent case is the limit of this, giving the tangent-secant theorem.

The alternate segment theorem states that the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. It is proved by drawing the radius to the point of contact and using the tangent-radius property together with the angle at the centre theorem.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 6 · 6.4 · Worked example 1

Chords, secants and the alternate segment

Worked example 6.4.1

Problem. Two chords AB and CD intersect at X inside a circle, with AX = 3, XB = 4, CX = 2. Find XD.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the intersecting chords theorem and solve for the unknown length.

  1. By the intersecting chords theorem, AX × XB = CX × XD.
  2. So 3 × 4 = 2 × XD, giving 12 = 2 × XD.
  3. Hence XD = 6.
  4. Check: 2 × 6 = 12, which equals 3 × 4.
  5. The result is independent of where X lies along CD, so long as the products are formed correctly.

Final answer. XD = 6

Interpretation. The theorem converts a length problem into a product equation, and the check is the equality of the two products.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 6 · 6.4 · Worked example 2

Chords, secants and the alternate segment

Worked example 6.4.2

Problem. Prove the alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent at A and a chord AB equals the angle in the alternate segment.

Mathematical reasoning. Express both angles in terms of the base angle of the isosceles triangle and compare.

  1. Let the tangent at A meet the chord AB, and let C be a point on the circle in the alternate segment.
  2. The radius OA is perpendicular to the tangent, so the angle between the tangent and AB is 90 degrees minus angle OAB.
  3. Triangle OAB is isosceles, so angle OAB = angle OBA.
  4. The angle at the centre AOB is 180 degrees minus twice angle OAB, and it is twice angle ACB.
  5. So angle ACB is 90 degrees minus angle OAB, which equals the angle between the tangent and the chord.

Final answer. the angle between the tangent and the chord equals the angle in the alternate segment

Interpretation. The proof is a chain of three theorems, and each link is named.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.5
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.5

Constructing and writing proofs

Inquiry question

What makes a geometric argument a proof?

Your task

Take four circle theorems from this chapter: the angle at the centre theorem, the angle in a semicircle, the tangent-radius property and the perpendicular from the centre to a chord. For each, write out a complete proof with a reason beside every step, and then state the converse and decide whether it is true.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.5
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.5

Constructing and writing proofs

What do you notice?
  • Two proofs used congruent triangles and two used a contradiction or a reduction to an earlier result.
  • Every converse turned out to be true, but each needed its own proof.
  • The angle in a semicircle was the quickest, because it was a special case.
  • Writing the reasons beside the steps exposed the assumptions immediately.
Observation. A proof is a chain of justified statements, and the converse of a true statement is a separate claim.
Mathematical conclusion

A geometric proof is a sequence of statements each justified by a definition, a given, or a previously proved result, and the justification is what distinguishes it from a description. The converse of a proved result is a separate claim requiring its own proof, and all four converses here were true.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.5 · Constructing and writing proofs
Chapter 6 · 6.5

Constructing and writing proofs

A proof is a sequence of statements, each justified by a definition, a previously proved result, or a given fact. The logic of the chain is the proof: a list of true statements without reasons is a description.

Proofs in circle geometry are usually written in two columns, or as a numbered chain with the reason beside each step. Either form is acceptable provided every step is justified and the conclusion follows by logic alone.

A proof by contradiction assumes the opposite of what is to be proved and derives a statement that contradicts a known fact. It is the natural form for the tangent-radius property, because the definition of a tangent is a statement about the number of intersection points.

The converse of a proved result is a separate claim that needs its own proof. The angle-in-a-semicircle theorem and its converse are both true, but neither follows from the other.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 6 · 6.5 · Worked example 1

Constructing and writing proofs

Worked example 6.5.1

Problem. Prove that if a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is supplementary then the quadrilateral is cyclic.

Mathematical reasoning. Assume the fourth vertex is off the circle, construct the point on the circle, and show the two must coincide.

  1. Let ABCD have angle DAB + angle BCD = 180 degrees.
  2. Suppose D is not on the circle through A, B and C.
  3. Let that circle meet the line BD again at E, so ABCE is cyclic.
  4. Then angle AEB = 180 degrees minus angle BCD, which equals angle ADB.
  5. So D and E make the same angle with AB while lying on the same line, and hence coincide.
  6. This contradicts the assumption, so D lies on the circle and ABCD is cyclic.

Final answer. the quadrilateral is cyclic

Interpretation. The proof is by contradiction, and the contradiction is that two points with the same position must be distinct.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 6 · 6.5 · Worked example 2

Constructing and writing proofs

Worked example 6.5.2

Problem. Write a proof that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

Mathematical reasoning. Form two congruent right-angled triangles and read off the equal segments.

  1. Let M be the foot of the perpendicular from the centre O to the chord AB.
  2. The radii OA and OB are equal, and OM is common.
  3. Both triangles OMA and OMB are right-angled at M.
  4. So they are congruent by the right angle, hypotenuse, side criterion.
  5. Hence AM = MB, so M bisects the chord.

Final answer. the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord

Interpretation. The proof is short because the congruency is immediate, and every step cites its reason.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.6
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.6

Investigation: circle theorems under transformation

Inquiry question

Which circle properties survive a transformation?

Your task

Draw a circle with a chord and an inscribed angle. Apply a translation, a rotation, a reflection and an enlargement to the whole figure, and measure the inscribed angle in each image. Then repeat with the alternate segment theorem, and record which quantities change and which stay the same.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.6
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.6

Investigation: circle theorems under transformation

What do you notice?
  • The inscribed angle survived every transformation.
  • The isometries left every measurement unchanged.
  • The enlargement multiplied the lengths by 3 but left the angles alone.
  • The alternate segment angle was likewise unchanged in every case.
Observation. Angles are preserved by all four transformations, and lengths only by the isometries.
Mathematical conclusion

Translations, rotations and reflections preserve both angles and lengths, and enlargements preserve angles while scaling lengths. Every circle theorem is therefore invariant under all of them, which is why a single diagram is enough to establish a circle theorem: any other configuration is obtained by a transformation, and the transformation preserves the quantities the theorem relates.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.6 · Investigation: circle theorems under transformation
Chapter 6 · 6.6

Investigation: circle theorems under transformation

A circle is defined by a centre and a radius, so any transformation that preserves distances preserves circles. Translations, rotations and reflections all send circles to circles, and enlargements send circles to circles with a scaled radius.

An enlargement with centre on the circle sends the circle to a line, which is the tangent at that centre in the limit. This is the transformation view of a tangent: it is the image of a circle under an enlargement about a point of the circle.

Angles are preserved by all of these transformations, so every circle theorem is invariant under them. A theorem proved for one configuration is therefore proved for every configuration obtained by a transformation, which is why one diagram is enough.

Inversion in a circle is a transformation that sends circles to circles and lines to circles, and it is the transformation in which the intersecting chords theorem becomes most transparent. It is the tool behind many advanced results in circle geometry.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 6 · 6.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: circle theorems under transformation

Worked example 6.6.1

Problem. A circle of radius 3 with centre (2, 5) is translated by the vector (−4, 1) and then enlarged by factor 2 about the origin. Find the final centre and radius.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply each transformation to the centre and scale the radius by the enlargement factor.

  1. The original centre is (2, 5) and the radius is 3.
  2. Translation by (−4, 1) moves the centre to (−2, 6).
  3. An enlargement of factor 2 about the origin multiplies every distance from the origin by 2.
  4. So the centre moves to (−4, 12) and the radius becomes 6.
  5. The image is a circle, because translations and enlargements preserve circles.

Final answer. centre (−4, 12), radius 6

Interpretation. Tracking the centre and the radius is enough, because the shape of a circle is determined by those two quantities.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 6 · 6.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: circle theorems under transformation

Worked example 6.6.2

Problem. Explain why a tangent can be regarded as the limit of circles under an enlargement about a point of the circle.

Mathematical reasoning. An enlargement about a point of the circle increases the radius without bound, and a circle of infinite radius is a line.

  1. An enlargement of factor k about a point P on the circle keeps P fixed and multiplies the radius by k.
  2. The curvature of a circle is the reciprocal of its radius, so the curvature is divided by k.
  3. As k grows, the curvature tends to zero and the circle becomes locally straight.
  4. The limiting line passes through P and is perpendicular to the radius OP.
  5. That line is the tangent, which is why the tangent is perpendicular to the radius.

Final answer. the tangent is the limit of the images, and it is perpendicular to the radius

Interpretation. The transformation view explains the tangent-radius property rather than merely restating it.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.7
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which theorem does this figure need?

Your task

Take a circle of radius 5 with a point P at distance 13 from the centre. Draw the two tangents from P and the chord of contact AB. Find the angle APB, the length of AB, the angle AOB and the area of the quadrilateral OAPB, and name the theorem used at each step.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 6.7
Chapter 6 · Investigation 6.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • Every quantity came from the tangent-radius property plus one further theorem.
  • The area of the quadrilateral was twice the area of one right-angled triangle.
  • The chord of contact was found from the isosceles triangle OAB.
  • Naming the theorem at each step made the whole solution checkable.
Observation. The tangent-radius property converts every tangent question into a right-angled triangle question.
Mathematical conclusion

A circle question is solved by naming the theorem that applies, stating it in full, and applying it to the named parts. The tangent-radius property, the equal-tangents theorem and the perpendicular-bisector property between them handle most tangent and chord questions, and each answer cites the property it uses. Here the tangent was 12, the angle APB was about 45.2 degrees and the chord of contact was about 9.23.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 6 · 6.7

Mixed practice

Every circle question begins by naming the theorem that applies. Naming it forces the relevant arc, chord or tangent to be identified, and the identification is most of the work.

A complete answer states the theorem in full, applies it to the named parts, and derives the required quantity. Omitting the statement of the theorem leaves the answer a calculation without a justification.

Proofs in this chapter are chains of at most five steps, each citing a definition, a given, or an earlier theorem. Writing the reason beside each step is the discipline that makes the chain checkable.

Mixed practice is where the theorem is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 6 · 6.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 6.7.1

Problem. A chord of length 8 cm is 3 cm from the centre of a circle. Find the radius.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the perpendicular-bisector property to form a right-angled triangle, then apply Pythagoras.

  1. The perpendicular from the centre to the chord bisects it, so half the chord is 4 cm.
  2. The distance from the centre to the chord is 3 cm.
  3. The radius, the half-chord and the distance form a right-angled triangle.
  4. So r² = 4² + 3² = 16 + 9 = 25.
  5. Hence r = 5 cm.

Final answer. radius 5 cm

Interpretation. The perpendicular-bisector property is what makes the right-angled triangle available, and it must be named.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook6.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 6 · 6.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 6.7.2

Problem. Two tangents from P touch a circle of radius 6 at A and B, and the angle APB is 70 degrees. Find the angle AOB and the length PA.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the tangent-radius property and the angle sum of the quadrilateral, then Pythagoras.

  1. The radii OA and OB are perpendicular to the tangents at A and B.
  2. So the quadrilateral OAPB has angles 90, 70, 90 and angle AOB.
  3. The angle sum is 360, so angle AOB = 360 − 250 = 110 degrees.
  4. The line OP bisects the angle APB, so angle APO is 35 degrees.
  5. In the right-angled triangle OAP, tan 35° = 6/PA, so PA = 6 ÷ tan 35° ≈ 8.56 cm.

Final answer. angle AOB = 110 degrees; PA ≈ 8.56 cm

Interpretation. The two properties used are the tangent-radius property and the equal-tangents theorem, and both must be named.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 6 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc.
  • Angles in the same segment are equal.
  • The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
  • Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
  • An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.
  • A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
  • The two tangents from an external point are equal in length.
  • The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.
  • For intersecting chords, AX × XB = CX × XD.
  • The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.

Vocabulary

circle · centre · radius · diameter · chord · arc · tangent · secant · point of contact · cyclic quadrilateral · alternate segment · angle at the centre · angle at the circumference · concyclic · proof by contradiction · congruent · similar
