MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 7 · Sine and Cosine Rules; Trigonometry in Three Dimensions
Chapter 7 · Part III · Spatial reasoning
07

Sine and Cosine Rules; Trigonometry in Three Dimensions

A triangle is determined by three independent measurements. The sine rule and the cosine rule are the two relationships that connect them, and together they solve every triangle and extend trigonometry into three dimensions.

Engage

A surveyor measures two angles and one side of a triangular plot. A colleague measures two sides and a non-included angle of a different plot and finds two possible positions for the third corner. Why does one set of measurements give one triangle and the other give two?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Relationships
Related concepts: Space · Change · Measurement
Global context: Orientation in space and time
Global context exploration: navigation, surveying and the geometry of place

Statement of inquiry: Triangles that are not right-angled can still be solved: the sine and cosine rules turn measurements of angle and distance into positions, areas and three-dimensional structure.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What do the sine rule and the cosine rule state, and when is each used?
  • Conceptual: Why can two sides and a non-included angle determine two triangles, and when does it determine none?
  • Debatable: If a navigation calculation gives two possible positions, which one should be acted on, and on what grounds?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to decide how many triangles a set of measurements determines, students must compare the given side with the perpendicular height, identify the zero, one or two-triangle cases, and justify the conclusion.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.1
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.1

The sine rule

Inquiry question

How do the sine rule and the ambiguous case fit together?

Your task

Take a fixed angle A = 40° and a fixed side b = 12. Vary a over the values 6, 8, 7.7, 7.71, 12 and 14. For each, compute b sin A, decide how many triangles exist, and where two exist, find both values of B. Record the case boundaries.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.1
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.1

The sine rule

What do you notice?
  • Below the height there were no triangles at all, however close the values were.
  • At the height there was exactly one triangle, and it was right-angled.
  • Between the height and b there were exactly two triangles, with supplementary values of B.
  • At and above b there was exactly one triangle again.
Observation. The number of triangles is decided by comparing a with b sin A and b, and the two-triangle case gives supplementary values of B.
Mathematical conclusion

Two sides and a non-included angle determine a triangle only when the given side is at least the perpendicular height b sin A. When b sin A = a there is exactly one triangle and it is right-angled; when b sin A < a < b there are two, with the two values of B supplementary; when a < b sin A there is none. Here the height was 7.713, and the cases were 0, 1 and 2 triangles around it.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.1 · The sine rule
Chapter 7 · 7.1

The sine rule

The sine rule states that a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C, where a is the side opposite the angle A. It is proved by dropping a perpendicular from one vertex and expressing its length in two ways.

The rule is used when a triangle has a side and its opposite angle, together with one further angle or side. It converts a known pair into an unknown one through a single ratio, which is why it is the rule for angle-side problems.

The ambiguous case arises when two sides and a non-included angle are given, written SSA. The given side opposite the given angle may be shorter than, equal to, or longer than the perpendicular height, and the three cases give two, one or no triangle.

The condition is exact: with A given and sides a and b given, the perpendicular height is b sin A. Two triangles exist when b sin A < a < b; exactly one right triangle exists when b sin A = a; no triangle exists when a < b sin A; and exactly one triangle exists when a ≥ b.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 7 · 7.1 · Worked example 1

The sine rule

Worked example 7.1.1

Problem. In triangle ABC, A = 38°, B = 64° and a = 9.4. Find b and c.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the third angle, then apply the sine rule twice.

  1. The third angle is C = 180° − 38° − 64° = 78°.
  2. By the sine rule, b = a sin B ÷ sin A.
  3. So b = 9.4 × sin 64° ÷ sin 38° = 9.4 × 0.8988 ÷ 0.6157 ≈ 13.72.
  4. Similarly c = 9.4 × sin 78° ÷ sin 38° = 9.4 × 0.9781 ÷ 0.6157 ≈ 14.93.
  5. Check: C is the largest angle, so c is the largest side, as found.

Final answer. b ≈ 13.72 and c ≈ 14.93

Interpretation. Two angles and one side determine exactly one triangle, so there is no ambiguity here.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 7 · 7.1 · Worked example 2

The sine rule

Worked example 7.1.2

Problem. In triangle ABC, A = 30°, a = 5 and b = 10. Determine how many triangles exist and find the remaining measurements.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the perpendicular height b sin A and compare it with the given side a to decide the number of triangles.

  1. The perpendicular height from C to the side AB extended is b sin A = 10 × sin 30° = 10 × 0.5 = 5.
  2. This equals the given side a = 5, so the height condition b sin A = a holds.
  3. Hence there is exactly one triangle, and it is right-angled at C.
  4. The remaining angles are B = 90° and C = 60°.
  5. Check: a/sin A = 5/0.5 = 10 and b/sin B = 10/1 = 10, so the sine rule is satisfied.

Final answer. exactly one triangle, right-angled at C, with B = 90° and C = 60°

Interpretation. The ambiguous case is decided before any angle is computed, and the check confirms the single solution.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.2
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.2

The cosine rule

Inquiry question

When is the cosine rule the right rule, and what does it generalise?

Your task

Take a triangle with sides 8 and 11 and included angle 55°. Compute the third side by the cosine rule, then all three angles, and check the angle sum. Then repeat with the included angle 125° and compare the two results.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.2
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.2

The cosine rule

What do you notice?
  • A larger included angle gave a much larger third side, from 9.22 to 16.87.
  • In both cases the largest angle was the given one, because it was opposite the largest side.
  • The angle sum was 180 degrees in both cases, confirming the calculations.
  • The change in the third side was far from proportional to the change in the angle, because the cosine is not linear.
Observation. The third side grows with the included angle, and fastest when the cosine is changing fastest.
Mathematical conclusion

The cosine rule a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A determines the third side from two sides and the included angle, and rearranged determines an angle from three sides. It is a generalisation of Pythagoras, to which it reduces when the included angle is a right angle. Here the third side was 9.22 for an included angle of 55 degrees and 16.87 for 125 degrees.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.2 · The cosine rule
Chapter 7 · 7.2

The cosine rule

The cosine rule states that a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A, and rearranged gives cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc). It is proved by placing the triangle in a coordinate system and applying Pythagoras to two right-angled triangles.

The rule is used when three sides are given, or two sides and the included angle. It is the only rule that handles the included angle directly, and it reduces to Pythagoras when the included angle is 90 degrees.

The cosine rule is a generalisation of Pythagoras: the term 2bc cos A vanishes when A is a right angle, and the formula becomes a² = b² + c². Every right-angled calculation is a special case of it.

When the cosine rule gives a quadratic in an unknown side, both roots must be considered and rejected if they are not positive. This happens when two sides and a non-included angle are given, and it is the algebraic form of the ambiguous case.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 7 · 7.2 · Worked example 1

The cosine rule

Worked example 7.2.1

Problem. In triangle ABC, b = 7, c = 10 and A = 47°. Find a and then find B.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the cosine rule for the side, then again for the angle.

  1. The cosine rule gives a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
  2. So a² = 49 + 100 − 140 cos 47° = 149 − 140(0.6820) ≈ 95.59.
  3. Hence a ≈ 9.78.
  4. For the angle, cos B = (a² + c² − b²)/(2ac) = (95.59 + 100 − 49)/(2 × 9.78 × 10) ≈ 0.7493.
  5. So B ≈ 41.5°, and C ≈ 180 − 47 − 41.5 = 91.5°.

Final answer. a ≈ 9.78 and B ≈ 41.5°

Interpretation. Two sides and the included angle determine exactly one triangle, so there is no ambiguity.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 7 · 7.2 · Worked example 2

The cosine rule

Worked example 7.2.2

Problem. Find the angles of the triangle with sides 5, 7 and 9.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the cosine rule three times, or twice and use the angle sum.

  1. For the angle opposite the side 9, cos A = (5² + 7² − 9²)/(2 × 5 × 7) = (25 + 49 − 81)/70 = −7/70 = −0.1.
  2. So A ≈ 95.7°, which is obtuse as the negative cosine indicates.
  3. For the angle opposite 7, cos B = (25 + 81 − 49)/(2 × 5 × 9) = 57/90 ≈ 0.6333, so B ≈ 50.7°.
  4. For the angle opposite 5, cos C = (49 + 81 − 25)/(2 × 7 × 9) = 105/126 ≈ 0.8333, so C ≈ 33.6°.
  5. The three angles sum to 180°, as required.

Final answer. approximately 95.7°, 50.7° and 33.6°

Interpretation. Three sides determine exactly one triangle, so the answer is unique and the angle sum is the check.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.3
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.3

Area and the included angle

Inquiry question

How is the area of a triangle found without a height?

Your task

Take a triangle with sides 6, 8 and 11. Compute its area using each of the three forms of the area formula, and check that all three agree. Then find the radius of its circumcircle using a = 2R sin A.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.3
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.3

Area and the included angle

What do you notice?
  • All three forms gave the same area, as they had to.
  • The angles were found first by the cosine rule, since only the sides were given.
  • The circumradius came from a = 2R sin A, which is the sine rule rearranged.
  • The area was about 22.4 square units, and the circumradius about 5.49.
Observation. The area formula is symmetric in the three pairs of sides, and the sine rule extends to the circumradius.
Mathematical conclusion

The area of a triangle is ½bc sin A, where A is the angle included between the sides b and c, and the formula is symmetric in the three pairs. The same relationship rearranged gives a = 2R sin A, where R is the circumradius. Here every form gave an area of about 22.4 square units and a circumradius of about 5.49.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.3 · Area and the included angle
Chapter 7 · 7.3

Area and the included angle

The area of a triangle is half the base times the perpendicular height. When the height is not given but two sides and the included angle are, the height is one side times the sine of the included angle, giving area = ½bc sin A.

The formula is symmetric: area = ½ab sin C = ½bc sin A = ½ca sin B. Any pair of sides with the angle between them gives the same area, which is a check on the calculation.

The formula is derived by dropping the perpendicular and using the definition of sine in the resulting right-angled triangle. The derivation is short, and it explains why the included angle is the one that appears.

The same formula applied to a sector or a segment gives the area of a circular sector as ½r²θ in radians, and the segment as the sector minus the triangle. The radian measure is what makes the sector formula simple.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 7 · 7.3 · Worked example 1

Area and the included angle

Worked example 7.3.1

Problem. Find the area of a triangle with sides 9 and 13 and included angle 52°.

Mathematical reasoning. Drop the perpendicular and express the height with the sine of the included angle.

  1. Take the sides 9 and 13 with the included angle 52°.
  2. The height on the base 13 is 9 sin 52° ≈ 9 × 0.7880 ≈ 7.09.
  3. The area is ½ × 13 × 7.09 ≈ 46.1 square units.
  4. Check with the formula: ½ × 9 × 13 × sin 52° ≈ 46.1.
  5. The two calculations agree, as they must.

Final answer. about 46.1 square units

Interpretation. The direct formula is faster, and the height calculation explains where it comes from.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 7 · 7.3 · Worked example 2

Area and the included angle

Worked example 7.3.2

Problem. A sector of a circle of radius 8 has angle 0.7 radians. Find its area and the area of the segment cut off by the chord.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the sector formula with radians and subtract the triangle.

  1. The sector area is ½r²θ = ½ × 64 × 0.7 = 22.4.
  2. The triangle formed by the two radii and the chord has area ½r² sin θ = ½ × 64 × sin 0.7.
  3. sin 0.7 ≈ 0.6442, so the triangle area is 32 × 0.6442 ≈ 20.5.
  4. The segment is the sector minus the triangle: 22.4 − 20.5 ≈ 1.9.
  5. The segment is much smaller than the sector because the angle is small.

Final answer. sector 22.4, segment about 1.9

Interpretation. The radian measure makes the sector formula ½r²θ, and the same triangle formula gives the correction.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.4
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.4

Bearings and navigation

Inquiry question

How do bearings turn a triangle into a position?

Your task

Set up a navigation problem of your own with two legs and a turn, solve it by the cosine rule, and then solve the same problem by resolving each leg into north and east components. Compare the two answers and record which method you found more reliable.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.4
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.4

Bearings and navigation

What do you notice?
  • Both methods gave the same distance and the same bearing.
  • The component method made the sign of the northward distance visible, which the cosine rule hid.
  • The cosine rule was fewer steps once the included angle was found.
  • The component method needed the angle of each leg measured from north, which is what a bearing gives directly.
Observation. Bearings are angles from north, so they suit the component method; the cosine rule suits a triangle with a known included angle.
Mathematical conclusion

A bearing is a direction measured clockwise from north, and a navigation problem is a triangle whose sides are distances and whose angles come from bearings. The interior angles must be extracted carefully, and the two solution methods — the cosine rule and resolving into components — must agree. Here both gave a distance of 34.7 on a bearing of 137 degrees.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.4 · Bearings and navigation
Chapter 7 · 7.4

Bearings and navigation

A bearing is a direction measured clockwise from north, written as a three-figure angle. Bearings are the language in which positions are described, and they convert a diagram into a set of numbers that can be transmitted.

A navigation problem is a triangle in which the sides are distances and the angles are bearings. The sine and cosine rules solve it exactly as they solve any triangle, once the interior angles have been extracted from the bearings.

The interior angle between two bearings is the difference of the bearings, or 360 degrees minus that difference, depending on which way round the triangle goes. Getting this wrong is the commonest navigation error, and drawing the diagram prevents it.

Speed, distance and time enter as a scale on the sides: a ship travelling at 12 knots for 3 hours covers 36 nautical miles. The bearing gives the direction and the distance the magnitude, and together they give a position vector.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 7 · 7.4 · Worked example 1

Bearings and navigation

Worked example 7.4.1

Problem. A ship sails 40 km on a bearing of 060° and then 30 km on a bearing of 150°. Find its distance and bearing from the start.

Mathematical reasoning. Extract the interior angle from the bearings, then apply Pythagoras and trigonometry.

  1. The bearings differ by 150 − 60 = 90 degrees, so the turn is a right angle.
  2. The two legs are perpendicular, so the distance is √(40² + 30²) = √2500 = 50 km.
  3. The bearing of the resultant is 060° + arctan(30/40) = 060° + 36.87° = 096.87°.
  4. So the ship is 50 km away on a bearing of approximately 097°.
  5. Check: the eastward distance is 40 sin 60° + 30 sin 150° = 34.64 + 15 = 49.64, and the northward is 40 cos 60° + 30 cos 150° = 20 − 25.98 = −5.98, which gives the same distance.

Final answer. 50 km on a bearing of about 097°

Interpretation. The bearing difference is the interior angle, and the components check is a different route to the same position.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 7 · 7.4 · Worked example 2

Bearings and navigation

Worked example 7.4.2

Problem. Two ports A and B are 80 km apart, with B on a bearing of 035° from A. A ship leaves A and a second leaves B at the same time, the first on a bearing of 080° at 20 km/h and the second on a bearing of 200° at 15 km/h. Find the distance between them after 2 hours.

Mathematical reasoning. Extract the two distances and the included angle from the bearings, then apply the cosine rule.

  1. After 2 hours the first ship has travelled 40 km and the second 30 km.
  2. The angle at A between AB and the first ship's course is 080° − 035° = 45°.
  3. The second ship's course from B is on a bearing of 200°, so the angle between the two courses at the triangle's vertices is 180° − 45° − (200° − 180°) = 140°.
  4. By the cosine rule, the distance squared is 40² + 30² − 2(40)(30) cos 140°.
  5. That is 1600 + 900 + 1838.5 = 4338.5, so the distance is about 65.9 km.

Final answer. about 65.9 km

Interpretation. The included angle must be extracted from the bearings carefully, and drawing the diagram is what prevents the error.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.5
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.5

Trigonometry in three dimensions

Inquiry question

How does a three-dimensional problem become a two-dimensional one?

Your task

Take a cone of radius 5 and vertical height 12. Find the slant height, the angle between the slant height and the base, the angle between the slant height and the axis, and the area of the curved surface. Then repeat for a cone of radius 5 and height 5, and compare.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.5
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.5

Trigonometry in three dimensions

What do you notice?
  • The two angles were complementary in each cone, as they had to be in a right-angled triangle.
  • Halving the height halved the slant height only partly, from 13 to 7.07.
  • The curved surface area fell by nearly half, because it is proportional to the slant height.
  • The second cone had equal base radius and height, so its angles were both 45 degrees.
Observation. Every angle in a cone is read from the right-angled triangle formed by the radius, the height and the slant height.
Mathematical conclusion

A three-dimensional problem is solved by choosing a plane that contains the required lengths and solving the two-dimensional triangle in it. In a cone that plane gives the radius, the vertical height and the slant height, and from them every angle and the curved surface area. Here the slant heights were 13 and about 7.07, with curved surface areas of about 204.2 and 111.1.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.5 · Trigonometry in three dimensions
Chapter 7 · 7.5

Trigonometry in three dimensions

A three-dimensional problem is solved by finding a plane that contains the required lengths and angles, solving the two-dimensional triangle in that plane, and then relating it back to the solid. The choice of plane is the whole skill.

In a cuboid with edges a, b and c, the space diagonal is √(a² + b² + c²) and the angle between the diagonal and an edge is found from a right-angled triangle containing both. The face diagonal is an intermediate step.

The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its projection onto the plane, and it is found in the right-angled triangle formed by the line, its projection and the perpendicular. It is never the angle the line makes with the plane's normal.

In a pyramid or cone, the slant height, the vertical height and the radius of the base form a right-angled triangle, and every angle in the solid is found from that triangle or from a triangle in a face.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 7 · 7.5 · Worked example 1

Trigonometry in three dimensions

Worked example 7.5.1

Problem. A cuboid has edges 6, 8 and 24. Find the space diagonal and the angle it makes with the longest edge.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the face diagonal, then use it to find the space diagonal and the angle.

  1. The face diagonal on the 6 by 8 face is √(36 + 64) = 10.
  2. The space diagonal is √(10² + 24²) = √676 = 26.
  3. The angle with the longest edge has cosine 24/26, because the edge and the diagonal are in the same right-angled triangle.
  4. So the angle is arccos(24/26) ≈ 22.6°.
  5. Check: 6² + 8² + 24² = 36 + 64 + 576 = 676 = 26².

Final answer. space diagonal 26; angle about 22.6°

Interpretation. The two-step Pythagoras is the standard way through a cuboid, and the angle is read from the final triangle.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 7 · 7.5 · Worked example 2

Trigonometry in three dimensions

Worked example 7.5.2

Problem. A square pyramid has a base of side 10 and a vertical height of 12. Find the slant height and the angle between a sloping face and the base.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the right-angled triangle through the apex and the midpoint of a base edge.

  1. The perpendicular from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge, the vertical height and half the base side form a right-angled triangle.
  2. The legs are 12 and 5, so the slant height is √(144 + 25) = 13.
  3. The angle between the face and the base has tangent 12/5.
  4. So the angle is arctan(12/5) ≈ 67.4°.
  5. This is the angle between the planes, measured in the perpendicular cross-section.

Final answer. slant height 13; angle about 67.4°

Interpretation. The angle between two planes is measured in the plane perpendicular to their line of intersection, which is the cross-section used here.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.6
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.6

Investigation: measuring the unmeasurable

Inquiry question

How can a distance be found without measuring it directly?

Your task

Measure the height of an object in your school grounds without measuring it directly. Choose a baseline, measure two angles of elevation, compute the height, and repeat with a different baseline. Compare the two results and comment on the accuracy of the method.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.6
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.6

Investigation: measuring the unmeasurable

What do you notice?
  • The two baselines gave heights within 4 cm of each other.
  • The longer baseline gave a slightly different answer, because the angles were measured with the same instrument but over a longer distance.
  • The repeat measurement was identical, which showed the calculation was being done consistently.
  • The method's accuracy was limited by the angle measurement, not by the baseline.
Observation. Two angles of elevation and a baseline determine a height, and the accuracy is limited by the angles.
Mathematical conclusion

A distance that cannot be measured directly is found by measuring a baseline and two angles and solving the triangle, which is triangulation. The accuracy is limited by the angle measurement and by the conditioning of the triangle, and long baselines need correction for the curvature of the Earth. Here the two baselines gave heights of 8.42 m and 8.46 m.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.6 · Investigation: measuring the unmeasurable
Chapter 7 · 7.6

Investigation: measuring the unmeasurable

A distance that cannot be measured directly — across a river, to a mountain top, to a star — is found by measuring a baseline and two angles, and solving the resulting triangle. The method is triangulation, and it is the basis of surveying.

The accuracy of the result depends on the accuracy of the angles and on the shape of the triangle. A long thin triangle amplifies angle errors, so surveyors choose baselines and angles that give a well-conditioned triangle.

The same method with a very long baseline and very small angles measures stellar distances in parsecs, where one parsec is the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends one second of arc. The scale changes; the method does not.

Triangulation is limited by the curvature of the Earth over long baselines and by atmospheric refraction in astronomy. Both are corrections to the ideal triangle, and both must be stated when the method is used.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 7 · 7.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: measuring the unmeasurable

Worked example 7.6.1

Problem. A baseline AB of 200 m is measured on one bank of a river. From A a tree T on the far bank is sighted at 35° from the baseline, and from B at 65°. Find the distance from A to T.

Mathematical reasoning. Find the third angle, then apply the sine rule.

  1. The angles at A and B are 35° and 65°, so the angle at T is 180 − 35 − 65 = 80°.
  2. By the sine rule, AT ÷ sin 65° = AB ÷ sin 80°.
  3. So AT = 200 × sin 65° ÷ sin 80° = 200 × 0.9063 ÷ 0.9848.
  4. Hence AT ≈ 184.1 m.
  5. Check the angle sum: 35 + 65 + 80 = 180°, so the triangle is consistent.

Final answer. about 184 m

Interpretation. The angle sum check confirms the readings are consistent, and it is performed before any length is computed.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 7 · 7.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: measuring the unmeasurable

Worked example 7.6.2

Problem. A mountain is observed from two stations 3 km apart on a level plain. From the nearer station the angle of elevation to the summit is 22° and from the further one 18°. Find the height of the mountain.

Mathematical reasoning. Write the horizontal distance to the summit from each station and equate the difference to the baseline.

  1. Let h be the height and d the distance from the nearer station to the point below the summit.
  2. From the nearer station, tan 22° = h/d, so d = h ÷ tan 22° ≈ 2.475h.
  3. From the further station, tan 18° = h/(d + 3), so d + 3 = h ÷ tan 18° ≈ 3.078h.
  4. Subtracting gives 3 ≈ 0.603h, so h ≈ 4.97 km.
  5. Check: the nearer distance is about 12.3 km and the further about 15.3 km, differing by 3 km as required.

Final answer. about 4.97 km

Interpretation. Two angles of elevation from a known baseline give the height, and the check is the difference of the two horizontal distances.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.7
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which rule, and how many triangles?

Your task

Take A = 35°, a = 8 and b = 11. Determine how many triangles exist, find all solutions, and then repeat with a = 7, a = 6.30 and a = 14. Record the case boundaries and explain how you decided each one.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 7.7
Chapter 7 · Investigation 7.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • The height was about 6.31, and every case was decided by comparing a with it.
  • Two values of a gave two triangles each, with supplementary values of B.
  • One value of a gave no triangle, because it fell just below the height.
  • One value of a gave exactly one triangle, because it exceeded b.
Observation. The comparison of a with b sin A and with b decides the number of triangles before any angle is computed.
Mathematical conclusion

Two sides and a non-included angle determine a triangle only when the given side is at least the perpendicular height b sin A. The comparison is made first, and only then are angles computed: b sin A = a gives one right triangle, b sin A < a < b gives two, a < b sin A gives none, and a ≥ b gives one. Here the height was 6.31 and the cases were 2, 2, 0 and 1 triangles.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 7 · 7.7

Mixed practice

Every non-right-angled triangle question begins by asking what is given: three sides, two sides and the included angle, or two sides and a non-included angle. The answer decides the rule and whether the ambiguous case must be checked.

The ambiguous case is checked by comparing the given side with the perpendicular height. Skipping the check is how two-triangle problems are answered with one answer, and it is the defect this chapter repairs.

Three-dimensional problems are solved by choosing a plane. Naming the plane and the triangle in it is the first line of the solution, and it is what makes the rest of the solution checkable.

Mixed practice is where the rule is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 7 · 7.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 7.7.1

Problem. In triangle ABC, A = 40°, a = 7 and b = 12. Determine how many triangles exist and find all solutions.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute b sin A and compare it with a before doing anything else.

  1. The perpendicular height is b sin A = 12 × sin 40° ≈ 12 × 0.6428 ≈ 7.713.
  2. The given side a = 7 is less than 7.713, so no triangle exists.
  3. The case b sin A = a does not hold, since 7.713 ≠\neq= 7.
  4. The case b sin A < a < b does not hold either, since 7.713 > 7.
  5. Hence there is no triangle with these measurements.

Final answer. no triangle exists

Interpretation. The comparison is the whole solution, and it takes one multiplication.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook7.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 7 · 7.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 7.7.2

Problem. In triangle ABC, A = 40°, a = 9 and b = 12. Find both solutions.

Mathematical reasoning. Confirm the two-triangle case, then find both values of B from the sine rule.

  1. The height is b sin A = 12 sin 40° ≈ 7.713, and 7.713 < 9 < 12, so there are two triangles.
  2. By the sine rule, sin B = b sin A ÷ a = 7.713 ÷ 9 ≈ 0.857.
  3. So B ≈ 58.9° or B ≈ 180° − 58.9° = 121.1°.
  4. For the first, C ≈ 180 − 40 − 58.9 = 81.1° and c = 9 sin 81.1° ÷ sin 40° ≈ 13.82.
  5. For the second, C ≈ 18.9° and c = 9 sin 18.9° ÷ sin 40° ≈ 4.07.

Final answer. two solutions: B ≈ 58.9°, C ≈ 81.1°, c ≈ 13.82; and B ≈ 121.1°, C ≈ 18.9°, c ≈ 4.07

Interpretation. Both solutions are reported, and the supplementary pair of angles is the reason there are two.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 7 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • The sine rule is a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
  • The cosine rule is a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
  • The area of a triangle is ½ab sin C, where C is the included angle.
  • Two sides and a non-included angle give zero, one or two triangles.
  • Two triangles exist when b sin A < a < b.
  • b sin A = a gives exactly one right triangle.
  • a < b sin A gives no triangle.
  • A bearing is measured clockwise from north as a three-figure angle.
  • A three-dimensional problem is solved by choosing a plane.
  • The angle between a line and a plane uses the line's projection onto the plane.

Vocabulary

sine rule · cosine rule · included angle · non-included angle · ambiguous case · perpendicular height · bearing · angle of elevation · space diagonal · slant height · triangulation · baseline · projection · circumradius

The sine and cosine rules and triangulation.

A figure that was guessed becomes a figure that is justified.

08

Vectors and Matrices

A vector is a quantity with magnitude and direction, and a matrix is an array that transforms one. Together they describe displacements, forces and the transformations that move a plane onto itself.

Engage

A computer graphics program rotates a shape, then stretches it, then rotates it back. The programmer needs one matrix that does all three. How are the three matrices combined, and how can the program tell whether the result can still be undone?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Form
Related concepts: Space · Representation · Systems
Global context: Scientific and technical innovation
Global context exploration: computer graphics, navigation and engineering

Statement of inquiry: Vectors encode displacement by magnitude and direction, while matrices encode transformations of the plane as arrays of numbers; the determinant measures how a transformation stretches or collapses area, and decides whether it can be undone.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What do the magnitude of a vector, the scalar product and the determinant of a matrix measure?
  • Conceptual: Why does the determinant of a product equal the product of the determinants, and what does a zero determinant mean?
  • Debatable: If a transformation collapses a shape to a line, has it destroyed information or merely hidden it?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to decide whether a transformation can be reversed, students must compute the determinant, connect its value to the area scale factor, and justify when an inverse exists.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.1
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.1

Vectors: notation and operations

Inquiry question

What does a vector record that a number cannot?

Your task

Take the vectors a = (2, 1), b = (−3, 4), c = (1, −2) and d = (0, 5). Compute a + b, a − c, 2b + d, |a|, |b|, the unit vector in the direction of a, and the scalar products a · b, a · c and b · d. Record which pairs are perpendicular.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.1
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.1

Vectors: notation and operations

What do you notice?
  • The scalar product a · c was zero, so those two vectors were perpendicular.
  • The scalar product a · b was negative, so the angle between them was obtuse.
  • The unit vector had magnitude 1 and the same direction as a.
  • Vector addition and subtraction were component-wise throughout.
Observation. Vectors combine component-wise, and the scalar product measures the alignment of a pair.
Mathematical conclusion

A vector records magnitude and direction, and its arithmetic is component-wise: addition and subtraction combine the components, and scalar multiplication scales them. The magnitude is recovered by Pythagoras and the scalar product measures alignment, being zero exactly for perpendicular vectors. Here a · c was 0, so a and c were perpendicular.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.1 · Vectors: notation and operations
Chapter 8 · 8.1

Vectors: notation and operations

A vector is a quantity with magnitude and direction, written as a column vector or in bold, and it describes a displacement in space. Two vectors are equal when they have the same magnitude and direction, wherever they are drawn.

Vectors add by the triangle rule: the sum of a and b is the displacement from the start of a to the end of b when they are placed head to tail. Scalar multiplication scales the magnitude and leaves the direction unchanged, or reverses it when the scalar is negative.

The magnitude of a vector a = (x, y) is |a| = √(x² + y²), which is its length. A unit vector has magnitude 1, and dividing a vector by its magnitude gives the unit vector in the same direction.

The scalar product a · b = |a||b| cos θ is a number, not a vector. It is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular, which makes it the standard test for right angles.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.1 · Worked example 1

Vectors: notation and operations

Worked example 8.1.1

Problem. Given a = (3, −2) and b = (−1, 5), find 3a − 2b and its magnitude.

Mathematical reasoning. Scale each vector, then combine component by component.

  1. 3a = 3 × (3, −2) = (9, −6).
  2. 2b = 2 × (−1, 5) = (−2, 10).
  3. So 3a − 2b = (9, −6) − (−2, 10) = (11, −16).
  4. The magnitude is √(11² + 16²) = √(121 + 256) = √377 ≈ 19.42.
  5. The direction is given by the angle arctan(−16/11), which is below the positive x-axis.

Final answer. 3a − 2b = (11, −16), magnitude about 19.42

Interpretation. Vector arithmetic is component-wise, and the magnitude is recovered from the components by Pythagoras.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.1 · Worked example 2

Vectors: notation and operations

Worked example 8.1.2

Problem. Show that the vectors (4, 3) and (−6, 8) are perpendicular.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the scalar product and check whether it is zero.

  1. The scalar product is u · v = 4(−6) + 3(8) = −24 + 24 = 0.
  2. Since the scalar product is zero, the vectors are perpendicular.
  3. Check with the formula u · v = |u||v| cos θ: 0 = 5 × 10 × cos θ gives cos θ = 0.
  4. So θ = 90°, confirming the result.
  5. The magnitudes were 5 and 10, but only the product mattered.

Final answer. they are perpendicular

Interpretation. The scalar product test is faster than finding the angle, and it is exact.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.2
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.2

Vectors and geometry

Inquiry question

How does vector notation prove a geometric claim?

Your task

Take the points A(0, 0), B(6, 2), C(9, 7) and D(3, 5). Determine whether ABCD is a parallelogram, find the midpoints of the diagonals, and check whether the diagonals are perpendicular. Then find the area of the quadrilateral.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.2
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.2

Vectors and geometry

What do you notice?
  • The diagonals shared a midpoint, which proved the parallelogram.
  • The scalar product of the diagonals was −6, not zero, so they were not perpendicular.
  • The area came from the determinant of the two side vectors.
  • Both conditions — parallel opposite sides and shared midpoint — held.
Observation. A parallelogram is detected by equal opposite sides or by a shared diagonal midpoint, and perpendicularity is a scalar product test.
Mathematical conclusion

Vector notation turns a geometric claim into an algebraic one: collinearity is a scalar multiple, a parallelogram is equal opposite sides or a shared diagonal midpoint, and perpendicularity is a zero scalar product. The area of a parallelogram is the magnitude of the determinant of its side vectors. Here the area was 26 and the diagonals were not perpendicular.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.2 · Vectors and geometry
Chapter 8 · 8.2

Vectors and geometry

A position vector gives the position of a point relative to an origin, and the vector between two points is the difference of their position vectors. Writing geometry in vectors is a representation that turns a diagram into an algebra.

Three points are collinear exactly when the vector between two of them is a scalar multiple of the vector between another pair. This is a single equation in two components, and it is the standard collinearity test.

The midpoint of AB has position vector (a + b)/2, and the point dividing AB in the ratio m : n has position vector (n a + m b)/(m + n). Both formulas come from a single linear combination.

The scalar product proves perpendicularity and computes angles, and the vector product in three dimensions gives a vector perpendicular to two others. These tools make vector proofs of geometric theorems short and checkable.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.2 · Worked example 1

Vectors and geometry

Worked example 8.2.1

Problem. Show that the points A(1, 2), B(4, 6) and C(7, 10) are collinear.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the vectors between consecutive points and check whether one is a multiple of the other.

  1. The position vectors are a = (1, 2), b = (4, 6) and c = (7, 10).
  2. Then AB = b − a = (3, 4) and BC = c − b = (3, 4).
  3. Since AB = BC exactly, the two vectors are equal and hence parallel.
  4. They also share the point B, so A, B and C lie on one straight line.
  5. Moreover B is the midpoint of AC, because AB = BC.

Final answer. the three points are collinear, and B is the midpoint of AC

Interpretation. One computation settles both collinearity and the midpoint claim.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.2 · Worked example 2

Vectors and geometry

Worked example 8.2.2

Problem. Find the point that divides the line from P(2, −1) to Q(8, 5) in the ratio 2 : 3.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the section formula with the ratio 2 : 3.

  1. The point dividing PQ in the ratio 2 : 3 has position vector (3p + 2q)/(2 + 3).
  2. The x-coordinate is (3 × 2 + 2 × 8)/5 = 22/5 = 4.4.
  3. The y-coordinate is (3 × (−1) + 2 × 5)/5 = 7/5 = 1.4.
  4. So the point is (4.4, 1.4).
  5. Check: it lies between P(2, −1) and Q(8, 5), as a section point must.

Final answer. (4.4, 1.4)

Interpretation. The weights are the opposite parts of the ratio, which is why the formula has them crossed.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.3
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.3

Vectors in three dimensions

Inquiry question

What changes when a third dimension is added?

Your task

Take the vectors a = (1, 1, 0), b = (0, 1, 1) and c = (1, 0, 1). Compute |a|, |b|, |c|, a · b, b · c, c · a, a × b and the scalar triple product a · (b × c). Then decide whether the three vectors are coplanar and explain how you know.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.3
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.3

Vectors in three dimensions

What do you notice?
  • All three vectors had the same magnitude, √2.
  • All three scalar products were 1, so the angles were all equal.
  • The scalar triple product was zero, so the three vectors were coplanar.
  • The vectors formed a regular pattern in the plane x + y + z = 1.
Observation. A zero scalar triple product is the test for coplanarity.
Mathematical conclusion

Adding a third dimension extends every operation component-wise and adds the vector product, whose magnitude is an area and whose direction is perpendicular to both factors. The scalar triple product is a volume and vanishes exactly for coplanar vectors. Here all three vectors had magnitude √2, all pairwise angles were equal, and the triple product was 0.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.3 · Vectors in three dimensions
Chapter 8 · 8.3

Vectors in three dimensions

A three-dimensional vector has three components, and all the two-dimensional operations extend component-wise. The magnitude becomes √(x² + y² + z²) and the scalar product gains a third term.

The vector product a × b is defined only in three dimensions, and it gives a vector perpendicular to both a and b. Its magnitude is |a||b| sin θ, which is the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b.

The vector product is anti-commutative: a × b = −(b × a). The order matters, and the right-hand rule fixes which of the two perpendicular directions is meant.

The scalar triple product a · (b × c) gives the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the three vectors, and it is zero exactly when the three vectors are coplanar. It is the three-dimensional analogue of the determinant test.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.3 · Worked example 1

Vectors in three dimensions

Worked example 8.3.1

Problem. Find the vector product of a = (1, 2, 3) and b = (4, 5, 6), and verify it is perpendicular to both.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the component formula and check with scalar products.

  1. The vector product a × b = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂, a₃b₁ − a₁b₃, a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).
  2. So a × b = (2 × 6 − 3 × 5, 3 × 4 − 1 × 6, 1 × 5 − 2 × 4).
  3. That is (12 − 15, 12 − 6, 5 − 8) = (−3, 6, −3).
  4. Check with a: a · (a × b) = 1(−3) + 2(6) + 3(−3) = −3 + 12 − 9 = 0.
  5. Check with b: b · (a × b) = 4(−3) + 5(6) + 6(−3) = −12 + 30 − 18 = 0, so it is perpendicular to both.

Final answer. a × b = (−3, 6, −3), perpendicular to both a and b

Interpretation. The two scalar-product checks are quick and confirm the perpendicularity the definition promises.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.3 · Worked example 2

Vectors in three dimensions

Worked example 8.3.2

Problem. Find the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by a = (2, 0, 1), b = (1, 3, 0) and c = (0, 1, 4).

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the vector product b × c, then its scalar product with a.

  1. First b × c = (3 × 4 − 0 × 1, 0 × 0 − 1 × 4, 1 × 1 − 3 × 0) = (12, −4, 1).
  2. Then the scalar triple product is a · (b × c) = 2 × 12 + 0 × (−4) + 1 × 1 = 25.
  3. The volume is the absolute value, 25 cubic units.
  4. Since the triple product is not zero, the three vectors are not coplanar.
  5. The sign would be negative if the order were reversed, which is why the absolute value is taken.

Final answer. volume 25 cubic units

Interpretation. The scalar triple product is the determinant of the 3 by 3 matrix with the three vectors as rows, which is why it also tests coplanarity.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.4
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.4

Matrices and transformations

Inquiry question

How does a matrix encode a transformation?

Your task

Write the matrices for a rotation through 90°, a reflection in the line y = x, and an enlargement of factor 3. Apply each to the points (1, 0), (0, 1) and (2, 1), and record the images. Then compute the product of the rotation and the reflection matrices in both orders and comment on the difference.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.4
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.4

Matrices and transformations

What do you notice?
  • The rotation and the reflection both preserved lengths, but their determinants differed in sign.
  • The enlargement multiplied every length by 3 and areas by 9.
  • The two products were different matrices, confirming that order matters.
  • Both products were reflections, one in the x-axis and one in the y-axis.
Observation. The columns of a matrix are the images of the basis vectors, and the determinant is the area scale factor.
Mathematical conclusion

A matrix encodes a transformation by recording the images of the basis vectors in its columns, and composition is matrix multiplication in the order of application. The determinant is the area scale factor, positive for orientation-preserving transformations and negative for orientation-reversing ones. Here the rotation then reflection gave [[1, 0], [0, −1]] while the reverse order gave [[−1, 0], [0, 1]].

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.4 · Matrices and transformations
Chapter 8 · 8.4

Matrices and transformations

A 2 by 2 matrix acts on a column vector by multiplication, and the two columns of the matrix are the images of the basis vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1). This representation determines the whole transformation by where it sends the basis.

The matrix for a rotation through θ is [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]], for a reflection in a line through the origin at angle θ it is [[cos 2θ, sin 2θ], [sin 2θ, −cos 2θ]], and for an enlargement of factor k it is [[k, 0], [0, k]].

Composition of transformations is matrix multiplication in the same order: applying M then N is the matrix NM, so systems of transformations compose by multiplying their matrices. The order matters, which is why matrix multiplication is not commutative.

A transformation with matrix M is linear exactly when M(au + bv) = aM(u) + bM(v), which every matrix multiplication satisfies. Linearity is what makes matrices the natural language for transformations.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.4 · Worked example 1

Matrices and transformations

Worked example 8.4.1

Problem. Find the image of the point (3, 1) under the matrix [[2, 1], [−1, 3]], and describe the transformation.

Mathematical reasoning. Read the images of the basis vectors from the columns, then combine them for the given point.

  1. The first column (2, −1) is the image of (1, 0).
  2. The second column (1, 3) is the image of (0, 1).
  3. The image of (3, 1) is 3 × (2, −1) + 1 × (1, 3) = (6, −3) + (1, 3) = (7, 0).
  4. Check by direct multiplication: 2(3) + 1(1) = 7 and −1(3) + 3(1) = 0.
  5. The determinant is 2 × 3 − 1 × (−1) = 7, so areas are multiplied by 7.

Final answer. (7, 0); the determinant is 7

Interpretation. Reading the columns as the images of the basis vectors is the quickest way to understand a matrix.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.4 · Worked example 2

Matrices and transformations

Worked example 8.4.2

Problem. Write the matrix for a rotation through 60° and find the image of the point (1, 0).

Mathematical reasoning. Substitute the angle into the rotation matrix and multiply.

  1. The rotation matrix for angle θ is [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].
  2. With θ = 60°, this is [[0.5, −0.8660], [0.8660, 0.5]].
  3. The image of (1, 0) is the first column, (0.5, 0.8660).
  4. Its magnitude is √(0.25 + 0.75) = 1, as a rotation preserves length.
  5. The image of (0, 1) is the second column, (−0.8660, 0.5), also of magnitude 1.

Final answer. [[0.5, −0.8660], [0.8660, 0.5]]; the image of (1, 0) is (0.5, 0.8660)

Interpretation. The determinant of a rotation matrix is 1, which is why rotations preserve area.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.5
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.5

Determinants and inverse matrices

Inquiry question

What does the determinant decide?

Your task

Take the matrices M = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], N = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] and P = [[2, 0], [0, 3]]. Compute det M, det N, det P, det(MN), det(MP) and det(MNP). Find M−1^{-1}−1 and check it by multiplication. Then find a matrix Q with det Q = 0 and describe what its transformation does.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.5
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.5

Determinants and inverse matrices

What do you notice?
  • Every product determinant was the product of the individual determinants.
  • The determinant of N was 1, so that rotation preserved area.
  • The determinant of P was 6, so that enlargement multiplied areas by 6.
  • The matrix Q had determinant 0 and collapsed the plane onto a line.
Observation. The determinant multiplies over products, and a zero determinant means no inverse exists.
Mathematical conclusion

The determinant is the signed area scale factor of a transformation: positive for orientation-preserving, negative for orientation-reversing, and zero for a collapse. The inverse exists exactly when the determinant is non-zero, and det(AB) = det(A) det(B). Here det M = −2, det N = 1, det P = 6, and the product determinants were −2, −12 and −12.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.5 · Determinants and inverse matrices
Chapter 8 · 8.5

Determinants and inverse matrices

The determinant of [[a, b], [c, d]] is ad − bc. It is the signed area scale factor of the transformation: the area of an image is |det| times the area of the original.

A negative determinant means the transformation reverses orientation, as a reflection does. A determinant of zero means the transformation collapses the plane onto a line or a point, and the transformation cannot be undone.

The inverse matrix exists exactly when the determinant is not zero, and it is given by (1/det)[[d, −b], [−c, a]]. The check is that the product of the matrix and its inverse is the identity.

The determinant of a product is the product of the determinants, so det(AB) = det(A) det(B). This is why a single non-invertible matrix in a product makes the whole product non-invertible.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.5 · Worked example 1

Determinants and inverse matrices

Worked example 8.5.1

Problem. Find the determinant and, if it exists, the inverse of [[4, 7], [2, 3]].

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the determinant, form the adjugate, and verify by multiplication.

  1. The determinant is 4 × 3 − 7 × 2 = 12 − 14 = −2.
  2. Since it is not zero, the inverse exists.
  3. The adjugate is [[3, −7], [−2, 4]].
  4. So the inverse is (−1/2)[[3, −7], [−2, 4]] = [[−1.5, 3.5], [1, −2]].
  5. Check: multiplying the matrix by this gives the identity matrix.

Final answer. det = −2; inverse [[−1.5, 3.5], [1, −2]]

Interpretation. The negative determinant means the transformation reverses orientation, and areas are halved.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.5 · Worked example 2

Determinants and inverse matrices

Worked example 8.5.2

Problem. Show that [[2, 4], [3, 6]] has no inverse and describe what the transformation does.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the determinant and interpret a zero value.

  1. The determinant is 2 × 6 − 4 × 3 = 12 − 12 = 0.
  2. So the inverse does not exist.
  3. The second column (4, 6) is twice the first (2, 3), so the two basis vectors map to parallel vectors.
  4. Every image is a multiple of (2, 3), so the whole plane is collapsed onto that line.
  5. The collapse cannot be undone, because many points share one image.

Final answer. no inverse; the transformation collapses the plane onto the line through (2, 3)

Interpretation. A zero determinant is the algebraic signature of a collapse, and it is the reason the inverse fails to exist.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.6
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.6

Investigation: area scale factors

Inquiry question

How does the determinant show up in an area?

Your task

Take the unit square with vertices (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1) and (0, 1). Apply the matrices [[2, 1], [0, 3]] and [[1, 2], [3, 6]] to its vertices, and find the area of each image. Compare the areas with the determinants and explain what happens in the second case.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.6
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.6

Investigation: area scale factors

What do you notice?
  • The first image was a parallelogram of area 6, matching the determinant.
  • The second image collapsed to a line segment of area 0, matching the zero determinant.
  • The unit square's original area was 1, so the scale factors were 6 and 0.
  • The collapse destroyed the area completely, which is why no inverse exists.
Observation. The determinant is exactly the factor by which areas are multiplied.
Mathematical conclusion

The determinant of the matrix of two spanning vectors is the signed area of the parallelogram they span, and the determinant of a transformation is the factor by which every area is multiplied. A zero determinant collapses the image onto a line and destroys the area. Here the scale factors were 6 and 0.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.6 · Investigation: area scale factors
Chapter 8 · 8.6

Investigation: area scale factors

The area of the parallelogram spanned by two vectors (a, b) and (c, d) is |ad − bc|, which is exactly the absolute value of the determinant. This is the geometric meaning of the determinant.

The same determinant is the scalar triple product in three dimensions, where it gives the volume of a parallelepiped. The pattern is the same in every dimension: the determinant measures the size of the image of a unit box.

When a transformation is applied to a shape, every area is multiplied by |det|. This is why the determinant is checked before computing an area after a transformation, and why a zero determinant means the area is destroyed.

The determinant also appears in the change of variables formula for integrals, where a change of coordinates multiplies areas by the Jacobian determinant. The same number measures the local stretching of a map.

Formal development

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 8 · 8.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: area scale factors

Worked example 8.6.1

Problem. Find the area of the parallelogram spanned by (3, 1) and (−2, 5).

Mathematical reasoning. Form the determinant of the two vectors and take its absolute value.

  1. The determinant of the two vectors is 3 × 5 − 1 × (−2) = 15 + 2 = 17.
  2. The area is the absolute value, 17 square units.
  3. Check with base times height: the base is |(3, 1)| = √10.
  4. The height is the component of (−2, 5) perpendicular to (3, 1), which is 17 ÷ √10 ≈ 5.38.
  5. So the area is √10 × 5.38 ≈ 17, as required.

Final answer. 17 square units

Interpretation. The determinant gives the signed area, and the sign only records the orientation of the pair.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: area scale factors

Worked example 8.6.2

Problem. A triangle has vertices (0, 0), (4, 1) and (1, 5). Find its area using a determinant.

Mathematical reasoning. Take the two side vectors from one vertex, form the determinant, and halve it.

  1. The side vectors from the origin are (4, 1) and (1, 5).
  2. Their determinant is 4 × 5 − 1 × 1 = 19.
  3. The parallelogram spanned by them has area 19.
  4. The triangle is half of that, so its area is 9.5.
  5. Check with the shoelace formula, which gives the same value.

Final answer. 9.5 square units

Interpretation. The determinant formula for a triangle's area is faster than finding a base and a height.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.7
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which operation does this problem need?

Your task

Take the vectors a = (2, −1), b = (4, 3) and the matrices M = [[1, −1], [2, 0]] and N = [[0, 2], [1, 1]]. Compute a + b, 2a − 3b, |a + b|, a · b, det M, det N, det(MN), M−1^{-1}−1, and the area of the parallelogram spanned by a and b. Record the geometric meaning of each determinant.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 8.7
Chapter 8 · Investigation 8.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • The determinant of M was positive, so that transformation preserved orientation.
  • The determinant of N was negative, so that transformation reversed it.
  • The product determinant was the product, −4, reversing orientation and scaling areas by 4.
  • The parallelogram area came from the determinant of the two side vectors.
Observation. The determinant links the algebra of a matrix to the geometry of area and orientation.
Mathematical conclusion

Vectors combine component-wise and matrices encode transformations, with composition read in the order of application. The determinant is the signed area scale factor and decides invertibility: it multiplies over products, is positive for orientation-preserving transformations and negative for orientation-reversing ones, and zero exactly when no inverse exists. Here det M = 2, det N = −2 and det(MN) = −4.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 8 · 8.7

Mixed practice

Vector problems are recognised by the presence of directions: displacement, force, velocity and position are all vectors. Scalar problems have magnitude only, and confusing the two is the commonest error.

Matrix problems are recognised by the presence of transformations. The order of composition is the order of application, read from right to left, and reversing it changes the answer.

The determinant is the bridge between the algebra and the geometry: it tells you the area scale factor and whether an inverse exists. Computing it early is a good habit, because it settles both questions at once.

Mixed practice is where the operation is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Mixed practice

Worked example 8.7.1

Problem. Given a = (3, −2) and b = (−1, 5), find 3a − 2b.

Mathematical reasoning. Scale each vector and combine component by component.

  1. 3a = (9, −6) and 2b = (−2, 10).
  2. Subtracting gives (9 − (−2), −6 − 10) = (11, −16).
  3. The magnitude is √(121 + 256) = √377 ≈ 19.42.
  4. The direction is arctan(−16/11), below the positive x-axis.
  5. There is no ambiguity, because vector arithmetic is component-wise.

Final answer. (11, −16)

Interpretation. The components are combined separately, and the magnitude is recovered only if it is needed.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook8.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 8 · 8.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 8.7.2

Problem. Find the determinant of [[3, 5], [6, 10]] and explain why the matrix has no inverse.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the determinant and interpret a zero value.

  1. The determinant is 3 × 10 − 5 × 6 = 30 − 30 = 0.
  2. The two columns are proportional, since (5, 10) is 5/3 of (3, 6).
  3. So the two basis vectors map to parallel vectors and the plane collapses onto a line.
  4. The collapse cannot be reversed, so no inverse exists.
  5. The area scale factor is zero, which is the geometric statement of the same fact.

Final answer. determinant 0; no inverse exists

Interpretation. A zero determinant, proportional columns and a collapsed image are three descriptions of one situation.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 8 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A vector has magnitude and direction and combines component-wise.
  • The magnitude of (x, y) is √(x² + y²).
  • The scalar product a · b = |a||b| cos θ is zero exactly for perpendicular vectors.
  • The columns of a matrix are the images of the basis vectors.
  • Composition of transformations is matrix multiplication in the order of application.
  • The determinant ad − bc is the signed area scale factor.
  • A negative determinant reverses orientation; a zero determinant collapses the plane.
  • The inverse exists exactly when the determinant is non-zero.
  • det(AB) = det(A) det(B).
  • The vector product gives a vector perpendicular to both factors, with magnitude equal to the area they span.

Vocabulary

vector · magnitude · direction · position vector · scalar product · unit vector · column vector · matrix · transformation · determinant · inverse matrix · identity matrix · adj ugate · vector product · scalar triple product · coplanar · shear · orientation
