MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 9 · Statistics: Dispersion, Correlation and Regression
Chapter 9 · Part IV · Reasoning with data
09

Statistics: Dispersion, Correlation and Regression

A single average describes a group's centre and nothing else. Dispersion describes how the group is spread, and association describes how two variables move together, and neither can say more than the data allows.

Engage

Two classes have the same mean test score. One class has every student within two marks of the mean; the other has scores from the lowest to the highest possible. Are the two classes equally well taught, and what would you need to know to decide?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Relationships
Related concepts: Patterns · Representation · Measurement
Global context: Identities and relationships
Global context exploration: how groups differ, and how claims about them are made

Statement of inquiry: Two groups can share a centre and differ in every other respect; measuring dispersion and association describes those differences precisely, while the origin of the data limits what the description can prove.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What do the range, the interquartile range, the variance and the standard deviation measure?
  • Conceptual: Why can two data sets share a mean and differ completely, and what does a correlation coefficient measure?
  • Debatable: If a correlation is strong, is a causal claim justified?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to judge a claim made about two groups, students must compare a measure of centre with a measure of dispersion, consider the origin of the data, and justify what the comparison can and cannot show.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.1
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.1

Measuring spread

Inquiry question

Why is a single average not enough to describe a group?

Your task

Take six data sets of your own, each with the same mean of 10: one with no spread at all, one with a small spread, one with a large spread, one with one extreme outlier, one with two clusters, and one symmetric. Compute the range, the interquartile range and the standard deviation of each, and record which measure best captures the difference.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.1
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.1

Measuring spread

What do you notice?
  • The data set with an outlier had a huge range but a zero interquartile range.
  • The two-cluster set had a large interquartile range but a standard deviation similar to the wide set.
  • The set with no spread had every measure equal to zero.
  • No single measure described all six sets adequately, which is why more than one is reported.
Observation. Different measures of spread respond to different features of a data set, and an outlier distorts the range and the standard deviation but not the interquartile range.
Mathematical conclusion

A single average describes a centre and nothing else, so a measure of dispersion is needed alongside it. The range is sensitive to extremes, the interquartile range is resistant to them, and the standard deviation uses every value in the same units as the data. Here the outlier set had range 30 with interquartile range 0.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.1 · Measuring spread
Chapter 9 · 9.1

Measuring spread

The range is the difference between the largest and smallest values, and it is sensitive to every extreme value. It is quick to compute and quick to mislead, because one unusual observation can change it completely.

The interquartile range is the difference between the upper and lower quartiles, and it describes the middle half of the data. It is resistant to outliers, which is why it is preferred when the data contain extreme values.

The variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean, and the standard deviation is its square root. The standard deviation is in the same units as the data, which is what makes it interpretable.

There are two conventions for variance: the population variance divides by n and the sample variance divides by n − 1. The sample version is unbiased for estimating the population variance, and the convention in use must always be stated.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.1 · Worked example 1

Measuring spread

Worked example 9.1.1

Problem. Find the range, the interquartile range and the standard deviation of the data 4, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 16.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the mean, then the range, the quartiles and the deviations.

  1. The mean is (4 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 11 + 13 + 16)/7 = 68/7 ≈ 9.714.
  2. The range is 16 − 4 = 12.
  3. The lower quartile is 7.5 and the upper quartile is 12.5, so the interquartile range is 5.
  4. The squared deviations sum to 82.857, so the population variance is 82.857/7 ≈ 11.837.
  5. The population standard deviation is √11.837 ≈ 3.44, and the sample standard deviation is √(82.857/6) ≈ 3.72.

Final answer. range 12, interquartile range 5, population standard deviation about 3.44

Interpretation. The interquartile range is much smaller than the range because the extremes are excluded, which is exactly its purpose.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.1 · Worked example 2

Measuring spread

Worked example 9.1.2

Problem. Two data sets both have mean 50. Set A has standard deviation 2 and set B has standard deviation 12. Explain what this means for the two groups.

Mathematical reasoning. Compare the standard deviations while noting the equal means.

  1. Both sets have the same mean of 50, so their centres agree.
  2. Set A has a standard deviation of 2, so most of its values lie close to 50.
  3. Set B has a standard deviation of 12, so its values are typically 12 units from the mean.
  4. The two groups therefore differ completely even though their means are identical.
  5. A report giving only the means would hide the difference entirely.

Final answer. the means agree but the spreads differ by a factor of 6

Interpretation. This is the case the inquiry statement describes: a shared centre with a complete difference in every other respect.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.2
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.2

Standard deviation and grouped data

Inquiry question

How is dispersion computed when the data are grouped?

Your task

Take a data set of your own with at least 20 values, group it into classes of equal width, and compute the mean and standard deviation from the grouped table. Then compute them from the raw values and compare, explaining any difference.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.2
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.2

Standard deviation and grouped data

What do you notice?
  • The narrower the classes, the closer the grouped answers were to the raw answers.
  • The widest classes gave the largest errors in both measures.
  • The mean was always slightly affected by the mid-point assumption.
  • The standard deviation was affected less, because within-class variation partly cancels.
Observation. Grouping replaces each value by its class mid-point, and the error shrinks as the classes narrow.
Mathematical conclusion

For grouped data the mid-point of each class stands in for every value in it, and the mean and standard deviation are computed from the frequency table with the formula variance = (sum of f x²)/(sum of f) − mean². The mid-point assumption introduces an error that narrows the classes reduce. Here the raw mean was 31.4 and the grouped estimates were 31.0, 31.3 and 30.0.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.2 · Standard deviation and grouped data
Chapter 9 · 9.2

Standard deviation and grouped data

For grouped data with frequencies, the mean is the sum of each value times its frequency divided by the total frequency. The standard deviation is computed from the same table, using the squared deviations.

The coding shortcut replaces each value x by (x − a)/h for a convenient a and class width h, computes the standard deviation of the coded values, and multiplies by h. The shift does not affect the spread, and the scale multiplies it.

For a frequency table, the variance is (sum of f x²)/(sum of f) − mean². This form is faster than summing squared deviations and is the one used in practice.

When data are grouped into classes, the mid-point of each class represents every value in it. This introduces a within-class error that the standard deviation cannot detect, and it is stated as a limitation of the calculation.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.2 · Worked example 1

Standard deviation and grouped data

Worked example 9.2.1

Problem. Find the mean and standard deviation of the data summarised by x = 2, 4, 6, 8 with frequencies 3, 5, 2, 1.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the frequency-table formula for the mean and the variance.

  1. The total frequency is 3 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 11.
  2. The sum of f x is 6 + 20 + 12 + 8 = 46, so the mean is 46/11 ≈ 4.18.
  3. The sum of f x² is 12 + 80 + 72 + 64 = 228.
  4. The variance is 228/11 − (46/11)² ≈ 20.73 − 17.50 ≈ 3.23.
  5. The standard deviation is √3.23 ≈ 1.80.

Final answer. mean about 4.18, standard deviation about 1.80

Interpretation. The frequency table formula is the same calculation written in a form that avoids listing every observation.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.2 · Worked example 2

Standard deviation and grouped data

Worked example 9.2.2

Problem. The heights of 40 plants are grouped into classes 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–29 with frequencies 4, 12, 16, 8. Estimate the mean and standard deviation.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the mid-points as representative values and apply the frequency formula.

  1. The mid-points are 12, 17, 22 and 27.
  2. The total frequency is 40 and the sum of f times mid-point is 48 + 204 + 352 + 216 = 820.
  3. So the estimated mean is 820/40 = 20.5.
  4. The sum of f times mid-point squared is 4(144) + 12(289) + 16(484) + 8(729) = 576 + 3468 + 7744 + 5832 = 17 620.
  5. The variance is 17 620/40 − 20.5² = 440.5 − 420.25 = 20.25, so the standard deviation is 4.5.

Final answer. estimated mean 20.5, estimated standard deviation 4.5

Interpretation. The mid-point assumption is an estimate, and the true standard deviation within each class is hidden by it.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.3
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.3

Comparing distributions

Inquiry question

How are two distributions compared fairly?

Your task

Collect two data sets of your own from different sources — for example reaction times and test scores. Compute the mean, median, standard deviation and interquartile range of each, draw box plots of both, and write a comparison that states what the comparison can and cannot show.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.3
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.3

Comparing distributions

What do you notice?
  • The two sets had different units, so their standard deviations could not be compared directly.
  • Comparing each standard deviation with its own mean showed that the second set was more spread relative to its centre.
  • The first set was roughly symmetric, so the mean and median were close.
  • The second set was skewed right, so its mean exceeded its median.
Observation. A fair comparison uses centre, dispersion and shape together, and notes the units.
Mathematical conclusion

Two distributions are compared by a measure of centre, a measure of dispersion and a statement of shape, and the sample sizes and the origin of the data limit what the comparison can show. Where the distributions are skewed, the median is the better centre. Here the second set was more spread relative to its mean and skewed to the right.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.3 · Comparing distributions
Chapter 9 · 9.3

Comparing distributions

Two distributions are compared by a measure of centre, a measure of dispersion, and a statement of the shape. Reporting only the means is the commonest statistical error, and it hides exactly the difference the inquiry statement describes.

A box plot displays the minimum, the lower quartile, the median, the upper quartile and the maximum, so it shows centre, spread and shape at once, and it is a representation of a whole distribution in five numbers. Comparing two box plots side by side is the standard visual comparison.

The shape of a distribution is described as symmetric, skewed to the left or skewed to the right. When a distribution is skewed, the median is a better measure of centre than the mean, because the mean is pulled towards the tail.

A comparison must state the sample sizes and the origin of the data, because a difference between two small samples may not be a difference between the populations they came from.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.3 · Worked example 1

Comparing distributions

Worked example 9.3.1

Problem. Two groups of seven values each are recorded. Group A has mean 50 and standard deviation 2; group B has mean 50 and standard deviation 12. Write a comparison of the two groups.

Mathematical reasoning. Compare centre, dispersion and shape in turn.

  1. Both groups have the same mean of 50, so their centres agree.
  2. Group A has a standard deviation of 2 and group B of 12, so group B is six times as spread.
  3. The interquartile ranges tell the same story: 3 against 18.
  4. The shapes differ too, with group A tightly clustered and group B widely spread.
  5. So the two groups are completely different despite an identical mean, and any report giving only the mean would be misleading.

Final answer. the means agree; group B is six times as dispersed as group A

Interpretation. The comparison names all three aspects, and it states what the shared mean hides.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.3 · Worked example 2

Comparing distributions

Worked example 9.3.2

Problem. A distribution has mean 40, median 34 and mode 28. Describe its shape and say which measure of centre to report.

Mathematical reasoning. Compare the three measures and use their order to identify the skew.

  1. The three measures are 28, 34 and 40.
  2. The mean is the largest, so the distribution is skewed to the right.
  3. A right skew means a long tail of large values pulling the mean upwards.
  4. The median is the better measure of centre here, because it is not affected by the tail.
  5. So the report should give the median, 34, with a note that the distribution is skewed.

Final answer. skewed to the right; report the median, 34

Interpretation. The order of the three measures diagnoses the skew, and the skew decides which measure to report.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.4
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.4

Scatter graphs and correlation

Inquiry question

What does a correlation coefficient measure, and what does it not?

Your task

Collect ten paired observations of your own on two variables you suspect are related. Draw a scatter graph, compute the correlation coefficient, and then write a paragraph on whether the correlation supports a causal claim, giving at least one alternative explanation.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.4
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.4

Scatter graphs and correlation

What do you notice?
  • The scatter graph was roughly linear and sloped upwards.
  • The correlation coefficient was 0.78, indicating a strong positive linear association.
  • A third variable, time of day, could plausibly explain both.
  • The data supported a claim of association only.
Observation. A strong correlation establishes association, not causation, and an alternative explanation is always available.
Mathematical conclusion

The correlation coefficient r measures the strength of a linear association and lies between −1 and 1, and it is unchanged by a change of units. It says nothing about causation: a common cause, a reverse cause or coincidence can all produce a strong r. Here r was 0.78 and the causal claim was not supported.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.4 · Scatter graphs and correlation
Chapter 9 · 9.4

Scatter graphs and correlation

A scatter graph plots one variable against another, and its overall patterns are described by direction, strength and shape. A straight-line pattern suggests linear correlation; a curved pattern suggests a non-linear relationship, and the eye reads the patterns before any number is computed.

The product-moment correlation coefficient r lies between −1 and 1. Values near 1 indicate strong positive linear correlation, values near −1 strong negative linear correlation, and values near 0 little or no linear correlation, so the number summarises the pattern of the scatter.

The coefficient is computed from the covariance of the two variables divided by the product of their standard deviations, which is why it is unaffected by the units of measurement, and it is a representation of the pattern in a single number. Changing metres to centimetres does not change r.

Correlation is not causation. Two variables may be correlated because one causes the other, because both are caused by a third, or by coincidence, and the data alone cannot distinguish these cases.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.4 · Worked example 1

Scatter graphs and correlation

Worked example 9.4.1

Problem. Compute the correlation coefficient for the paired data (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 6).

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the summary sums and substitute into the formula.

  1. The means are x̄ = 3 and ȳ = 4.2.
  2. The sum of x y is 2 + 8 + 15 + 16 + 30 = 71.
  3. The sum of x² is 55 and the sum of y² is 97.
  4. The correlation is (5 × 71 − 15 × 21) ÷ √((5 × 55 − 225)(5 × 97 − 441)) = 80 ÷ √(50 × 44) ≈ 0.855.
  5. So r ≈ 0.855, indicating strong positive linear correlation.

Final answer. r ≈ 0.855

Interpretation. The coefficient is dimensionless, so it is unaffected by a change of units in either variable.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.4 · Worked example 2

Scatter graphs and correlation

Worked example 9.4.2

Problem. Explain why a correlation of 0.93 between ice-cream sales and drowning deaths does not show that ice cream causes drowning.

Mathematical reasoning. Consider the possible explanations for a correlation and identify the plausible one.

  1. A correlation of 0.93 is strong, so the two variables really do move together.
  2. But correlation measures association, not causation.
  3. Both ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise in hot weather, so temperature is a common cause.
  4. Once temperature is accounted for, the association between the other two largely disappears.
  5. So the data support a claim of association only, and any causal claim needs further evidence.

Final answer. temperature is a common cause; correlation is not causation

Interpretation. The origin of the data limits what the correlation can show, which is the second half of the inquiry statement.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.5
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.5

Regression and prediction

Inquiry question

How is a line of best fit used, and what are its limits?

Your task

Take ten paired observations of your own, compute the regression line of y on x, and use it to predict y at a value of x inside the data range and one outside. Then compute the line of x on y and compare the two lines, and comment on the reliability of each prediction.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.5
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.5

Regression and prediction

What do you notice?
  • The two regression lines were different, as expected with |r| < 1.
  • The interpolation gave a value inside the observed range.
  • The extrapolation gave a value far outside it, and assumed the relationship continued.
  • The two gradients were not reciprocals, because the lines minimise different distances.
Observation. The regression line of y on x predicts y from x, and extrapolation assumes the relationship continues beyond the data.
Mathematical conclusion

The regression line of y on x minimises the vertical distances and predicts y from x, and it is computed from the same summary sums as the correlation coefficient. Interpolation within the range of the data is reliable; extrapolation beyond it assumes the relationship continues. The line of x on y is different whenever |r| < 1. Here the two gradients were 0.78 and about 1.64.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.5 · Regression and prediction
Chapter 9 · 9.5

Regression and prediction

The regression line of y on x is the line that minimises the sum of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line. It is written y = a + bx, and it is the line used to predict y from x.

The gradient is b = covariance ÷ variance of x, and the intercept is a = ȳ − b x̄. Both are computed from the same summary sums as the correlation coefficient, and r is the normalised version of b.

Interpolation is prediction within the range of the data, and it is usually reliable. Extrapolation is prediction beyond that range, and it assumes the relationship continues, which is an assumption and not a fact.

The regression line of x on y is a different line from the regression line of y on x, unless the correlation is exactly ±1. The two lines answer different questions, and using the wrong one gives a wrong prediction.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.5 · Worked example 1

Regression and prediction

Worked example 9.5.1

Problem. Find the regression line of y on x for the data (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 6), and predict y when x = 6.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the summary sums, then the gradient and intercept.

  1. The means are x̄ = 3 and ȳ = 4.2.
  2. The gradient is (5 × 71 − 15 × 21)/(5 × 55 − 225) = 80/50 = 1.6.
  3. The intercept is ȳ − b x̄ = 4.2 − 1.6(3) = −0.6.
  4. So the line is y = 1.6x − 0.6.
  5. At x = 6 the prediction is y = 9.0, which is an extrapolation beyond the data and so less reliable.

Final answer. y = 1.6x − 0.6; prediction 9.0 at x = 6

Interpretation. The prediction is labelled as extrapolation, and the assumption it makes is stated.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.5 · Worked example 2

Regression and prediction

Worked example 9.5.2

Problem. A student uses the regression line of x on y to predict y from x. Explain the error.

Mathematical reasoning. Identify which distances each line minimises and which prediction it supports.

  1. The line of y on x minimises the vertical distances, so it is the line for predicting y from x.
  2. The line of x on y minimises the horizontal distances, so it is the line for predicting x from y.
  3. The two lines coincide only when |r| = 1, that is when the points lie exactly on a line.
  4. In general they are different, and using the wrong one gives a biased prediction.
  5. So the student must use the line of y on x.

Final answer. the wrong line was used; the line of y on x is required

Interpretation. Naming which variable is being predicted is the first step in any regression question.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.6
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.6

Investigation: correlation, causation and reliability

Inquiry question

What limits a statistical description?

Your task

Take a published correlation claim from a newspaper or a website. Identify the variables, the sample, the correlation coefficient and the causal claim, if any. Then write an evaluation stating what the data support, what they do not, and at least one alternative explanation.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.6
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.6

Investigation: correlation, causation and reliability

What do you notice?
  • Both variables were self-reported, which introduced a common measurement bias.
  • The sample came from one country, so the association might not generalise.
  • The coefficient of 0.4 indicated a moderate association only.
  • The causal claim was not supported, and a common cause was plausible.
Observation. The origin of the data limits the description, and a causal claim needs more than a correlation.
Mathematical conclusion

A statistical description describes the sample measured and extends to a wider population only if the sample was representative. A correlation may arise from a common cause, a reverse cause or coincidence, and distinguishing these needs an experiment rather than a larger sample. Reporting the coefficient with and without influential points is the standard robustness check.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.6 · Investigation: correlation, causation and reliability
Chapter 9 · 9.6

Investigation: correlation, causation and reliability

A statistical description describes the relationships within the sample that was measured, and it extends to a wider population only if the sample was representative. The origin of the data is therefore part of the result, not a footnote.

A correlation may arise from a common cause, from a reverse cause, or from coincidence. Distinguishing these requires an experiment or a controlled study, not a larger sample of the same kind.

The reliability of an estimate is described by a confidence interval, which is a range of values consistent with the data. A narrow interval means the estimate is precise; it says nothing about whether the estimate is unbiased.

An outlier can change a correlation coefficient substantially, because the coefficient is computed from sums of products. Reporting the coefficient with and without the outlier is a standard robustness check.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: correlation, causation and reliability

Worked example 9.6.1

Problem. A data set of nine points gives r = 0.32, but adding a tenth point changes r to 0.91. Investigate what has happened.

Mathematical reasoning. Compare the coefficient with and without the added point and identify its role.

  1. With nine points the correlation is 0.32, indicating weak linear association.
  2. Adding the point (30, 30) raises the correlation to 0.91.
  3. The added point is far from the cluster of the other nine, so it pulls the line towards itself.
  4. Such a point is called an influential outlier, and it changes the coefficient without changing the other data.
  5. The honest report gives both values and identifies the outlier.

Final answer. the tenth point is an influential outlier; report both values

Interpretation. The robustness check is reporting the coefficient with and without the influential point.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: correlation, causation and reliability

Worked example 9.6.2

Problem. A study of 1000 people finds a correlation of 0.6 between hours of television watched and reading score. State what the study shows and what it does not.

Mathematical reasoning. Separate the claim the data support from the claims they do not.

  1. The study shows an association, with r = 0.6 over 1000 people.
  2. The large sample makes the estimate of the association reasonably precise.
  3. It does not show causation, because correlation measures association only.
  4. It does not show the association holds for groups outside the sample, unless the sample was representative of them.
  5. A third variable, such as socioeconomic status, could explain both.

Final answer. an association is shown; causation and generalisation are not

Interpretation. The origin of the data limits the description, which is the second half of the inquiry statement.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.7
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

Which measure, and what does it support?

Your task

Take a data set of at least ten paired observations from a source you choose. Compute the mean and standard deviation of each variable, the correlation coefficient, and the regression line of y on x. Then write an evaluation stating what the analysis supports, what it does not, and one limitation of the data source.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 9.7
Chapter 9 · Investigation 9.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • The correlation was strong, at 0.82.
  • The regression line allowed predictions within the observed range.
  • The sample was self-selected, so the association might not generalise.
  • The analysis supported a claim of association only.
Observation. A complete statistical report gives the centre, the spread, the association and the limitation together.
Mathematical conclusion

A statistics question is answered by choosing the measure that matches what is being described: a centre, a dispersion, an association or a prediction. Skewed data call for the median and the interquartile range, and every association is reported as an association rather than a cause. Here the correlation was 0.82 and the regression line was y = 1.97x + 15.8.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 9 · 9.7

Mixed practice

Every statistics question begins by asking what is being described: a centre, a spread, an association or a prediction. The four need different measures, and using the wrong one is the commonest error.

When data are skewed, the median and the interquartile range are the appropriate measures, because they are resistant to extreme values. When data are symmetric, the mean and the standard deviation use more of the information.

A regression prediction must state whether it is interpolation or extrapolation, and an association must be reported as an association rather than a cause. Both statements are part of the answer.

Mixed practice is where the measure is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 9 · 9.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 9.7.1

Problem. Find the mean and standard deviation of 12, 15, 18, 20, 23.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the mean, then the squared deviations, then the variance.

  1. The mean is (12 + 15 + 18 + 20 + 23)/5 = 88/5 = 17.6.
  2. The deviations are −5.6, −2.6, 0.4, 2.4 and 5.4.
  3. Their squares sum to 31.36 + 6.76 + 0.16 + 5.76 + 29.16 = 73.2.
  4. The population variance is 73.2/5 = 14.64.
  5. The standard deviation is √14.64 ≈ 3.83.

Final answer. mean 17.6, standard deviation about 3.83

Interpretation. The sample standard deviation would divide by 4 instead of 5, and the convention must be stated.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook9.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 9 · 9.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 9.7.2

Problem. A line of best fit is y = 2.4x + 8. Predict y when x = 15 and comment on the prediction if the data ranged from x = 5 to x = 12.

Mathematical reasoning. Substitute, then classify the prediction by comparing x with the data range.

  1. The prediction is y = 2.4(15) + 8 = 44.
  2. The data ranged from x = 5 to x = 12.
  3. Since 15 is outside that range, the prediction is an extrapolation.
  4. Extrapolation assumes the linear relationship continues beyond the observed data.
  5. The prediction should therefore be reported with that assumption stated.

Final answer. 44, an extrapolation assuming the relationship continues

Interpretation. The classification of the prediction is part of the answer, not an optional remark.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 9 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A single average describes a centre and nothing else.
  • The range is the largest minus the smallest value.
  • The interquartile range is the difference of the quartiles and resists outliers.
  • The population variance divides by n; the sample variance divides by n − 1.
  • The standard deviation is the square root of the variance and is in the units of the data.
  • For grouped data, class mid-points stand in for the individual values.
  • The correlation coefficient r lies between −1 and 1 and measures linear association.
  • Correlation is not causation.
  • The regression line of y on x minimises vertical distances.
  • Interpolation is reliable; extrapolation assumes the relationship continues.

Vocabulary

range · interquartile range · variance · standard deviation · population · sample · frequency table · mid-point · skew · symmetric · box plot · scatter graph · correlation coefficient · covariance · regression line · interpolation · extrapolation · outlier · influential point

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 10 · Probability: Conditional Probability and Counting
Chapter 10 · Part IV · Reasoning with data
10

Probability: Conditional Probability and Counting

Probability measures how likely an outcome is on a stated set of possibilities. Conditioning restricts that set, and counting tells us how large the set is, and both decide what a probability means.

Engage

A medical test is 99 per cent accurate. A patient tests positive. What is the probability that the patient has the disease? Most people answer 99 per cent, and they are usually wrong. Why?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Logic
Related concepts: Relationships · Representation · Patterns
Global context: Fairness and development
Global context exploration: risk, screening and fair decisions

Statement of inquiry: Probability is a measure on a set of outcomes; conditioning restricts that set, and the difference between P(A ∣\mid∣ B) and P(B ∣\mid∣ A) is often the difference between a sound decision and a misleading one.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What do conditional probability, independence and the total probability rule state?
  • Conceptual: Why can P(A ∣\mid∣ B) and P(B ∣\mid∣ A) differ enormously, and what decides the difference?
  • Debatable: If a screening test is 99 per cent accurate, is it fair to act on a positive result?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to judge a screening result, students must identify the conditioned set, compute the conditional probability, and justify the conclusion against the reverse conditional probability.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.1
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.1

Sets, tables and probability

Inquiry question

What set is a probability a measure on?

Your task

Take a survey of your own class or group on two yes-or-no questions. Build a two-way table, draw a Venn diagram, and compute the probability of each event, of the union, of the intersection and of the complement. Check that the probabilities sum to one.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.1
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.1

Sets, tables and probability

What do you notice?
  • The four groups of the Venn diagram summed to 30, the whole class.
  • The union was 21, and the intersection was 5.
  • The addition rule gave 14/30 + 11/30 − 5/30 = 20/30, which disagreed with the direct count of 21/30.
  • The disagreement came from a mis-transcribed count, and re-checking gave 14/30 + 11/30 − 4/30 = 21/30.
Observation. The addition rule and the direct count must agree, and a disagreement locates an error.
Mathematical conclusion

A probability is a measure on a stated set of outcomes, and for equally likely outcomes it is a count divided by the total. Two-way tables and Venn diagrams are two representations of the same partition, and the addition rule corrects the double-counted overlap. Here the union was 21 out of 30.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.1 · Sets, tables and probability
Chapter 10 · 10.1

Sets, tables and probability

A probability is a measure on a set of outcomes, and it is only meaningful once the set is stated. The same event can have different probabilities on different sets, and the logic of the calculation depends entirely on which set is meant, which is why the sample space is named first.

For equally likely outcomes, the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. The formula is a counting statement, and its correctness depends entirely on the outcomes being equally likely.

Two-way tables organise two categorical variables, and the probability of an event is a count divided by the relevant total. This representation makes the relationships between the categories visible, and reading the correct total is the whole skill, because the denominator changes with the conditioning.

Venn diagrams display the union, intersection and complement of events, and their patterns of overlap are what the rules of probability encode. The addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) corrects for the double-counted overlap, and mutually exclusive events have no overlap and simply add.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.1 · Worked example 1

Sets, tables and probability

Worked example 10.1.1

Problem. A fair die is rolled. Find the probability that the score is even or greater than 4.

Mathematical reasoning. Count the favourable outcomes directly, and check with the addition rule.

  1. The sample space is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, with six equally likely outcomes.
  2. The even outcomes are 2, 4, 6, so P(even) = 3/6.
  3. The outcomes greater than 4 are 5, 6, so P(> 4) = 2/6.
  4. The overlap is 6 alone, so P(even and > 4) = 1/6.
  5. By the addition rule, P(even or > 4) = 3/6 + 2/6 − 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3.

Final answer. 2/3

Interpretation. The direct count and the addition rule agree, and the overlap is the reason the rule subtracts.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.1 · Worked example 2

Sets, tables and probability

Worked example 10.1.2

Problem. In a class of 30, 18 study French and 14 study Spanish, and 6 study both. Find the probability that a student studies at least one language.

Mathematical reasoning. Partition the class and add the three relevant groups.

  1. French only is 18 − 6 = 12 students.
  2. Spanish only is 14 − 6 = 8 students.
  3. Both is 6, and neither is 30 − 12 − 8 − 6 = 4.
  4. So at least one language is 12 + 8 + 6 = 26 students.
  5. The probability is 26/30 = 13/15.

Final answer. 13/15

Interpretation. The four groups sum to the whole class, which is the check that the partition is complete.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.2
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.2

Conditional probability

Inquiry question

What does conditioning change?

Your task

Take a screening scenario of your own with a stated prevalence and a stated accuracy. Build the two-way table, compute P(positive ∣\mid∣ disease), P(disease ∣\mid∣ positive), and the two false-positive and false-negative rates. Then repeat with the prevalence ten times higher and explain the change.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.2
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.2

Conditional probability

What do you notice?
  • The accuracy P(positive ∣\mid∣ disease) stayed at 0.90, because it depends only on the test.
  • The predictive value P(disease ∣\mid∣ positive) stayed near 0.5, because the false positives grew with the population.
  • Raising the prevalence tenfold increased both predictive values, but only slightly.
  • The false-negative rate stayed at 10 per cent, again because it depends only on the test.
Observation. The test's accuracy is a property of the test, and the predictive value is a property of the test together with the prevalence.
Mathematical conclusion

Conditioning restricts the set of outcomes, and the conditional probability is computed on the restricted set. The two conditional probabilities P(A ∣\mid∣ B) and P(B ∣\mid∣ A) are generally different, and the difference is governed by the prevalence of the conditioning event. Here the test was 90 per cent accurate, but the predictive value was only about 0.5.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.2 · Conditional probability
Chapter 10 · 10.2

Conditional probability

The conditional probability P(A ∣\mid∣ B) is the probability of A given that B has occurred, and it is defined as P(A and B)/P(B). The denominator is the probability of the conditioning event, not the whole sample space.

Conditioning restricts the set of outcomes under consideration. Every probability is computed on a smaller set, and the answer is a probability on that restricted set rather than on the original one.

The definition is a ratio, and it can be rearranged as the multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(B) × P(A ∣\mid∣ B). This is the form used in tree diagrams, where the second branch is conditional.

The reverse conditional probability is found from Bayes' theorem, P(B ∣\mid∣ A) = P(A ∣\mid∣ B)P(B)/P(A). The two conditional probabilities are generally different, and confusing them is the error the inquiry statement names.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.2 · Worked example 1

Conditional probability

Worked example 10.2.1

Problem. A fair die is rolled. Given that the score is even, find the probability that it is greater than 4.

Mathematical reasoning. Restrict the sample space to the conditioning event and count within it.

  1. The conditioning event is that the score is even, so the restricted set is 2, 4, 6.
  2. This set has three equally likely outcomes.
  3. The favourable ones, greater than 4, are just 6.
  4. So P(> 4 ∣\mid∣ even) = 1/3.
  5. Check with the formula: P(> 4 and even)/P(even) = (1/6)/(3/6) = 1/3.

Final answer. 1/3

Interpretation. The denominator changed from 6 to 3, and that change is the whole content of conditioning.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.2 · Worked example 2

Conditional probability

Worked example 10.2.2

Problem. In a group of 100 people, 10 have a disease. A test is positive for 9 of the 10 who have it and for 9 of the 90 who do not. Find the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease.

Mathematical reasoning. Condition on the event of testing positive and divide by the number who test positive.

  1. The number who test positive is 9 + 9 = 18.
  2. Of those, the number who actually have the disease is 9.
  3. So P(disease ∣\mid∣ positive) = 9/18 = 0.5.
  4. Note that P(positive ∣\mid∣ disease) = 9/10 = 0.9, which is a different number.
  5. The difference arises because the disease is rare, so the false positives are numerous.

Final answer. 0.5

Interpretation. This is the base-rate effect: a very accurate test on a rare condition still gives many false positives among the positives.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.3
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.3

Independence

Inquiry question

When does conditioning make no difference?

Your task

Take six pairs of events from a single experiment of your own — for example two dice, a pack of cards, or a spinner. For each pair, decide whether the events are independent, justifying the answer with the product rule. Include at least one pair that feels independent but is not, and one that feels related but is.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.3
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.3

Independence

What do you notice?
  • The pair that felt independent but was not was 'first die even, total is 7', because the total depends on both dice.
  • The pair that felt related but was independent was 'card is a heart, card is a king', since the suits and ranks are separate.
  • Every decision was made by the product rule, not by intuition.
  • Containment always forces dependence, as the heart-and-red pair showed.
Observation. Independence is decided by the product rule, and intuition about it is unreliable.
Mathematical conclusion

Two events are independent exactly when P(A and B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently when conditioning on one does not change the probability of the other. Independence must be justified in the model, because intuition about it is unreliable, and mutually exclusive events are independent only in the trivial case. Here four of the six pairs were independent.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.3 · Independence
Chapter 10 · 10.3

Independence

Two events are independent when P(A ∣\mid∣ B) = P(A), which is equivalent to P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). Conditioning on one event does not change the probability of the other, and that is the whole content of independence.

Independence is a property of a pair of events in a stated model, and it must be justified rather than assumed. Two events that feel unrelated can be dependent, and two that feel related can be independent.

Mutually exclusive events are different from independent events. If A and B cannot both occur, then P(A and B) = 0, so they are independent only if one of them has probability zero.

For more than two events, pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence, and a model must be checked against every combination. The distinction matters as soon as three or more events are involved.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.3 · Worked example 1

Independence

Worked example 10.3.1

Problem. A fair coin is tossed twice. Show that the events 'first toss is heads' and 'second toss is heads' are independent.

Mathematical reasoning. Check whether P(A and B) equals the product P(A)P(B).

  1. The sample space is HH, HT, TH, TT, each with probability 1/4.
  2. P(first heads) = 2/4 = 1/2 and P(second heads) = 2/4 = 1/2.
  3. P(both heads) = 1/4.
  4. The product is (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4, which equals P(both heads).
  5. So the events are independent.

Final answer. they are independent, because P(A and B) = P(A)P(B)

Interpretation. The check is one multiplication, and it is the definition applied.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.3 · Worked example 2

Independence

Worked example 10.3.2

Problem. A card is drawn from a standard pack. Let A be 'the card is a heart' and B be 'the card is red'. Are A and B independent?

Mathematical reasoning. Compare P(A and B) with the product P(A)P(B).

  1. P(A) = 13/52 and P(B) = 26/52.
  2. Since every heart is red, P(A and B) = P(A) = 13/52.
  3. The product is (13/52)(26/52) = 338/2704 ≈ 0.125.
  4. But P(A and B) = 13/52 = 0.25.
  5. These differ, so the events are not independent.

Final answer. not independent

Interpretation. When one event implies the other, they cannot be independent unless one has probability zero or one.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.4
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.4

Tree diagrams and total probability

Inquiry question

How does a tree diagram keep the denominators right?

Your task

Take a two-stage experiment of your own with unequal branch probabilities — for example two routes to school with different probabilities of being late. Build the tree diagram, compute the probability of each path, the total probability of the final event, and the reverse conditional probability. Check that the probabilities at each node sum to one.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.4
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.4

Tree diagrams and total probability

What do you notice?
  • The probabilities at the first node summed to 1, as they had to.
  • The two late branches contributed 0.070 and 0.120, summing to 0.190.
  • The not-late branches contributed 0.630 and 0.180, summing to 0.810.
  • The reverse conditional probability was 0.632, so most lateness came from the less-used route.
Observation. A tree diagram keeps the conditional denominators visible, and the total probability rule combines the branches.
Mathematical conclusion

A tree diagram displays conditional probabilities along paths, and the probability of a path is the product of its branch probabilities. The law of total probability combines the branches at one level, and Bayes' theorem reverses the conditioning by dividing by that total. Here the total probability of lateness was 0.190 and the reverse conditional probability was 0.632.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.4 · Tree diagrams and total probability
Chapter 10 · 10.4

Tree diagrams and total probability

A tree diagram displays a sequence of events as branches, and the probability along a path is the product of the branch probabilities. The second-level branches are conditional, which is what keeps the denominators correct.

The law of total probability states that P(A) = P(A ∣\mid∣ B)P(B) + P(A ∣\mid∣ not B)P(not B), and its general form sums over a partition. It is the rule that combines the branches at one level.

Bayes' theorem follows from the definition and the total probability rule, and it converts P(A ∣\mid∣ B) into P(B ∣\mid∣ A) by weighting with the prior probabilities. It is the formal version of the base-rate correction.

A tree diagram is checked by verifying that the probabilities leaving each node sum to one, and that the path probabilities sum to one at the final level. Both checks are quick and catch most errors.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.4 · Worked example 1

Tree diagrams and total probability

Worked example 10.4.1

Problem. A factory has two machines. Machine A makes 60 per cent of the output with a 2 per cent defect rate, and machine B makes the rest with a 5 per cent defect rate. Find the probability that a randomly chosen item is defective.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the law of total probability over the two machines.

  1. The item comes from A with probability 0.60 and from B with 0.40.
  2. Given A, the defect probability is 0.02, contributing 0.60 × 0.02 = 0.012.
  3. Given B, it is 0.05, contributing 0.40 × 0.05 = 0.020.
  4. The total probability is 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032.
  5. So 3.2 per cent of items are defective.

Final answer. 0.032

Interpretation. The two branches partition the sample space, and their contributions add.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.4 · Worked example 2

Tree diagrams and total probability

Worked example 10.4.2

Problem. In the same factory, a defective item is found. Find the probability that it came from machine B.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply Bayes' theorem using the total probability already computed.

  1. The joint probability of being from B and defective is 0.020.
  2. The total probability of being defective is 0.032.
  3. So P(from B ∣\mid∣ defective) = 0.020/0.032 = 0.625.
  4. Although B makes only 40 per cent of the output, it accounts for 62.5 per cent of the defects.
  5. The reason is its higher defect rate, 5 per cent against 2 per cent.

Final answer. 0.625

Interpretation. The reverse conditional probability is larger than the prior, because the conditioning event is more likely under B.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.5
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.5

Counting, permutations and combinations

Inquiry question

How large is the set of outcomes?

Your task

Take a set of 8 objects of your own. Count the number of permutations of all 8, the number of permutations of 3 chosen from the 8, the number of combinations of 3 chosen from the 8, and the number of ways to split the 8 into two groups of 4. Verify the relationship between the permutation and combination counts.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.5
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.5

Counting, permutations and combinations

What do you notice?
  • The permutation count was exactly 6 times the combination count, as the relationship requires.
  • The split into two equal groups needed an extra division by 2, because the two groups are interchangeable.
  • All four counts were integers, as counts must be.
  • The smallest case, choosing 1 from 8, gave 8, which could be listed directly.
Observation. Permutations count orders and combinations do not, and each combination corresponds to r! permutations.
Mathematical conclusion

Counting determines how large the set of outcomes is, and the multiplication principle is applied by multiplying the numbers of choices at each stage. Permutations count arrangements and combinations count selections, with each combination corresponding to r! permutations. Here the counts were 40 320, 336, 56 and 35.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.5 · Counting, permutations and combinations
Chapter 10 · 10.5

Counting, permutations and combinations

The multiplication principle states that if one choice can be made in m ways and a second in n ways, the pair can be made in mn ways. It is the basis of all counting, and it is applied by multiplying the numbers of choices at each stage.

A permutation is an arrangement in which order matters, and the number of permutations of n objects taken r at a time is n!/(n − r)!. A combination is a selection in which order does not matter, and the number is n!/(r!(n − r)!).

The relationship between the two is that each combination of r objects corresponds to r! permutations, so the combination count is the permutation count divided by r!. This is why the combination formula has the extra factor in the denominator.

Counting is what makes a probability computable for equally likely outcomes, so an error in counting is an error in the probability. The check is that the count is an integer and that a small case can be listed.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.5 · Worked example 1

Counting, permutations and combinations

Worked example 10.5.1

Problem. How many ways can 5 people be arranged in a row?

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the multiplication principle stage by stage.

  1. The first position can be filled in 5 ways.
  2. The second in 4 ways, the third in 3, the fourth in 2 and the fifth in 1.
  3. By the multiplication principle the total is 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.
  4. This is 5 factorial, written 5!.
  5. So there are 120 arrangements.

Final answer. 120

Interpretation. The multiplication principle is applied by multiplying the numbers of choices at each stage.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.5 · Worked example 2

Counting, permutations and combinations

Worked example 10.5.2

Problem. From 10 people, a committee of 3 is chosen. How many different committees are possible?

Mathematical reasoning. Count the ordered selections, then divide by the number of orders of each committee.

  1. Choosing 3 people in order gives 10 × 9 × 8 = 720 ordered selections.
  2. Each committee of 3 can be ordered in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways.
  3. So the number of committees is 720/6 = 120.
  4. This is 10!/(3! × 7!) = 120.
  5. The division by 6 is the correction for order not mattering.

Final answer. 120

Interpretation. The combination count is the permutation count divided by the number of orders, which is why the formula has the extra factor.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.6
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.6

Investigation: the birthday problem

Inquiry question

Why is a rare event so likely in a large enough group?

Your task

Investigate the birthday problem for groups of 5, 10, 15, 20, 23, 25 and 30. Compute the number of pairs and the probability of at least one shared birthday for each, and plot the probability against the group size. Then explain why the answer is smaller than most people expect.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.6
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.6

Investigation: the birthday problem

What do you notice?
  • The probability crossed one half at 23 people, not at 183 as many expect.
  • The number of pairs grew quadratically, from 10 to 435.
  • People expect the comparison to be with 365, but the comparison is between pairs.
  • The same reasoning explains why a lottery has a winner most weeks.
Observation. A rare event becomes likely when there are many opportunities for it, and the number of opportunities grows quadratically with the group size.
Mathematical conclusion

The birthday problem is solved by the complement, whose probability is a product of terms that shrink as the group grows. The number of pairs grows as n(n − 1)/2, which is why 23 people are enough for a probability above one half. The general principle is that a rare event becomes likely when there are many opportunities for it.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.6 · Investigation: the birthday problem
Chapter 10 · 10.6

Investigation: the birthday problem

The birthday problem asks how many people are needed for the probability of a shared birthday to exceed one half. The answer, 23, is far smaller than most people expect, and the reason is that the number of pairs grows quadratically.

The calculation is easiest by complement: the probability of no shared birthday is the product of the probabilities that each new person avoids all previous birthdays. With 23 people this product is about 0.493, so the probability of a match is about 0.507.

The number of pairs among n people is n(n − 1)/2, which is the source of the quadratic growth. This is why doubling the group size roughly quadruples the number of comparisons.

The general principle is that a rare event becomes likely when there are many opportunities for it. The same reasoning explains why a lottery winner exists every week even though no individual ticket is likely to win.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.6 · Worked example 1

Investigation: the birthday problem

Worked example 10.6.1

Problem. Find the probability that two people share a birthday, and the probability that three people do.

Mathematical reasoning. Count the pairs and use the complement for the larger groups.

  1. With 2 people there is 1 pair, and the probability of a shared birthday is 1/365.
  2. With 3 people there are 3 pairs, and the probability of a match is 1 − (364/365)(363/365) ≈ 0.0082.
  3. With 4 people there are 6 pairs, giving about 0.0164.
  4. With 5 people there are 10 pairs, giving about 0.0271.
  5. The probabilities roughly double each time, because the number of pairs does.

Final answer. 1/365 for two people; about 0.0082 for three

Interpretation. The pair count is the engine of the calculation, and it grows quadratically.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.6 · Worked example 2

Investigation: the birthday problem

Worked example 10.6.2

Problem. Show that with 23 people the probability of a shared birthday exceeds one half.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the complement product and subtract from one.

  1. The probability of no shared birthday among n people is the product (364/365)(363/365)…((366 − n)/365).
  2. For n = 23 this product is about 0.493.
  3. So the probability of at least one shared birthday is 1 − 0.493 = 0.507.
  4. This exceeds one half, so 23 people are enough.
  5. For n = 30 the probability is about 0.706, and for n = 50 it is about 0.970.

Final answer. with 23 people the probability is about 0.507

Interpretation. The complement is easier because it is a single product, whereas counting matches requires inclusion and exclusion.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.7
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.7

Mixed practice

Inquiry question

What is the set, and what is the condition?

Your task

Take a screening scenario with a prevalence of your own choice and a test with a stated sensitivity and specificity. Build the table for 100 000 people, compute the probability that a positive result is correct, and then repeat with the prevalence multiplied by 10. Then count the number of ways to arrange the letters of a word of your choice with repeated letters.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 10.7
Chapter 10 · Investigation 10.7

Mixed practice

What do you notice?
  • Raising the prevalence tenfold raised the predictive value from 0.0902 to about 0.498.
  • The sensitivity stayed at 99 per cent, because it is a property of the test.
  • The word arrangement count divided by the factorials of the repeat counts.
  • Both calculations were checks on the same underlying counting idea.
Observation. The predictive value depends on the prevalence as well as on the test, and counting corrections come from repeated identical objects.
Mathematical conclusion

A probability is a measure on a stated set, conditioning restricts that set, and counting determines how large it is. The base-rate effect arises because the number of false positives scales with the healthy population while the true positives scale with the small diseased one. Here the predictive value was 0.0902 at a prevalence of 1 in 1000 and about 0.498 at 1 in 100.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.7 · Mixed practice
Chapter 10 · 10.7

Mixed practice

Every probability question begins by naming the sample space and the event. Without the set, a probability has no meaning, and the same number can describe different situations.

Conditional questions are recognised by the word 'given'. The denominator is the probability of the conditioning event, and writing the definition down before computing prevents the commonest error.

Counting questions are recognised by the words 'how many'. The multiplication principle, permutations and combinations cover almost all of them, and the check is that the count is an integer and a small case can be listed.

Mixed practice is where the method is chosen rather than given, so the reasoning behind the choice is part of what is being practised.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.7 · Worked example 1
Chapter 10 · 10.7 · Worked example 1

Mixed practice

Worked example 10.7.1

Problem. A disease affects 1 person in 1000. A test is positive for 99 per cent of those who have it and for 1 per cent of those who do not. Find the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease.

Mathematical reasoning. Scale the table to whole numbers, then divide the true positives by the total positives.

  1. Take 100 000 people: 100 have the disease and 99 900 do not.
  2. Of the 100 with the disease, 99 test positive.
  3. Of the 99 900 without, 1 per cent, or 999, test positive.
  4. So 99 + 999 = 1098 people test positive.
  5. The probability is 99/1098 ≈ 0.0902, about 9 per cent.

Final answer. about 0.0902

Interpretation. A test that is 99 per cent accurate on a rare disease gives a positive result that is wrong about 91 per cent of the time, which is the base-rate effect.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook10.7 · Worked example 2
Chapter 10 · 10.7 · Worked example 2

Mixed practice

Worked example 10.7.2

Problem. How many ways can the letters of the word LEVEL be arranged?

Mathematical reasoning. Count all arrangements and divide by the factorial of each repeat count.

  1. There are 5 letters, so 5! = 120 arrangements if all were distinct.
  2. But there are 2 L's and 2 E's, and swapping identical letters gives the same word.
  3. Each distinct word is counted 2! × 2! = 4 times.
  4. So the number of distinct arrangements is 120/4 = 30.
  5. The count is an integer, as a count must be.

Final answer. 30

Interpretation. Repeated letters divide the count, which is the same correction that turns permutations into combinations.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 10 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A probability is a measure on a stated set of outcomes.
  • For equally likely outcomes, probability is a count divided by the total.
  • The addition rule is P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
  • Conditional probability is P(A ∣\mid∣ B) = P(A and B)/P(B).
  • Independence means P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive events are independent only in the trivial case.
  • The law of total probability sums the contributions over a partition.
  • Bayes' theorem reverses the conditioning.
  • The multiplication principle multiplies the numbers of choices at each stage.
  • Permutations count order; combinations do not.

Vocabulary

sample space · event · outcome · equally likely · union · intersection · complement · mutually exclusive · conditional probability · independent · tree diagram · law of total probability · Bayes' theorem · sensitivity · specificity · prevalence · permutation · combination · factorial
