MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 11 · Capstone: A Mathematical Modelling Project
Chapter 11 · Part V · Integrated modelling
11

Capstone: A Mathematical Modelling Project

A capstone project applies the whole of the course to a real decision. The mathematics is only part of the work: naming the problem, stating the assumptions and defending the model are the rest.

Engage

A school is deciding whether to install a water tank. The tank costs money, saves money, and takes up space. Three students build three models and reach three different conclusions from the same arithmetic. What went wrong?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Relationships
Related concepts: Change · Representation · System
Global context: Globalization and sustainability
Global context exploration: decisions about shared resources, access and long-term cost

Statement of inquiry: A mathematical model is an argument about the world: its value depends as much on the assumptions it makes and the evidence it ignores as on the accuracy of its arithmetic.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What are the stages of the modelling cycle, and what is produced at each?
  • Conceptual: Why can two correct models of the same situation give different recommendations?
  • Debatable: Is a model that ignores an important factor more or less honest than one that includes it approximately?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to defend a model of a shared resource, students must state its assumptions, test it against data, and justify which evidence it leaves out and why.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.1
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.1

The modelling cycle

Inquiry question

What are the stages of a modelling project, and what does each produce?

Your task

Choose a decision in your school or community that involves a cost over time. Work through the five stages of the modelling cycle, producing an artefact at each stage. Then find a second model of the same decision that differs from yours in exactly one assumption, and explain how the conclusion changes.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.1
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.1

The modelling cycle

What do you notice?
  • Defining the problem first made the rest of the work easier, because the variables were fixed.
  • Listing five assumptions exposed two that were doing most of the work.
  • Testing against three data points showed an error of about 8 per cent, which set the confidence in the recommendation.
  • Changing one assumption moved the conclusion, which showed how sensitive the answer was.
Observation. Each stage of the cycle produces an artefact, and the artefacts are what a reader examines.
Mathematical conclusion

The modelling cycle runs from defining the problem, through assumptions and building, to testing and reporting, and each stage produces a specific artefact. Two models of the same situation can both be correct and reach different conclusions when they differ in an assumption, and the disagreement is settled by evidence about that assumption.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.1 · The modelling cycle
Chapter 11 · 11.1

The modelling cycle

The modelling cycle has five stages: define the problem, make assumptions, build the model, test and evaluate it, and report the result. Each stage produces something specific, and skipping one leaves a gap that shows up later.

The first stage defines the variables, the units, the quantity to be optimised or predicted, and the audience for the answer. A problem that has not been defined cannot be solved, however good the mathematics.

Assumptions are the bridge between the situation and the mathematics, and every one of them is a choice that can be challenged. Listing them explicitly is what allows a reader to disagree with a specific claim rather than with the whole model.

Testing compares the model's predictions with data, and evaluation reports where the model fails. A model that has never failed a test has not been tested, and a model that has not been evaluated has not been finished.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 11 · 11.1 · Worked example 1

The modelling cycle

Worked example 11.1.1

Problem. A school models the cost of running a bus service. List the variables, the units and the assumptions a first model would need.

Mathematical reasoning. Work through the stages in order and name the output of each.

  1. Define: the quantity is the weekly cost, the variables are the distance and the number of services, and the units are currency units and kilometres.
  2. Assume: the fuel price is constant, the route is fixed, and maintenance is ignored in a first model.
  3. Build: the cost is a fixed part plus a part proportional to distance, so C = 50 + 1.2d.
  4. Test: compare the model's predictions with three past invoices.
  5. Report: give the recommendation and state that the model ignores driver overtime and maintenance.

Final answer. variables, units, assumptions, formula, test and report, each named

Interpretation. The list of assumptions is the part that lets a reader challenge a specific claim rather than the whole model.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 11 · 11.1 · Worked example 2

The modelling cycle

Worked example 11.1.2

Problem. Two students model the same bus service and reach different conclusions. One included a term for maintenance and one did not. Explain how both can be correct.

Mathematical reasoning. Identify the assumption that differs and trace its effect on the conclusion.

  1. Both students used correct arithmetic on the same data.
  2. Student 1 assumed no maintenance cost; student 2 assumed maintenance proportional to distance.
  3. The second model has an extra term, 0.3d, which student 1 omitted.
  4. So the two models make different predictions, and both are internally correct.
  5. The disagreement is about an assumption, and it is settled by evidence about maintenance, not by arithmetic.

Final answer. the two models differ in an assumption, so both can be correct

Interpretation. This is the inquiry statement in action: the value of a model depends on its assumptions, not only on its arithmetic.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.2
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.2

Defining the problem

Inquiry question

What has to be settled before any mathematics is done?

Your task

Take a real decision in your community that involves a cost over time. Write a full problem definition with the five named parts. Then list three factors the situation involves that your definition excludes, and for each state the effect on the conclusion and what data would repair it.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.2
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.2

Defining the problem

What do you notice?
  • Naming the objective first showed that a different objective, such as maximising carbon saving, would give a different answer.
  • Each excluded factor changed the saving, not the cost, so the conclusion was sensitive to all three.
  • Two of the three could be repaired with published data.
  • The third, the resale value, had no reliable data and had to be left as a stated range.
Observation. A definition fixes what the model will answer, and the excluded factors set the limits of the answer.
Mathematical conclusion

A problem definition names the decision, the objective, the variables with units, the constraints and the audience, and anything not named is an unstated assumption. Excluded factors are part of the model's value: each one limits the conclusion, and the honest report names them and says what data would repair them.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.2 · Defining the problem
Chapter 11 · 11.2

Defining the problem

A problem definition names the decision to be made, the quantity to be optimised or predicted, the variables with their units, and the constraints. Anything not named is assumed, and an unstated assumption is an undefended one.

The quantity to be optimised is a choice, and different choices lead to different models. Minimising cost and maximising access describe different relationships between the resources, and a model built for one does not answer the other.

Constraints come from the limits of the situation, and each becomes an inequality in the model. A constraint that is not stated is a constraint that has been assumed away, which is the commonest reason a model fails in practice.

The audience for the answer decides the form of the report. A recommendation to a school council is stated in the council's terms, with the limits named, and not in the terms of the calculation that produced it.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 11 · 11.2 · Worked example 1

Defining the problem

Worked example 11.2.1

Problem. Define the problem of deciding whether a school should install a water tank, naming the decision, the objective, the variables and the constraints.

Mathematical reasoning. Name each part of the definition and state why it matters.

  1. The decision is whether to install a tank of a given size.
  2. The objective is to minimise the total cost over ten years, counting the purchase, the installation and the water saved.
  3. The variables are the tank volume in litres and every cost in currency units per year.
  4. The constraints are the available roof area, the budget and the space on the site.
  5. The audience is the school council, so the report is in currency units and years, with the limits named.

Final answer. decision, objective, variables, constraints and audience all named

Interpretation. The definition is a contract: it fixes what the model will and will not answer.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 11 · 11.2 · Worked example 2

Defining the problem

Worked example 11.2.2

Problem. A student's model of the tank ignores the rainfall pattern because no local data were available. Evaluate the model.

Mathematical reasoning. Identify the omission, trace its effect, and state what would repair it.

  1. The model computes cost from tank volume but omits rainfall.
  2. Rainfall determines how much water the tank actually collects, so it determines the saving.
  3. Without it, the saving is an estimate with an unknown error, and the recommendation is unsafe.
  4. The repair is local rainfall data, or a stated range of rainfall with the recommendation for each.
  5. The honest report names the omission and gives the recommendation as conditional on it.

Final answer. the omission makes the recommendation unsafe, and it must be named

Interpretation. An ignored factor is part of the model's value, which is the second half of the inquiry statement.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.3
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.3

Building and testing a model

Inquiry question

How is a model built, and how is it shown to work?

Your task

Build a model for a decision of your own with at least three parameters. Fit it to three data points, test it against a fourth, and then carry out a sensitivity analysis on each parameter, reporting the percentage change in the conclusion for a 10 per cent change in each.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.3
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.3

Building and testing a model

What do you notice?
  • The unit price was the most sensitive parameter, so its data mattered most.
  • The usage and the lifetime had comparable effects, in opposite directions.
  • The discount rate had the smallest effect, so its estimate could be crude.
  • Testing against the fourth data point gave an error of 6 per cent, consistent with the sensitivity ranking.
Observation. A sensitivity analysis ranks the parameters by their effect on the conclusion, and the ranking says where better data are needed.
Mathematical conclusion

A model is built by choosing a form for each relationship and fitting its parameters, and it is tested against data not used in the fit. The relative error says whether the model is good enough, and a sensitivity analysis ranks the parameters by their effect on the conclusion. Here the unit price was the most sensitive parameter.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.3 · Building and testing a model
Chapter 11 · 11.3

Building and testing a model

A model is built by choosing a mathematical form for each relationship, fitting its parameters to data, and combining the parts into a system. The form is chosen for simplicity first, and complexity is added only when the data demand it.

Testing compares the model's predictions with data that were not used to fit it. A model that predicts new data well is useful; one that only reproduces the data it was fitted to has learned nothing.

A sensitivity analysis varies each parameter and reports the effect on the conclusion. The parameters with the largest effect are the ones that most need better data, and the sensitivity report says where the effort should go.

A model is tested by attempting to break it: with extreme values, with values outside the fitted range, and against known special cases. A model that survives these is ready to report; one that does not needs repair.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 11 · 11.3 · Worked example 1

Building and testing a model

Worked example 11.3.1

Problem. A model for the tank's saving is S = 0.002rV, where r is the annual rainfall in millimetres and V the tank volume in litres. Test it against r = 800, V = 5000 and a measured saving of 7800 currency units.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the prediction, the error and the relative error.

  1. The model predicts S = 0.002 × 800 × 5000 = 8000.
  2. The measured saving is 7800.
  3. The absolute error is 8000 − 7800 = 200.
  4. The relative error is 200/7800 ≈ 0.0256, about 2.6 per cent.
  5. An error under 3 per cent is acceptable for a planning model, so the model passes this test.

Final answer. the model predicts 8000 against a measured 7800, an error of about 2.6 per cent

Interpretation. The relative error is the useful measure, because it says whether the error matters for the decision.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 11 · 11.3 · Worked example 2

Building and testing a model

Worked example 11.3.2

Problem. In the same model, find the sensitivity of the saving to the rainfall when r changes from 800 to 900.

Mathematical reasoning. Compute the change in the saving and express it relatively.

  1. At r = 800 the saving is 8000, and at r = 900 it is 9000.
  2. The change is 1000, which is 12.5 per cent of 8000.
  3. Since the model is linear in r, the relative change in the saving equals the relative change in the rainfall.
  4. A 12.5 per cent rise in rainfall gives a 12.5 per cent rise in the saving, so the model is highly sensitive to rainfall.
  5. This means the rainfall data matter more than any other input.

Final answer. a 12.5 per cent change in the saving for a 12.5 per cent change in rainfall

Interpretation. The sensitivity analysis says where to spend effort on better data, and here it is unambiguously the rainfall.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.4
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.4

Optimising and evaluating

Inquiry question

How is a model's recommendation chosen and defended?

Your task

Take a model you have built and optimise it. Report the optimal point, the optimal value and the feasibility check. Then test the robustness of the recommendation to a 10 per cent change in each parameter, and state whether the recommendation survives.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.4
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.4

Optimising and evaluating

What do you notice?
  • The optimal plan did not change under any single 10 per cent perturbation.
  • The optimal value changed by up to about 7 per cent.
  • The most sensitive parameter was the profit from x, as the earlier sensitivity analysis had predicted.
  • The recommendation was therefore robust, and this was reported with the value range.
Observation. A recommendation is a point, a value and a robustness statement, and all three are needed.
Mathematical conclusion

A recommendation from a model is the optimal point, the optimal value and the justification that the point is feasible, together with a robustness statement. A recommendation that reverses under a reasonable change in a parameter is not a recommendation. Here the plan survived every single perturbation, with the value ranging from 260 to 300.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.4 · Optimising and evaluating
Chapter 11 · 11.4

Optimising and evaluating

When a model has a linear objective and linear constraints, the optimum is found at a vertex of the feasible region. When the objective is non-linear, the optimum is found numerically and reported with the interval that contains it.

An optimal recommendation is a point, a value and a justification that the point is feasible. The value alone is not a recommendation, because it does not say what to do.

Evaluation compares the model's recommendation with what a decision-maker would do without it. If the model adds nothing, it has failed, and the reason should be reported.

Robustness asks whether the recommendation survives reasonable changes in the parameters. A recommendation that reverses under a 10 per cent change in one input is not a recommendation but a coin toss, and it must be reported as such.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 11 · 11.4 · Worked example 1

Optimising and evaluating

Worked example 11.4.1

Problem. A model of a community garden gives a profit of P = 40x + 30y subject to x + 2y ≤ 12, 2x + y ≤ 12, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0. Find the optimal plan and test its robustness to a 10 per cent fall in the profit from x.

Mathematical reasoning. Evaluate the objective at the vertices, then perturb the profit from x.

  1. The vertices are (0, 0), (6, 0), (4, 4) and (0, 6).
  2. Evaluating P gives 0, 240, 280 and 180, so the optimum is (4, 4) with P = 280.
  3. If the profit from x falls by 10 per cent to 36, then P(4, 4) = 36(4) + 30(4) = 264.
  4. The other vertices give 216 and 180, so (4, 4) is still optimal.
  5. The recommendation is therefore robust to a 10 per cent fall in the profit from x.

Final answer. optimal plan (4, 4) with profit 280, robust to a 10 per cent fall in the profit from x

Interpretation. The robustness test is part of the recommendation, because it says how much the conclusion can be trusted.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 11 · 11.4 · Worked example 2

Optimising and evaluating

Worked example 11.4.2

Problem. A model recommends a plan that a gardener rejects because it ignores the volunteers' availability. Evaluate the model.

Mathematical reasoning. Identify the omission, trace its effect, and state the repair.

  1. The model optimises profit subject to land and money only.
  2. It omits volunteer availability, which caps the labour available.
  3. The recommended plan needs more labour than the volunteers can supply, so it cannot be carried out.
  4. The model is not wrong in its arithmetic, but it is incomplete, and an incomplete model can recommend an impossible plan.
  5. The repair is to add the labour constraint and solve again.

Final answer. the model is incomplete; adding the labour constraint repairs it

Interpretation. An omitted constraint is more dangerous than an omitted cost, because it can make the recommendation impossible rather than merely inaccurate.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.5
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.5

Presenting and defending

Inquiry question

What does a defensible report contain?

Your task

Write a full report on a model you have built, with the six sections in order. Then find the strongest objection a reader could make and write a defence of it in five steps: restate, concede, quantify, state the consequence, and repair.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.5
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.5

Presenting and defending

What do you notice?
  • Writing the assumptions section first made the rest easier, because the challenges were already visible.
  • The strongest objection was about the assumption with the largest sensitivity, which the earlier analysis had identified.
  • Quantifying the objection showed it did not change the recommendation, only the size of the benefit.
  • The report was about four pages, which was the right length for the audience.
Observation. A report is an argument with a fixed order, and a defence answers the strongest objection in five steps.
Mathematical conclusion

A modelling report states the problem, the assumptions, the model, the test results, the recommendation and the limits, in that order, and each section answers the question the previous one raises. A defence restates the strongest objection, concedes what is true, quantifies the effect, states the consequence and gives the repair.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.5 · Presenting and defending
Chapter 11 · 11.5

Presenting and defending

A modelling report states the problem, the assumptions, the model, the test results, the recommendation and the limits, in that order. This representation of the work is the argument, and each section answers the question the previous one raises.

A defence is a response to the strongest objection, not a summary of the work. Anticipating the objection and answering it is what makes a report defensible, and the objection is usually about an assumption.

Every claim in a report is traceable either to a calculation or to a stated assumption. A claim that is neither is removed, because it cannot be defended.

The audience decides the level of detail. A council needs the recommendation, the limits and one number each for the cost and the benefit; a mathematics audience needs the model and its test.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 11 · 11.5 · Worked example 1

Presenting and defending

Worked example 11.5.1

Problem. Write the structure of a report on the water-tank decision, naming what each section contains.

Mathematical reasoning. Name the sections in order and state what each answers.

  1. The problem section states the decision and the objective.
  2. The assumptions section lists the five simplifications, so a reader can challenge one specifically.
  3. The model section gives the formula and its parameters, with the source of each.
  4. The test section gives the error against four data points.
  5. The recommendation gives the plan and the value, and the limits section names what the model omits.

Final answer. problem, assumptions, model, test, recommendation and limits, in that order

Interpretation. Each section answers the question the previous one raises, which is why the order matters.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 11 · 11.5 · Worked example 2

Presenting and defending

Worked example 11.5.2

Problem. A reviewer objects that the tank model assumes a constant water price, which has risen 8 per cent a year for a decade. Write the defence.

Mathematical reasoning. Restate the objection, concede what is true, quantify the effect, and state the repair.

  1. The objection is that the model assumes a constant water price.
  2. This is conceded: the price has in fact risen about 8 per cent a year.
  3. The effect is quantified: over ten years the saving is understated by about 40 per cent.
  4. The consequence is that the recommendation is unchanged, and the reported saving is too small.
  5. The repair is to model the price rise explicitly and report both figures.

Final answer. the objection is conceded, quantified and repaired, and the recommendation survives

Interpretation. A defence that concedes and quantifies is stronger than one that denies, because it shows the objection was understood.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.6
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.6

The capstone project brief

Inquiry question

What must a capstone project contain?

Your task

Plan your capstone project. Choose a real decision, write the problem definition, list the assumptions you expect to make, name the data you will need and where you will get it, and write the reflection you expect to end with. Present the plan to a peer and record the strongest objection they raise.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 11.6
Chapter 11 · Investigation 11.6

The capstone project brief

What do you notice?
  • Choosing the decision first made the data needs obvious.
  • Listing the assumptions before collecting data showed which data actually mattered.
  • The peer objection matched the most sensitive parameter, which the plan had already identified.
  • The expected reflection named something the model could not answer, which is the most transferable part of the work.
Observation. A capstone plan is a problem definition, an assumption list, a data list and an expected reflection, tested against a peer's objection.
Mathematical conclusion

A capstone project contains a problem definition, a numbered list of assumptions, a model with sourced parameters, a test against data, a recommendation with a robustness statement, and a reflection on what the model could not answer. The evidence behind each element is what distinguishes a project from an essay, and the assumptions are assessed as heavily as the arithmetic.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.6 · The capstone project brief
Chapter 11 · 11.6

The capstone project brief

The capstone project is an extended piece of work on a real decision, and it must contain all six elements of a modelling report together with the evidence behind them. The evidence is what distinguishes a project from an essay.

The project is assessed on the mathematics, on the quality of the assumptions, on the testing, and on the communication. A project with excellent arithmetic and unstated assumptions scores badly, because the assumptions are the model.

Every number in a project is either computed, measured or estimated, and its status is stated. An estimate with no stated basis is a guess, and a guess cannot be defended.

The project ends with a reflection on what the model could not answer. That reflection is the most valuable part of the work, because it is what transfers to the next problem.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 11 · 11.6 · Worked example 1

The capstone project brief

Worked example 11.6.1

Problem. List the required elements of a capstone project and the evidence each needs.

Mathematical reasoning. List the elements and state the evidence each requires.

  1. The problem definition needs the decision, the objective, the variables and the constraints, all named.
  2. The assumptions need to be a numbered list with a reason for each, so a reader can challenge one specifically.
  3. The model needs the formula, the parameters and the source of each parameter.
  4. The test needs the comparison with data and the resulting error.
  5. The recommendation needs the plan, the value and the robustness, and the limits and reflection need what the model omits.

Final answer. six elements, each with its required evidence

Interpretation. The evidence is what distinguishes a project from an essay, and it is what is assessed.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook11.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 11 · 11.6 · Worked example 2

The capstone project brief

Worked example 11.6.2

Problem. A student's project has excellent arithmetic but no stated assumptions. Evaluate it against the capstone requirements.

Mathematical reasoning. Assess each criterion and state the consequence of the omissions.

  1. The mathematics is excellent, so that criterion earns full credit.
  2. But the assumptions are absent, so the reader cannot challenge any specific claim.
  3. The testing is absent too, so there is no evidence the model works.
  4. The communication is clear but undefended, which earns only partial credit.
  5. The project fails the capstone requirements, because the assumptions are the model.

Final answer. the project fails the requirements despite excellent arithmetic

Interpretation. This is the inquiry statement applied to assessment: the value of a model depends on its assumptions, not only on its arithmetic.

A1 · The tank decision

A school is deciding whether to install a water tank. The tank costs 6000 currency units, lasts 15 years, and is expected to save 500 currency units a year. A community has a shared budget of 2400 currency units and 60 volunteer hours for a summer programme. MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 11 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • The modelling cycle runs from defining the problem to reporting the result.
  • A problem definition names the decision, objective, variables, constraints and audience.
  • Assumptions are the bridge between the situation and the mathematics, and each is challengeable.
  • A model is tested against data not used in the fit.
  • The relative error against the decision's margin is the verdict.
  • A sensitivity analysis ranks the parameters by their effect.
  • A recommendation is a point, a value and a robustness statement.
  • An omitted constraint can make a recommendation impossible.
  • A report's six sections in order form the argument.
  • A defence restates, concedes, quantifies, states the consequence and repairs.

Vocabulary

modelling cycle · problem definition · objective · variable · constraint · assumption · parameter · fitting data · test data · relative error · sensitivity analysis · robustness · recommendation · limit · defence · payback time · margin

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter 12 · Cumulative Revision and the Transition to DP Mathematics
Chapter 12 · Part V · Integrated modelling
12

Cumulative Revision and the Transition to DP Mathematics

This chapter revises the whole course and looks forward. The habit that matters is not recalling a formula but choosing a method, justifying it, and knowing where it stops.

Engage

A DP mathematics paper contains a question nobody has seen before. Two students recognise the structure; one recalls a formula and the other does not. Which student does better, and why?

Framing the inquiry

Key concept: Logic
Related concepts: Generalisation · Representation · Justification
Global context: Identities and relationships
Global context exploration: how mathematical habits shape the way we reason elsewhere

Statement of inquiry: Mathematical maturity is the ability to choose a method, justify it, connect it to other ideas, and recognise the limits of what has been shown.

Questions to guide us

  • Factual: What are the main methods of each strand of the course, and when is each used?
  • Conceptual: What does it mean to choose a method rather than recall one, and how is the choice justified?
  • Debatable: Is a correct answer without a justification worth more or less than a justified answer with a small error?
ATL · Critical thinking. In order for a student to choose a method for an unfamiliar problem, students must identify the structure of the problem, select and justify an approach, and state what the solution does not show.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.1
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.1

Cumulative practice: algebra and functions

Inquiry question

Which algebraic method fits this structure?

Your task

Take twelve algebra questions from earlier chapters of your own choice. For each, name the method you use, justify the choice in one sentence, solve it, and check the answer by a second method where one exists.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.1
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.1

Cumulative practice: algebra and functions

What do you notice?
  • Naming the method before solving exposed two cases where the chosen method was inefficient.
  • The quadratic formula was needed only where factorising failed.
  • Every answer was checked, and three checks found an error.
  • The justifications were one sentence each, which was enough to make the choice reviewable.
Observation. The structure of a question decides the method, and the justification makes the choice reviewable.
Mathematical conclusion

An algebra question is classified by its structure, and the structure decides the method: factorising, the quadratic formula, completing the square, substitution, elimination, rearrangement or a sign analysis. Each choice is justified by the structure of the question, and every answer is checked by a second route. Here six question types were classified and checked.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.1 · Cumulative practice: algebra and functions
Chapter 12 · 12.1

Cumulative practice: algebra and functions

Algebra questions are classified by their structure: a polynomial to factorise, an equation to solve, a function to transform, an inequality to bound, or a system to solve. The structure decides the method, and recognising the structure is the skill.

The quadratic formula, completing the square and factorising are three methods for one class of equation, and each is preferable in a different case. Completing the square also gives the vertex, which is why it is used when a graph is needed.

Function questions are classified by whether they ask for a value, an inverse, a composition or a transformation. Each is a different operation, and the commonest error is applying the wrong one.

Justification in algebra is the statement of the rule or property used at each step. A correct answer without the reasons is a computation, not a solution, and it cannot be checked by a reader.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.1 · Worked example 1
Chapter 12 · 12.1 · Worked example 1

Cumulative practice: algebra and functions

Worked example 12.1.1

Problem. Solve 2x² − 7x − 3 = 0 by completing the square.

Mathematical reasoning. Complete the square, then solve and check with the quadratic formula.

  1. Divide by 2: x² − (7/2)x = 3/2.
  2. Add (7/4)² = 49/16 to both sides: (x − 7/4)² = 24/16 + 49/16 = 73/16.
  3. Take square roots: x − 7/4 = ±√73/4.
  4. So x = (7 ± √73)/4.
  5. Check with the quadratic formula: x = (7 ± √(49 + 24))/4 = (7 ± √73)/4, as required.

Final answer. x = (7 ± √73)/4, about 3.886 or −0.386

Interpretation. The check uses a different method, which is what makes it a check.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.1 · Worked example 2
Chapter 12 · 12.1 · Worked example 2

Cumulative practice: algebra and functions

Worked example 12.1.2

Problem. Given f(x) = 2x − 3 and g(x) = x² + 1, find f(g(2)) and f−1^{-1}−1(5).

Mathematical reasoning. Evaluate the inner function first, then invert by rearranging.

  1. g(2) = 2² + 1 = 5.
  2. So f(g(2)) = f(5) = 2(5) − 3 = 7.
  3. For the inverse, write y = 2x − 3 and rearrange: x = (y + 3)/2.
  4. So f−1^{-1}−1(x) = (x + 3)/2.
  5. Hence f−1^{-1}−1(5) = 8/2 = 4.

Final answer. f(g(2)) = 7 and f−1^{-1}−1(5) = 4

Interpretation. The two operations are distinguished by what they act on: composition feeds one function into another, and inversion reverses the rule.

Inquiry question

Which geometric or trigonometric relationship applies?

Your task

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.2
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.2

Cumulative practice: geometry and trigonometry

What do you notice?
  • Drawing the figure first made the correct relationship obvious in every case.
  • The sine rule and the cosine rule were distinguished by whether the given angle was included.
  • The circle questions were distinguished by whether a chord, a tangent or an arc was involved.
  • Every answer was checked, and two checks found a sign error.
Observation. The figure decides the relationship, and naming the figure is the first step.
Mathematical conclusion

Geometry and trigonometry questions are classified by the figure: right-angled triangles, general triangles, circles, cuboids and cones. Each figure has its own relationships, the choice is justified by what is given, and three-dimensional problems are solved by choosing a plane. Here six figure types were classified and checked.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.2 · Cumulative practice: geometry and trigonometry
Chapter 12 · 12.2

Cumulative practice: geometry and trigonometry

Geometry and trigonometry questions are classified by the figure: a right-angled triangle, a general triangle, a circle, a cuboid or a cone. The figure decides the available relationships, and drawing it is the first step.

Right-angled triangles use Pythagoras and the trigonometric ratios; general triangles use the sine rule, the cosine rule or the area formula. The choice depends on whether the given angle is included.

Circle questions use the angle at the centre theorem, the tangent-radius property or the intersecting chords theorem, and the choice is made by naming the arc, the tangent or the chords involved.

Three-dimensional questions are solved by choosing a plane. Naming the plane and the triangle in it is the first line of the solution, and it is what makes the rest of the solution checkable.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.2 · Worked example 1
Chapter 12 · 12.2 · Worked example 1

Cumulative practice: geometry and trigonometry

Worked example 12.2.1

Problem. A triangle has sides 8 and 11 and included angle 47°. Find the area and the third side.

Mathematical reasoning. Apply the area formula and the cosine rule, then check the ordering.

  1. The area is ½ × 8 × 11 × sin 47° ≈ 44 × 0.7314 ≈ 32.2.
  2. The third side squared is 8² + 11² − 2(8)(11) cos 47° ≈ 185 − 176(0.6820) ≈ 65.0.
  3. So the third side is about 8.06.
  4. Check: 11 is the largest side, so it is opposite the largest angle, which is the given 47 degrees only if 47 is indeed largest.
  5. The angle opposite 11 is arccos((64 + 65 − 121)/(2 × 8 × 8.06)) ≈ 79.4 degrees, which is the largest, as required.

Final answer. area about 32.2, third side about 8.06

Interpretation. The check on the ordering of sides and angles is the standard verification for a triangle.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.2 · Worked example 2
Chapter 12 · 12.2 · Worked example 2

Cumulative practice: geometry and trigonometry

Worked example 12.2.2

Problem. A circle has a chord of length 24 at distance 7 from the centre. Find the radius and the angle the chord subtends at the centre.

Mathematical reasoning. Use the perpendicular-bisector property, then a sine ratio in the resulting triangle.

  1. The perpendicular from the centre to the chord bisects it, so half the chord is 12.
  2. The radius is √(12² + 7²) = √193 ≈ 13.89.
  3. In the right-angled triangle, sin(half the angle) = 12/13.89.
  4. So half the angle is about 59.7 degrees and the full angle is about 119.4 degrees.
  5. The angle is obtuse, as expected for a chord far from the centre.

Final answer. radius about 13.89; the angle is about 119.4 degrees

Interpretation. Two circle properties are used, and both are named in the solution.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.3
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.3

Cumulative practice: statistics and probability

Inquiry question

Which measure or rule fits this question?

Your task

Take eight statistics and probability questions from earlier chapters. For each, name the measure or rule you use, justify the choice in one sentence, solve it, and state one limit of the conclusion.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.3
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.3

Cumulative practice: statistics and probability

What do you notice?
  • Naming the measure before computing exposed one case where the mean had been used on skewed data.
  • The limit of each conclusion was stated in one clause.
  • The probability questions were distinguished by which conditional direction was needed.
  • Every answer was checked against a small case that could be listed.
Observation. Each statistics question has a measure matched to its purpose, and each conclusion has a stated limit.
Mathematical conclusion

Statistics questions are classified by whether they ask for a centre, a dispersion, an association or a prediction, and probability questions by which rule applies. Skewed data call for the median and the interquartile range, and every conclusion states the sample and its origin. Here the positive result meant only an 8.7 per cent chance of disease.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.3 · Cumulative practice: statistics and probability
Chapter 12 · 12.3

Cumulative practice: statistics and probability

Statistics questions are classified by whether they ask for a centre, a dispersion, an association or a prediction. Each needs a different measure, and using the wrong one is the commonest error.

When the data are symmetric the mean and the standard deviation use the most information; when they are skewed the median and the interquartile range are the appropriate measures, because they resist extremes.

Probability questions are classified by whether they ask for a simple probability, a conditional probability, an independence test, a total probability or a count. Each is a different rule, and naming the rule is the justification.

Every statistical conclusion states the sample and the origin of the data, because the description extends to a wider population only if the sample was representative.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.3 · Worked example 1
Chapter 12 · 12.3 · Worked example 1

Cumulative practice: statistics and probability

Worked example 12.3.1

Problem. A data set has mean 30, median 22 and mode 18. Describe its shape and say which measure of centre to report.

Mathematical reasoning. Compare the three measures and use their order to identify the skew.

  1. The three measures are 18, 22 and 30.
  2. The mean is the largest, so the distribution is skewed to the right.
  3. A right skew means a long tail of large values pulling the mean upwards.
  4. The median is the better measure of centre, because it is resistant to the tail.
  5. So the report gives the median, 22, with a note that the distribution is skewed.

Final answer. skewed to the right; report the median, 22

Interpretation. The order of the three measures is the diagnosis, and the skew decides which measure to report.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.3 · Worked example 2
Chapter 12 · 12.3 · Worked example 2

Cumulative practice: statistics and probability

Worked example 12.3.2

Problem. A disease affects 1 in 500. A test has sensitivity 95 per cent and a false-positive rate of 2 per cent. Find the probability that a person who tests positive has the disease.

Mathematical reasoning. Scale the table to whole numbers, then divide the true positives by the total positives.

  1. Take 100 000 people: 200 have the disease and 99 800 do not.
  2. Of the 200, 95 per cent, or 190, test positive.
  3. Of the 99 800, 2 per cent, or 1996, test positive.
  4. So 190 + 1996 = 2186 people test positive.
  5. The probability is 190/2186 ≈ 0.0869, about 8.7 per cent.

Final answer. about 0.0869

Interpretation. The base-rate effect is stark here: a 95 per cent sensitive test on a rare disease gives a positive result that is wrong about 91 per cent of the time.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.4
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.4

Unfamiliar problems and extended reasoning

Inquiry question

How is a problem with no familiar structure approached?

Your task

Take four unfamiliar problems, each from a different strand. For each, describe how you found the structure, set out the solution as a chain of justified steps, and state one thing your solution does not show.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.4
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.4

Unfamiliar problems and extended reasoning

What do you notice?
  • Drawing a small case was the most productive first move in three of the four problems.
  • Writing the chain of steps exposed one step that had been assumed rather than justified.
  • The ambiguous case had to be checked explicitly, which was the limit of one solution.
  • Every solution stated something it did not show.
Observation. An unfamiliar problem is approached by finding its structure, and the solution is a chain of justified steps with stated limits.
Mathematical conclusion

An unfamiliar problem is approached by simplifying it, solving a special case, examining a small instance or working backwards, and each is a way of finding the structure. The solution is then a chain of justified steps, and it states what it does not show. Examples suggest a conjecture; only an argument that covers every case proves it.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.4 · Unfamiliar problems and extended reasoning
Chapter 12 · 12.4

Unfamiliar problems and extended reasoning

An unfamiliar problem is approached by simplifying it, solving a special case, looking at a small instance, or working backwards from the answer. None of these is the method; all of them are ways of finding the structure, and the generalisation that follows is what is being looked for.

Extended reasoning is a chain of justified steps, each of which would be accepted on its own. The chain is only as strong as its weakest step, so each step is checked before the next is taken, and the representation chosen makes the chain easier to follow.

A conjecture is formed from examples and then justified. The examples suggest; only the justification proves, and a conjecture that has not been justified is a hypothesis.

Recognising the limits of what has been shown is part of the answer. A solution that states what it has not proved is complete; one that does not is incomplete, however correct the computation.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.4 · Worked example 1
Chapter 12 · 12.4 · Worked example 1

Unfamiliar problems and extended reasoning

Worked example 12.4.1

Problem. Find the number of diagonals of a polygon with n sides, and prove the formula.

Mathematical reasoning. Count the pairs of vertices, subtract the sides, and check on small cases.

  1. Every pair of vertices gives either a side or a diagonal.
  2. The number of pairs is n(n − 1)/2.
  3. Of these, n are sides, so the number of diagonals is n(n − 1)/2 − n.
  4. Simplifying gives n(n − 3)/2.
  5. Check: a quadrilateral has 4(1)/2 = 2 diagonals and a pentagon has 5(2)/2 = 5, as required.

Final answer. n(n − 3)/2 diagonals

Interpretation. The two small cases confirm the formula but do not prove it; the proof is the counting argument.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.4 · Worked example 2
Chapter 12 · 12.4 · Worked example 2

Unfamiliar problems and extended reasoning

Worked example 12.4.2

Problem. A student finds that 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 and conjectures that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n². Justify or refute the conjecture.

Mathematical reasoning. Justify the conjecture by an argument that covers every case, not by more examples.

  1. The examples support the conjecture but do not prove it.
  2. To prove it, write the sum as (2 × 1 − 1) + (2 × 2 − 1) + … + (2n − 1).
  3. This is 2(1 + 2 + … + n) − n.
  4. Using the formula for the sum of the first n integers, this is 2 × n(n + 1)/2 − n = n².
  5. So the conjecture is true, and the justification covers every n.

Final answer. the conjecture is true, and the proof is the algebraic simplification

Interpretation. Examples suggest and the argument proves, and the difference is what the inquiry statement calls mathematical maturity.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.5
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.5

Cumulative examination

Inquiry question

How is examination technique different from coursework?

Your task

Take a past examination paper. Attempt it under timed conditions, allocating time by marks. Afterwards, review each answer and record the check you used, the time spent, and one thing you would do differently.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.5
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.5

Cumulative examination

What do you notice?
  • The geometry question took three times its share of time, which cost marks elsewhere.
  • Two answers were wrong and were caught only by the checks, both of which took seconds.
  • The modelling question needed its assumptions stated early, because the marks were for the assumptions as much as the arithmetic.
  • Allocating time by marks rather than by order would have gained several marks.
Observation. Examination technique is a separate skill from the mathematics, and it is learned by review.
Mathematical conclusion

An examination rewards the choice and statement of a method, the allocation of time by marks, and the use of a check different from the route used to obtain the answer. A question that cannot be finished should still be started, because partial credit is awarded for a correct method. Here the doubling rate was about 9.05 per cent per year.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.5 · Cumulative examination
Chapter 12 · 12.5

Cumulative examination

An examination rewards the choice of method as much as the execution, and it rewards the statement of the method even when the arithmetic is imperfect. Writing down the intended method is the first thing to do on any question.

Time is allocated by marks, not by order. A question worth few marks is not worth many minutes, and leaving a hard question until last is a strategy rather than a defeat.

Every answer is checked by a route that is different from the one used to obtain it. Substitution, an estimate, a special case and a dimension check are the four standard checks, and each takes seconds.

A question that cannot be solved should still be started: the method is written down, the first step is taken, and the partial answer is left. Partial credit is awarded for a correct method, and an unanswered question scores nothing.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.5 · Worked example 1
Chapter 12 · 12.5 · Worked example 1

Cumulative examination

Worked example 12.5.1

Problem. Solve the question: a population doubles every 8 years. Find the annual percentage growth rate, to three significant figures.

Mathematical reasoning. Write the model, extract the annual factor, and convert to a percentage.

  1. The model is P(t) = P₀ × 2^(t/8), because the doubling period is 8 years.
  2. The annual factor is 2^(1/8), since t = 1 gives one year.
  3. 2^(1/8) ≈ 1.0905.
  4. So the annual rate is 1.0905 − 1 = 0.0905.
  5. As a percentage this is about 9.05 per cent per year.

Final answer. about 9.05 per cent per year

Interpretation. The error to avoid is dividing 100 per cent by 8, which gives 12.5 per cent and is wrong, because the growth compounds.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.5 · Worked example 2
Chapter 12 · 12.5 · Worked example 2

Cumulative examination

Worked example 12.5.2

Problem. A candidate has 20 minutes left and two questions remaining, one worth 3 marks and one worth 8. Advise on the order.

Mathematical reasoning. Allocate time in proportion to the marks and start the harder question with the method.

  1. The 3-mark question should take about a quarter of the remaining time.
  2. So it is done first, in about 5 minutes.
  3. The 8-mark question then has about 15 minutes, which is enough to write the method and several steps.
  4. If it cannot be finished, the method and the first step are left on the page.
  5. Partial credit is awarded for a correct method, so an unanswered question is the only one that scores nothing.

Final answer. the 3-mark question first, then start the 8-mark one with the method

Interpretation. The strategy is to secure the easy marks and to start the hard question with a stated method.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.6
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.6

From MYP to DP: expectations and readiness

Inquiry question

What changes in the transition to DP mathematics?

Your task

Assess your own readiness for DP mathematics on the four skills in the inquiry statement: choosing a method, justifying it, connecting it to other ideas, and recognising the limits of what has been shown. For each, give a rating, an example from your own work, and one thing you will practise.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookInvestigation 12.6
Chapter 12 · Investigation 12.6

From MYP to DP: expectations and readiness

What do you notice?
  • The four skills could each be rated against a concrete example.
  • The weakest skill was recognising limits, because it had rarely been asked for.
  • Connecting ideas was easier once a single idea, the determinant, was followed across two strands.
  • Each rating came with a specific practice, not a general intention.
Observation. Readiness is assessed by example, and each gap has a specific practice.
Mathematical conclusion

DP mathematics expects a student to choose a method, justify it, connect it to other ideas and recognise the limits of what has been shown, and the content is largely familiar. Readiness is assessed against those four skills rather than against recall, and each gap has a specific practice. Here the four skills were rated developing, developing, emerging and emerging.

Your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.6 · From MYP to DP: expectations and readiness
Chapter 12 · 12.6

From MYP to DP: expectations and readiness

DP mathematics expects a student to choose a method, justify it, and connect it to other ideas, and the logic of the argument is examined at every step. The content is largely familiar; the expectation of independent choice is what is new.

The DP courses are split by emphasis: one for students who need mathematics as a tool, one for students who will study it seriously, and one for those who will study it at depth. The choice depends on what the student will do next, not on how easy the course is.

Investigation and internal assessment are part of the DP, and the mathematical exploration rewards the same habits as the capstone project: a stated problem, stated assumptions, a test and a reflection on the limits.

Readiness is not the recall of formulas. It is the ability to read an unfamiliar question, identify its structure, select a method, and justify the selection, and those are the habits this course has been building.

Formal development

Work through the investigation above before reading this page: the statements here are the formal version of what you discovered.

In your own words
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.6 · Worked example 1
Chapter 12 · 12.6 · Worked example 1

From MYP to DP: expectations and readiness

Worked example 12.6.1

Problem. Compare the expectations of an MYP extended question with a DP examination question on the same content.

Mathematical reasoning. Compare the two forms on five aspects.

  1. An MYP extended question is usually signposted in parts, each pointing at a method.
  2. A DP question often presents a single unfamiliar stem and leaves the choice of method to the student.
  3. Justification is required for the top band in MYP and throughout in DP.
  4. Marks are awarded for the answer and the reasoning in both, but DP marks the method separately.
  5. So the transition is from following a signposted route to choosing one.

Final answer. the content is familiar; the independence and the continuous justification are new

Interpretation. Naming what is new makes the transition manageable, because the mathematics is already known.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebook12.6 · Worked example 2
Chapter 12 · 12.6 · Worked example 2

From MYP to DP: expectations and readiness

Worked example 12.6.2

Problem. A student can recall every formula in the course but cannot choose between them. Advise on what to practise.

Mathematical reasoning. Assess the four skills and name the practice each needs.

  1. Recall is strong, so no further practice is needed there.
  2. Recognition of structure is weak, so questions should be classified by type before solving.
  3. Choice of method is weak, so each type should be solved by two methods and the results compared.
  4. Justification is weak, so the reason should be written beside every step.
  5. The habit of stating limits is absent, and is practised by writing what each solution does not show.

Final answer. practise recognition, choice, justification and limits

Interpretation. The four skills are what the inquiry statement calls mathematical maturity, and recall is only the first.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookChapter review
Chapter 12 · Review

What you should now be able to do

Key ideas

  • A question is classified by its structure, and the structure decides the method.
  • Factorising, the quadratic formula and completing the square are three methods for one class of equation.
  • The sine rule and the cosine rule are distinguished by whether the given angle is included.
  • Two sides and a non-included angle give zero, one or two triangles.
  • Circle theorems are chosen by naming the arc, the tangent or the chords.
  • A three-dimensional problem is solved by choosing a plane.
  • Skewed data call for the median and the interquartile range.
  • Bayes' theorem reverses the conditioning, and the base rate decides the difference.
  • A linear program's optimum is at a vertex, with a robustness statement.
  • Examples suggest a conjecture; only an argument covering every case proves it.

Vocabulary

structure · method · justification · check · generalisation · representation · limit · conjecture · proof · extended reasoning · examination technique · readiness · transition · maturity · over-fitted

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookAnswers and reasoning
Chapter 1 · Criterion A · Knowing and understanding
1.A1
Degree 5, leading coefficient 3.
The degree is the highest power and the leading coefficient is its multiplier.
1.A2
x³ + 5x² − x + 2, degree 3.
Collect like terms.
1.A3
2x³ + 5x² − 7x + 2, degree 3.
Each term of the first multiplies each term of the second; degrees add.
1.A4
16 − 12 − 10 − 1 = −7.
Substitute and evaluate term by term.
1.A5
Quotient 3x² + 2x − 6, remainder 8.
Match leading terms and subtract; check with the division identity.
1.A6
Quotient x² + 2x + 4, remainder 0.
x − 2 is a factor, so the remainder is zero.
1.A7
p(1) = 2 − 5 + 3 = 0.
The remainder theorem replaces the division by substitution.
1.A8
p(−3) = −27 + 18 − 7 = −16.
The divisor x + 3 is x − (−3), so a = −3.
1.A9
(x − 1)(x − 2)(x + 1).
p(1) = 0, then divide and factorise the quadratic.
1.A10
(x − 2)/(x + 3), for x ≠\neq= −3 and x ≠\neq= −2.
Factorise both parts and cancel x + 2.
1.A11
x is not a factor of x + 3, so there is nothing to cancel.
Cancellation needs a common factor, not a common term.
1.A12
x = (−3 + √33)/2 or x = (−3 − √33)/2; neither is 0 nor −1, so both are valid.
Clear the fractions, solve the quadratic, then substitute each candidate.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookAnswers and reasoning
Chapter 1 · Criterion B · Investigating patterns
1.B1
Yes: substituting x = 1 gives 1N^{N}N − 1 = 0 for every n, so by the factor theorem x − 1 is always a factor.
One substitution covers every n.
1.B2
n = 2: (x − 1)(x + 1); n = 3: (x − 1)(x² + x + 1); n = 4: (x − 1)(x + 1)(x² + 1); n = 5: (x − 1)(x⁴ + x³ + x² + x + 1); n = 6: (x − 1)(x + 1)(x² + x + 1)(x² − x + 1).
Divide out x − 1 first, then factorise the quotient.
1.B3
The remainder is 1, because 1N^{N}N = 1 for every n.
The remainder theorem gives the remainder as p(1).
1.B4
n even gives 2 real roots (±1); n odd gives 1 real root (1).
A real nth root of 1 exists only for 1, and also −1 when n is even.
1.B5
The discriminant 4p³ + 27q² = 0; a double root forces it to vanish.
A double root means the factorised form contains a squared factor.
1.B6
Any correct answer, for example p(x) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 4) = x³ − 7x² + 14x − 8; dividing by x − 2 gives x² − 5x + 4 and (x − 2)(x² − 5x + 4) = p(x).
Use the division identity as the check.
1.B7
No: the degree of a sum is at most the larger degree, and here at most 3, because no term of degree 4 can be produced by adding.
Compare the possible powers in each term.
1.B8
The remainder is always 0, because x = 1 is a root of xN^{N}N − 1 for every positive integer n.
Use the factor theorem with p(1) = 1N^{N}N − 1.
1.B9
x² − y² = (x − y)(x + y); x³ − y³ = (x − y)(x² + xy + y²); x⁴ − y⁴ = (x − y)(x + y)(x² + y²). In every case x − y is a factor.

Chapter 11 · Criterion A · Knowing and understanding
11.A1
Define the problem, make assumptions, build the model, test and evaluate, report the result.
The cycle runs from definition to report.
11.A2
The decision, the objective, the variables with units, the constraints and the audience.
Anything not named is an unstated assumption.
11.A3
So that a reader can challenge a specific claim rather than the whole model, and so the model's limits are visible.
An unstated assumption is an undefended one.
11.A4
Fitting data, used to choose the parameters, and test data, not used in the fit, which show whether the model predicts.
A model that only reproduces its fitting data has learned nothing.
11.A5
The percentage change in the conclusion for a stated percentage change in each parameter, ranked by size.
The ranking says where better data are needed.
11.A6
Because an omitted cost makes the recommendation inaccurate, while an omitted constraint can make it impossible to carry out.
A constraint is a limit on what is feasible.
11.A7
The optimal point, the optimal value, and the justification that the point is feasible.
The value alone is not a recommendation.
11.A8
It says whether the recommendation survives reasonable changes in the parameters, which is how much the conclusion can be trusted.
A recommendation that reverses under a small change is a coin toss.
11.A9
Problem, assumptions, model, test, recommendation, limits.
The order is the argument.
11.A10
Restate the objection, concede what is true, quantify the effect, state the consequence, give the repair.
A defence that concedes is stronger than one that denies.
11.A11
Because an estimate with no stated basis is a guess, and a guess cannot be defended or challenged.
Every number is computed, measured or estimated.
11.A12
What the model could not answer, and what would be needed to answer it.
The reflection is the most transferable part of the work.

No: a model with more assumptions is more detailed but also more fragile, because each assumption can be challenged and each adds an error.

For a published transport model: constant travel demand, no new infrastructure, and unchanged fuel prices, each visible in the report's stated inputs.

A longer horizon favours plans with higher initial cost and lower running cost, because the running cost is saved for longer; a shorter horizon reverses the ranking.

11.B6
When the relationships are approximately proportional over the range of interest and the errors are small compared with the decision's margin; two test cases confirmed both conditions.

A model can be accurate and useless if it answers a question nobody asked, or useful and inaccurate if its errors are smaller than the decision's margin.
Compare the model's error with the margin between the options.
11.B8
A longer horizon favours plans with higher initial cost and lower running cost, because the running cost is saved for longer; a shorter horizon reverses the ranking.
Re-solve with two horizons and compare.
11.B9
The assumptions attached to the most sensitive parameters, which the sensitivity analysis identifies.
Rank the assumptions by the sensitivity of their parameters.
11.B10
No: more assumptions give more detail but also more fragility, because each assumption can be challenged and each adds an error.
Compare a simple and a detailed model against the same data.
11.B11
A model can be accurate and useless if it answers a question nobody asked, or useful and inaccurate if its errors are smaller than the decision's margin.
Compare the error with the margin between the options.

Chapter 11 · Criterion C · Communicating
11.C1
Decision: install or not. Objective: minimise the fifteen-year total cost. Variables: installed capacity in kW and costs in currency units per year. Constraints: roof area, budget and structural limits. Audience: the school council.
Name each part of the definition and state why it matters.
11.C2
Rank the parameters by the size of the change, and report the conclusion's percentage change for each; the largest is the parameter whose data most need improving.
Perturb each parameter by 10 per cent and record the effect.
11.C3
Compute the model's prediction, the absolute error and the relative error, and compare the relative error with the margin between the options being decided.
The relative error against the decision's margin is the verdict.
11.C4
Vertices (0, 0), (7, 0), (4, 6), (0, 10) give 0, 350, 440, 400; the optimum is (4, 6) with 440. With the profit from x at 45, the value is 420 and (4, 6) is still optimal, so the recommendation is robust.
Evaluate at the vertices, then perturb and re-evaluate.
11.C5
Restate the objection; concede that prices have in fact risen; quantify that the saving is understated by about 40 per cent over ten years; state that the recommendation is unchanged and the benefit larger; repair by modelling the price rise and reporting both.
Restate, concede, quantify, consequence, repair.
11.C6
The plan violates a constraint that the model omitted; the model is not wrong in its arithmetic but incomplete, and the repair is to add the constraint and re-solve.
Check the recommended plan against every constraint of the situation, not only those in the model.
11.C7
Problem, assumptions, model, test, recommendation and limits, each with the evidence named in the brief.
The evidence is what distinguishes a project from an essay.
11.C8
Decision, objective, variables with units, constraints and audience, each named with a reason.
Name each part of the definition and state why it matters.
11.C9
Rank the parameters by the size of the change; the largest identifies where better data are needed.
Perturb each parameter by 10 per cent and record the effect.
11.C10
Compute the prediction, the absolute error and the relative error, and compare the relative error with the margin between the options.
The relative error against the decision's margin is the verdict.
11.C11
The vertices are (0, 0), (6, 0), (3, 6) and (0, 9), giving 0, 360, 450 and 405; the optimum is (3, 6) with 450, and a 10 per cent fall in the profit from x gives 414 with (3, 6) still optimal.
Evaluate at the vertices, then perturb and re-evaluate.
11.C12
Restate, concede, quantify, state the consequence, repair.
Restate, concede, quantify, consequence, repair.

Chapter 11 · Criterion D · Applying mathematics in real-life contexts
11.D1
The total saving over 10 years is 6000 against a cost of 4000, so the payback time is 4000/600 ≈ 6.7 years; the model assumes the saving is constant, which a rising water price would change in the tank's favour.
Model the cost and the saving, then find the crossing.
11.D2
The optimum is (4, 4) with 280; with the profit from x at 36 the value is 264 and (4, 4) is still optimal, so the recommendation is robust.
Evaluate at the vertices, then perturb.
11.D3
The model is incomplete: it omits the labour constraint, so it recommends a plan that cannot be carried out. The repair is to add the labour constraint and re-solve, which lowers the optimum to 9 tonnes.
An omitted constraint is more serious than an omitted cost.
11.D4
The recommendation is robust, because the optimal plan is unchanged and only the value falls, by about 12 per cent.
Compare the plan, not only the value, after the perturbation.
11.D5
The largest error is 5 per cent, well inside the 15 per cent margin, so the model is good enough for the decision; the errors are reported alongside the recommendation.
Compare the largest error with the decision's margin.
11.D6
At n = 5 the model predicts 2250 against 2300, an error of 2.2 per cent; at n = 12 it predicts 2600 against 2650, an error of 1.9 per cent. The model is acceptable for planning.
Compute the prediction and the relative error at each point.
11.D7
The statement of whether the recommendation survives reasonable changes in the parameters; without it a reader cannot tell how much the conclusion can be trusted.
A recommendation is a point, a value and a robustness statement.
11.D8
The omission understates the saving from insulation during term time but overstates it over the holidays; the net effect is small, so the recommendation is probably unchanged, but the omission must be named and quantified.
Trace the effect of the omission on the quantity being optimised.
11.D9
Adopt the plan, which is expected to give a value of about 28 000, and which remains optimal for values between 25 000 and 31 000.
Give the plan, the value and the range, in the audience's terms.
11.D10
Not necessarily: if the decision's margin is 50 per cent, a 20 per cent error is well inside it and the model is useful. Usefulness depends on the error relative to the margin, not on the error alone.
Compare the error with the margin between the options.
11.D11
To the parameter with the 9 per cent effect, because improving its estimate improves the conclusion most; the other parameter's estimate can remain crude.
Rank the parameters by their effect on the conclusion.
11.D12
It is too vague to be useful: a reflection should name what the model could not answer, why, and what would be needed to answer it.
A reflection names a specific limit and a specific repair.

MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (1 of 5)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Number, accuracy and form

Index laws
aM^{M}M × aN^{N}N = aM+N^{M+N}M+N; aM^{M}M ÷ aN^{N}N = aM−N^{M-N}M−N; (aM^{M}M)N^{N}N = aMN^{MN}MN, for a ≠\neq= 0.
Zero and negative indices
a⁰ = 1 for a ≠\neq= 0; a−N^{-N}−N = 1/aN^{N}N.
Rational index
a^(1/n) is the nth root of a; a^(m/n) = (N^{N}N√a)M^{M}M.
Standard form
a × 10N^{N}N with 1 ≤ a < 10.
Surd rules
√a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b); (√a)² = a.
Rationalising
multiply by the conjugate so that the denominator becomes rational.
Error interval
a value given to the nearest unit lies within half a unit either side.
Bounds of a calculation
the lower bound uses the lower bounds of subtracted terms.
Percentage multiplier
an increase of r% multiplies by 1 + r/100; a decrease by 1 − r/100.
Logarithm laws
log(ab) = log a + log b; log(a/b) = log a − log b; log(aK^{K}K) = k log a.
Change of base
log_b a = log a ÷ log b, for any common base.
Continuous growth
N = N₀eKT^{KT}KT; the equivalent base is b = eK^{K}K and the rate is k = ln b.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (2 of 5)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Algebra and equations

Expanding
a(b + c) = ab + ac.
Difference of squares
a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
Perfect square
a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²; a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)².
Quadratic equation
ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠\neq= 0.
Quadratic formula
x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a.
Discriminant
b² − 4ac > 0 gives two real roots, = 0 one repeated root, < 0 none.
Completing the square
ax² + bx + c = a(x + b/2a)² + c − b²/4a.
Algebraic fraction
cancel only common factors, and state the excluded values first.
Quadratic inequality
solve the equation, mark the roots on a sign line, then test one interval.
Inequality rule
multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign.
Function
a rule giving exactly one output for each input of its domain.
Composite function
f(g(x)) applies g first; the inner function acts first.
Inverse function
f−1^{-1}−1 exists only when f is one-to-one; f−1^{-1}−1(f(x)) = x on the restricted domain.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (3 of 5)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Sequences, series and trigonometry

Arithmetic sequence
the nth term is u(n) = u₁ + (n − 1)d, with common difference d.
Arithmetic series
the sum of n terms is S(n) = n/2 (u₁ + u(n)) = n/2 (2u₁ + (n − 1)d).
Geometric sequence
the nth term is u(n) = u₁ rN−1^{N-1}N−1, with common ratio r.
Geometric series
the sum of n terms is S(n) = u₁(rN^{N}N − 1) ÷ (r − 1) for r ≠\neq= 1.
Convergent geometric series
the sum to infinity is u₁ ÷ (1 − r) when |r| < 1, and no sum otherwise.
Annuity
the accumulated value of equal regular payments, found by summing a geometric series.
Pythagoras
a² + b² = c² for the hypotenuse c of a right-angled triangle.
Trigonometric ratios
sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse; cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse; tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
Sine rule (sides)
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
Sine rule (angles)
sin A/a = sin B/b = sin C/c.
Cosine rule
a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.
Area of a triangle
½ab sin C, where C is the angle between sides a and b.
Ambiguous SSA case
b sin A < a < b gives two triangles; b sin A = a gives one right triangle; a < b sin A gives none.
Bearings
measured clockwise from north, written as three figures.
Space diagonal
d = √(l² + w² + h²) for a cuboid of length l, width w and height h.
Prism
volume = area of cross-section × length.
Cylinder
volume = πr²h; curved surface area = 2πrh.
Cone
volume = 13\frac{1}{3}31​πr²h; curved surface area = πrl for slant height l.
Sphere
volume = ⁴⁄₃πr³; surface area = 4πr².
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (4 of 5)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Vectors and matrices

Magnitude of a vector
|a| = √(x² + y²) for a = (x, y).
Vector addition
a + b = (x₁ + x₂, y₁ + y₂).
Scalar multiple
ka = (kx, ky).
Position vector
the vector from the origin to the point.
Matrix product
(AB)ij_{ij}ij​ is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.
Determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix
det [[a, b], [c, d]] = ad − bc.
Inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
A−1^{-1}−1 = 1/(ad − bc) [[d, −b], [−c, a]], when ad − bc ≠\neq= 0.
Area scale factor
|det M| multiplies every area under the transformation M.
MYP Mathematics 5 · Student coursebookFormula bank

Formula bank (5 of 5)

Key facts and formulas, chapter by chapter. Use them to check work, not to replace reasoning.

Statistics and probability

Mean
x̄ = Σx ÷ n for ungrouped data; for a frequency table use Σfx ÷ Σf.
Variance (population)
the mean of Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ n.
Standard deviation
the square root of the mean squared deviation; a sample divides by n − 1.
Grouped estimate
use the mid-interval value of each class as its representative.
Interquartile range
Q3 − Q1, a measure of spread that ignores the extremes.
Correlation coefficient
r = Sxy ÷ √(Sxx × Syy), where Sxx = Σ(x − x̄)².
Least-squares line
y = a + bx with b = Sxy ÷ Sxx and a = ȳ − b x̄.
Coefficient of determination
r² is the proportion of the variation in y explained by x.
Probability of an event
P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes.
Addition rule
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
Conditional probability
P(A given B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).
Independence
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), equivalently P(A given B) = P(A).
Total probability
P(B) = the sum, over each part A of a partition of the sample space, of P(A) × P(B given A).
Bayes' theorem
P(A ∣\mid∣ B) = P(B ∣\mid∣ A)P(A) ÷ P(B).
Multiplication principle
r successive choices with n₁, n₂, … options give n₁ × n₂ × … outcomes.
Permutations
nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)! counts ordered selections.
Combinations
nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!) counts unordered selections.
Expected value
E(X) = Σ x P(X = x) for a discrete random variable.

MYP Mathematics · Student coursebookSecond edition
About this book

Twelve chapters that take polynomials and algebraic fractions, functions and their inverses, exponential and logarithmic models, sequences and series, quadratic inequalities and linear programming, circle theorems and proof, the sine and cosine rules, vectors and matrices, dispersion and regression, and conditional probability and counting from first ideas to justified use. Each chapter opens with a task: you investigate, notice a pattern, state a mathematical conclusion you can defend, and only then meet the formal explanation — with worked examples that model a complete solution and practice separated into Criterion A, B, C and D sets so you can see which skill each task trains.

Year 5 reasoning is applied, not just correct: models are built from stated assumptions, checked against data and evaluated for their limitations, and Criterion B tasks ask you to justify a generalisation rather than to list cases. Every chapter closes with a reflection that returns to the statement of inquiry.

The book closes with a capstone: a sustained modelling task in which a claim about a shared resource becomes defensible only when it is modelled, tested and evaluated — and with a chapter that states plainly what the transition to DP Mathematics expects. Every chapter also closes with a Service as Action opportunity, a Community Project connection and a Personal Project extension. The back of the book carries complete student-facing answers with reasoning, a formula bank, a glossary and references.
